From a supplied example, identify resources, sinks/assimilative capacity, demand services and biospheric life-supporting services; preserve the slide’s resource taxonomy; explain why one place can provide several functions.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources
  • Four environmental functions
  • Resources
  • Sinks and assimilative capacity
  • Demand services
  • Global biospheric life-supporting services

Supported/completion work may use the finished note and named figure. Independent and delayed checks use no notes, figures, keys, web, AI or hints; a blank page is allowed. O003 may use a basic calculator for comparisons, without conceptual help. The tutor confirms known access/exposure conditions before scoring independence. Tasks describing a figure may be answered verbally or by drawing; the arrow legend and interpretation must still be produced unaided. original_sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

original_sections.html:
A forest can supply timber, enjoyment and systemic services. Asking only what it sells misses other ways it matters. A function describes a relationship, so the same site can have several functions.

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. In network lessons \(P\) denotes production, \(C\) denotes consumption, \(U\) denotes utility, \(R\) denotes natural resources, \(\mathrm{ER}\) denotes exhaustible resources, \(\mathrm{RR}\) denotes renewable resources, \(h\) denotes harvest rate, \(y\) denotes yield/growth, \(W\) denotes waste, \(A\) denotes assimilative capacity. These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.
original_sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

original_sections.html:
1. Ask whether the environmental feature supplies an input or possibility for economic activity: this is a resource. Wood/biomass are degradable renewable resources; fossil fuels/minerals are degradable non-renewable/exhaustible resources. Sunshine, wind and waves are separately classified as non-degradable in this source; space is also a resource.
  2. Ask whether the relationship concerns receiving undesirable outputs: this is the sink function, interpreted through assimilative capacity. A sink does not imply unlimited capacity.
  3. Ask whether people value aesthetic, cultural or recreational services directly: these are demand services. Forest recreation differs from timber production even at the same site.
  4. Ask whether the relationship concerns broad life-supporting systems: climate, the hydrologic cycle and soil production belong to the biospheric category.
  5. Keep categories distinct by mechanism while allowing coexistence. The source supplies this taxonomy, not a general formal definition of degradability; do not replace its wording with another taxonomy.
original_sections.title: Explanation steps

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Four environmental functions; fingerprint efb3d63bd3709f51261b845db081603746a89796298bbe89a4849ca6e0e84b23. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Four environmental functions

The slides distinguish four ways in which the environment matters to the economy. These functions can coexist in the same place. The forest example shows the distinction particularly clearly: wood is a resource, while aesthetic, cultural and recreational enjoyment belongs to the separate category of demand services. This comparison is an explanatory synthesis of the examples on slide 2. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 2

Resources

Resources provide inputs or possibilities for economic activity. Slide 2 distinguishes non-degradable resources, with sunshine, wind and waves as examples, from degradable resources. Within the latter group it distinguishes renewable resources, such as wood and biomass, from non-renewable or exhaustible resources, such as fossil fuels and minerals. It also lists space as a resource. Keep this source taxonomy when interpreting the later diagram: the slide uses “renewable” for the wood/biomass category and separately lists sunshine, wind and waves as non-degradable. It does not supply a broader taxonomy or a formal definition of “degradable.” 00_Intro.pptx, slide 2

The distinction becomes economically meaningful when resource use is compared with replenishment. An exhaustible resource can be reduced by extraction. For renewable resources, the diagram separately represents harvesting above and below yield or growth, so “renewable” alone does not establish that a particular pattern of use maintains the resource. The relevant question is how fast the resource is used relative to how fast it grows. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4

Sinks and assimilative capacity

A sink is a place where undesirable outputs, including emissions and wastes, may be placed. The source describes this function through assimilative capacity: the environment's capacity to receive or assimilate those outputs. The diagram later compares waste with that capacity. This makes waste disposal part of the environment–economy relationship, alongside resource extraction. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4

The capacity comparison matters because the diagram assigns different consequences to waste below capacity and waste above capacity. The existence of a sink therefore does not establish that every amount of waste has the same consequences. The source supplies a qualitative threshold comparison; it does not quantify a safe emissions level, a pollutant-specific assimilation rate, or the time needed for assimilation. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

Demand services

The environment also supplies services people value directly. Slide 2 names aesthetic, cultural and recreational services, such as those provided by a forest. In the full diagram, the environmental resource node has a positive amenity connection to utility. Thus the environment contributes to wellbeing through more than goods produced by firms and consumed by households. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 2 and 4

Utility, denoted by \(U\), is the diagram's representation of wellbeing or benefit. The source identifies utility flows but gives no numerical utility scale, utility function, or valuation method. The positive amenity arrow establishes a direction of effect in this schematic framework; it does not report a measured monetary benefit. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

Global biospheric life-supporting services

The fourth category concerns the systems that support life more generally. The source names the climate system, hydrologic cycle and soil production. These services place the production-and-consumption relationship in a wider biospheric setting. They explain why environmental economics considers systemic conditions as well as individual resource inputs and enjoyable amenities. This final sentence is a synthesis of the category's role in the introductory framework. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 2

original_sections.html:
O001-W1 v1, instruction only. An agent-created forest example combines timber, recreation, receipt of undesirable outputs, and the hydrologic cycle. Classify each and compare wood, fossil fuels and wind in the source taxonomy.

Worked solution: Step 1: timber supplies an input, so resource. Step 2: recreation gives direct enjoyment, so demand service. Step 3: receipt/assimilation of outputs is sink service, without an unlimited-capacity claim. Step 4: the hydrologic cycle is a biospheric life-supporting service. Wood is degradable renewable; fossil fuels are degradable exhaustible; wind is non-degradable in the slide. The same place supports several relationships; its identity does not force one exclusive category.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Every I and D task explicitly tests all indexed components: identify_four_functions, apply_source_resource_taxonomy, distinguish_coexisting_functions. Acquisition requires passes on two distinct fresh unassisted current-criterion tasks, I1 and I2. This is an operational acquisition threshold, not a personalized retention guarantee. These route restrictions ensure all components receive two complete checks. No numeric point scale is invented.

A missing keyed reason/limit is partial, even if labels or inequalities are right. Wrong mechanism, reversed sign, conflated arrow/service categories, unsupported equality/optimal-policy/universal-safety claim, or invented verified definition is a critical conceptual error and fails the relevant whole task. Unknown help/exposure conditions do not produce independent pass evidence. General source-faithful alternatives are acceptable; unsupported alternatives trigger a plan issue instead of improvised grading.
original_sections.title: Rubric and independence

original_sections.html:
Sign: all environmental benefits are called resources, or sunshine is silently recategorized. Treat one response as tentative; a repeated conflation across fresh tasks supports diagnosis. Correction: identify the relationship (input, waste reception, direct enjoyment, life support), then retain the slide’s labels. Hint 1: ask what role each feature plays. Hint 2: contrast timber with recreation at the same forest.

Score the original answer first; use at most the two hints above, then explain the prepared missing step. Corrective feedback creates exposure.

O001-C1 v1, fresh correction, assistance allowed: A learner says recreation and soil production are resources simply because nature provides them, and that wood and wind have the same source label. Correct both claims; also identify the timber and waste-reception functions and explain coexistence.

Key: In this taxonomy recreation is demand service and soil production biospheric life support; timber is resource and waste reception sink. Wood is degradable renewable; wind separately non-degradable. Nature can provide several distinct functions in one location; calling every service a resource erases the source distinction.

Rubric: the full keyed component set correct = correction pass; omitted reason/limit = partial; repeated critical mechanism error = fail. C1 is repair evidence and does not establish acquisition. If I1/I2 are already exposed or exhausted, stop and request new prepared variants from plan.

sections.html:
In this lesson, classify the four environmental functions.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • From a supplied example
  • Identify resources, sinks/assimilative capacity, demand services and biospheric life-supporting services; preserve the slide’s resource taxonomy;
  • Explain why one place can provide several functions.

2.2 Before you begin

  • No earlier lesson in this course is required. Review the definitions below before the worked example.
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Resource service: An environmental input to production or consumption.
  • Demand service: Direct environmental enjoyment, such as forest recreation, distinct from supplying a material input.
  • Sink service: Receipt or assimilation of undesirable outputs, with capacity limits.
  • Biospheric service: A life-supporting natural process, such as the hydrologic cycle.

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.

The capacity comparison matters because the diagram assigns different consequences to waste below capacity and waste above capacity. The existence of a sink therefore does not establish that every amount of waste has the same consequences. The source supplies a qualitative threshold comparison; it does not quantify a safe emissions level, a pollutant-specific assimilation rate, or the time needed for assimilation.

4.3 Demand services

The environment also supplies services people value directly. Slide 2 names aesthetic, cultural and recreational services, such as those provided by a forest. In the full diagram, the environmental resource node has a positive amenity connection to utility. Thus the environment contributes to wellbeing through more than goods produced by firms and consumed by households.

Utility, denoted by \(U\), is the diagram's representation of wellbeing or benefit. The source identifies utility flows but gives no numerical utility scale, utility function, or valuation method. The positive amenity arrow establishes a direction of effect in this schematic framework; it does not report a measured monetary benefit.

4.4 Global biospheric life-supporting services

The fourth category concerns the systems that support life more generally. The source names the climate system, hydrologic cycle and soil production.

These services place the production-and-consumption relationship in a wider biospheric setting. They explain why environmental economics considers systemic conditions as well as individual resource inputs and enjoyable amenities.

This final sentence is a synthesis of the category's role in the introductory framework.
sections.title: Four environmental functions

sections.html:
1. Ask whether the environmental feature supplies an input or possibility for economic activity: this is a resource. Wood/biomass are degradable renewable resources; fossil fuels/minerals are degradable non-renewable/exhaustible resources. Sunshine, wind and waves are separately classified as non-degradable in this source; space is also a resource.
  2. Ask whether the relationship concerns receiving undesirable outputs: this is the sink function, interpreted through assimilative capacity. A sink does not imply unlimited capacity.
  3. Ask whether people value aesthetic, cultural or recreational services directly: these are demand services. Forest recreation differs from timber production even at the same site.
  4. Ask whether the relationship concerns broad life-supporting systems: climate, the hydrologic cycle and soil production belong to the biospheric category.
  5. Keep categories distinct by mechanism while allowing coexistence. The source supplies this taxonomy, not a general formal definition of degradability; do not replace its wording with another taxonomy.

Check the prerequisites

Prompt: A simplified sketch shows nature supplying an input to production, receiving an unwanted output from production, and giving people direct scenic enjoyment. Name the environmental function for each relationship. Does drawing all three at the same location force one exclusive function? Explain.

Key and essential reasoning: Input to production is the resource function; reception of unwanted output is the sink/assimilative-capacity function; direct scenic enjoyment is a demand service. These are different relationships, so several functions can coexist at one location. A place label alone does not collapse them into one function. The question does not ask for a resource taxonomy or a fourth-function example.

original_sections.html:
More production is only one change within a network. Benefits from consumption, direct amenities and losses from environmental pressure travel along different paths, so one output measure cannot determine the whole welfare effect.

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. In network lessons \(P\) denotes production, \(C\) denotes consumption, \(U\) denotes utility, \(R\) denotes natural resources, \(\mathrm{ER}\) denotes exhaustible resources, \(\mathrm{RR}\) denotes renewable resources, \(h\) denotes harvest rate, \(y\) denotes yield/growth, \(W\) denotes waste, \(A\) denotes assimilative capacity. These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.

Relevant finished-note figure:
original_sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

original_sections.html:
1. In the core figure firms are production P and households consumption C. Labour, savings, wages and rent/interest are labels in that core. K is conventionally capital but is not separately defined by the source. The solid/dashed legend below belongs to the full network figure; do not apply it retroactively to every line of the simpler core.
  2. In the full network solid arrows carry materials/energy: natural resources R support P, P supplies C; solid paths from R, P and C join waste W.
  3. Waste connects to assimilative capacity A and can feed back to resources. The sign of the capacity branch is conditional; detailed inequalities are O003.
  4. Dashed arrows carry utility effects: C has a positive link to U; resources have positive amenity links to U; waste above capacity has a negative amenity path to U. U represents benefit/wellbeing without a numerical scale.
  5. Plus/minus denote qualitative direction, not coefficients, euro values or a sum that permits net-welfare calculation. The lower-case r appears on a material return path but has no supplied definition, rate or equation. Identifying that visible path is supported; assigning a verified recycling parameter is not.
original_sections.title: Explanation steps

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The economic core: firms and households; fingerprint efb3d63bd3709f51261b845db081603746a89796298bbe89a4849ca6e0e84b23. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The economic core: firms and households

Economic core reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 3, through a local LibreOffice PDF rendering. Firms represent production (\(P\)), households represent consumption (\(C\)), and the figure also labels \(K\), labour, savings, wages, and rent/interest. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 3

Read the figure first as an economic relationship. Firms produce what households consume. Labour and savings appear above the two groups, while wages and rent/interest appear below them. The loop beside firms is labelled \(K\), the conventional capital symbol; the source gives no separate definition or numerical relationship for \(K\). The point of the next slide is to place this compact economic core inside the wider resource, waste and utility network. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 3–4

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Reading the physical and utility network; fingerprint efb3d63bd3709f51261b845db081603746a89796298bbe89a4849ca6e0e84b23. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Reading the physical and utility network

Environment–economy network reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4. Solid arrows denote flows of materials/energy; dashed arrows denote utility flows. The blue highlight locates production and consumption within the wider network. Plus and minus signs show qualitative directions of effect. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

The symbols supplied by the slide are:

Symbol Source meaning
\(P\) Production
\(C\) Consumption
\(U\) Utility
\(R\) Natural resources
\(ER\) Exhaustible resources
\(RR\) Renewable resources
\(h\) Harvest rate
\(y\) Yield/growth
\(W\) Waste
\(A\) Assimilative capacity

The diagram also contains a lower-case \(r\) on the return path from waste toward resources. The source's printed legend does not define \(r\). The path can be identified visually as a material return path, but this note does not assign it a verified name, rate, or equation. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, lower-left return path and legend

Resource use and replenishment

The main horizontal physical path runs from natural resources (\(R\)) through production (\(P\)) to consumption (\(C\)). The resource branch separates exhaustible resources (\(ER\)) and renewable resources (\(RR\)). On the exhaustible branch, the displayed case \(h>y\) connects with a negative sign. On the renewable branch, \(h>y\) has a negative sign, whereas \(h<y\) has a positive sign. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, left resource branches

These inequalities compare harvesting with yield or growth. If harvesting exceeds growth, use runs ahead of replenishment and the diagram represents a reduction of the resource. If harvesting is below growth on the renewable branch, replenishment can exceed removal and the diagram represents a positive effect on that resource. For this interpretation, \(h\) and \(y\) must refer to comparable quantities over the same time interval. This comparability is a mathematical requirement of reading the inequality, rather than a separate numerical assumption supplied by the slide. The diagram does not specify a growth function, units, a time horizon, or an equality case \(h=y\). It therefore supports directional reasoning, rather than a calculation of a sustainable harvest level. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

Waste and capacity

Solid paths from the resource, production and consumption parts of the diagram join the waste node \(W\). Waste then connects to assimilative capacity \(A\). Two cases appear below it: \(W<A\) and \(W>A\). The \(W<A\) branch returns to resources with a positive sign. The \(W>A\) branch returns with a negative sign and also produces the dashed negative amenity connection to utility. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4, waste/capacity branches

Read \(W<A\) as waste remaining below the capacity represented in this schematic model, and \(W>A\) as waste exceeding it. The latter case makes the feedback explicit: undesirable output can impair the environmental resource base and reduce utility. As with harvesting and growth, the comparison requires a common basis of measurement. The slide gives no units or detailed physical law and does not discuss the equality case \(W=A\). It also does not establish that all waste below capacity is harmless in every setting. The diagram's positive and negative arrows represent its qualitative framework, not a universal empirical emissions rule. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

Several paths to wellbeing

Consumption has a positive dashed link to utility. Natural resources also connect to utility through the upper “Positive amenity (+)” path, while waste exceeding capacity connects through the lower-right “Negative amenity (−)” path. These distinct paths show why production or consumption alone cannot describe the whole environment–economy relationship: the same network contains benefits from consumption, benefits from environmental amenities, and losses associated with environmental pressures. This is an explanatory reading of the diagram, not a quantitative welfare formula. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, trace material, waste and utility paths.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Reconstruct the resource–production–consumption path, waste feedback and three utility paths;
  • Distinguish solid materials/energy arrows from dashed utility arrows and signs from quantities;
  • State the limits on K and r.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Classify the four environmental functions
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Material path: A directed resource/production/consumption flow in the conceptual diagram.
  • Amenity path: A pathway from environmental quality to utility.
  • Net welfare: The combined welfare effect, requiring more than uncalibrated arrow signs.

3.1 Notation and distinctions

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. In network lessons \(P\) denotes production, \(C\) denotes consumption, \(U\) denotes utility, \(R\) denotes natural resources, \(\mathrm{ER}\) denotes exhaustible resources, \(\mathrm{RR}\) denotes renewable resources, \(h\) denotes harvest rate, \(y\) denotes yield/growth, \(W\) denotes waste, \(A\) denotes assimilative capacity.

These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.

sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
Economic core reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 3, through a local LibreOffice PDF rendering. Firms represent production (\(P\)), households represent consumption (\(C\)), and the figure also labels \(K\), labour, savings, wages, and rent/interest.

Read the figure first as an economic relationship. Firms produce what households consume.

Labour and savings appear above the two groups, while wages and rent/interest appear below them. The loop beside firms is labelled \(K\), the conventional capital symbol;

the source gives no separate definition or numerical relationship for \(K\). The point of the next slide is to place this compact economic core inside the wider resource, waste and utility network.
sections.title: The economic core: firms and households

sections.html:
Environment–economy network reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 4. Solid arrows denote flows of materials/energy; dashed arrows denote utility flows. The blue highlight locates production and consumption within the wider network. Plus and minus signs show qualitative directions of effect.

The symbols supplied by the slide are:

Symbol Source meaning
\(P\) Production
\(C\) Consumption
\(U\) Utility
\(R\) Natural resources
\(ER\) Exhaustible resources
\(RR\) Renewable resources
\(h\) Harvest rate
\(y\) Yield/growth
\(W\) Waste
\(A\) Assimilative capacity

The diagram also contains a lower-case \(r\) on the return path from waste toward resources. The source's printed legend does not define \(r\). The path can be identified visually as a material return path, but this note does not assign it a verified name, rate, or equation.

5.1 Resource use and replenishment

The main horizontal physical path runs from natural resources (\(R\)) through production (\(P\)) to consumption (\(C\)). The resource branch separates exhaustible resources (\(ER\)) and renewable resources (\(RR\)). On the exhaustible branch, the displayed case \(h>y\) connects with a negative sign. On the renewable branch, \(h>y\) has a negative sign, whereas \(h<y\) has a positive sign.

These inequalities compare harvesting with yield or growth. If harvesting exceeds growth, use runs ahead of replenishment and the diagram represents a reduction of the resource.

If harvesting is below growth on the renewable branch, replenishment can exceed removal and the diagram represents a positive effect on that resource. For this interpretation, \(h\) and \(y\) must refer to comparable quantities over the same time interval.

This comparability is a mathematical requirement of reading the inequality, rather than a separate numerical assumption supplied by the slide. The diagram does not specify a growth function, units, a time horizon, or an equality case \(h=y\).

It therefore supports directional reasoning, rather than a calculation of a sustainable harvest level.

5.2 Waste and capacity

Solid paths from the resource, production and consumption parts of the diagram join the waste node \(W\). Waste then connects to assimilative capacity \(A\). Two cases appear below it: \(W<A\) and \(W>A\). The \(W<A\) branch returns to resources with a positive sign. The \(W>A\) branch returns with a negative sign and also produces the dashed negative amenity connection to utility.

Read \(W<A\) as waste remaining below the capacity represented in this schematic model, and \(W>A\) as waste exceeding it. The latter case makes the feedback explicit: undesirable output can impair the environmental resource base and reduce utility.

As with harvesting and growth, the comparison requires a common basis of measurement. The slide gives no units or detailed physical law and does not discuss the equality case \(W=A\).

It also does not establish that all waste below capacity is harmless in every setting. The diagram's positive and negative arrows represent its qualitative framework, not a universal empirical emissions rule.

5.3 Several paths to wellbeing

Consumption has a positive dashed link to utility. Natural resources also connect to utility through the upper “Positive amenity (+)” path, while waste exceeding capacity connects through the lower-right “Negative amenity (−)” path.

These distinct paths show why production or consumption alone cannot describe the whole environment–economy relationship: the same network contains benefits from consumption, benefits from environmental amenities, and losses associated with environmental pressures. This is an explanatory reading of the diagram, not a quantitative welfare formula.
sections.title: Reading the physical and utility network

sections.html:
1. In the core figure firms are production P and households consumption C. Labour, savings, wages and rent/interest are labels in that core. K is conventionally capital but is not separately defined by the source. The solid/dashed legend below belongs to the full network figure; do not apply it retroactively to every line of the simpler core.
  2. In the full network solid arrows carry materials/energy: natural resources R support P, P supplies C; solid paths from R, P and C join waste W.
  3. Waste connects to assimilative capacity A and can feed back to resources. The sign of the capacity branch is conditional; detailed inequalities are O003.
  4. Dashed arrows carry utility effects: C has a positive link to U; resources have positive amenity links to U; waste above capacity has a negative amenity path to U. U represents benefit/wellbeing without a numerical scale.
  5. Plus/minus denote qualitative direction, not coefficients, euro values or a sum that permits net-welfare calculation. The lower-case r appears on a material return path but has no supplied definition, rate or equation. Identifying that visible path is supported; assigning a verified recycling parameter is not.
sections.title: Connect the reasoning

sections.html:
instruction only. Hypothetical scenario: production and consumption rise while waste exceeds the capacity shown by the diagram. Explain what can be traced without calculating net wellbeing.

Worked solution: Step 1: trace resources \(R\to P\to C\) as material/energy. Step 2: outputs from economic activity join \(W\), then the \(W>A\) branch feeds back negatively to resources and through a negative amenity path to \(U\).

Step 3: \(C\) still has a positive utility path and \(R\) a positive amenity path. Step 4: positive and negative directions coexist;

no magnitude/utility function resolves their net effect. \(K\) has only a conventional interpretation; \(r\) remains undefined. This supports tracing mechanisms, not ranking the policy numerically.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, interpret harvest and waste capacity comparisons.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • For hypothetical comparable quantities, choose \(h>y\) or \(h<y\) and \(W>A\) or \(W<A\)
  • Explain the note’s directional resource/utility effects, and withhold unsupported equality cases, numerical limits and universal safety claims.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Classify the four environmental functions
  • Trace material, waste and utility paths
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Harvest h: The renewable-resource withdrawal flow over the declared time basis.
  • Growth y: The comparable renewable-resource regeneration flow.
  • Waste capacity A: The assimilation-capacity quantity compared with waste on compatible units/time bases.

3.1 Notation and distinctions

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. In network lessons \(P\) denotes production, \(C\) denotes consumption, \(U\) denotes utility, \(R\) denotes natural resources, \(\mathrm{ER}\) denotes exhaustible resources, \(\mathrm{RR}\) denotes renewable resources, \(h\) denotes harvest rate, \(y\) denotes yield/growth, \(W\) denotes waste, \(A\) denotes assimilative capacity.

These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.

Relevant finished-note figure:
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The main horizontal physical path runs from natural resources (\(R\)) through production (\(P\)) to consumption (\(C\)). The resource branch separates exhaustible resources (\(ER\)) and renewable resources (\(RR\)). On the exhaustible branch, the displayed case \(h>y\) connects with a negative sign. On the renewable branch, \(h>y\) has a negative sign, whereas \(h<y\) has a positive sign.

These inequalities compare harvesting with yield or growth. If harvesting exceeds growth, use runs ahead of replenishment and the diagram represents a reduction of the resource.

If harvesting is below growth on the renewable branch, replenishment can exceed removal and the diagram represents a positive effect on that resource. For this interpretation, \(h\) and \(y\) must refer to comparable quantities over the same time interval.

This comparability is a mathematical requirement of reading the inequality, rather than a separate numerical assumption supplied by the slide. The diagram does not specify a growth function, units, a time horizon, or an equality case \(h=y\).

It therefore supports directional reasoning, rather than a calculation of a sustainable harvest level.
sections.title: Resource use and replenishment

sections.html:
Solid paths from the resource, production and consumption parts of the diagram join the waste node \(W\). Waste then connects to assimilative capacity \(A\). Two cases appear below it: \(W<A\) and \(W>A\). The \(W<A\) branch returns to resources with a positive sign. The \(W>A\) branch returns with a negative sign and also produces the dashed negative amenity connection to utility.

Read \(W<A\) as waste remaining below the capacity represented in this schematic model, and \(W>A\) as waste exceeding it. The latter case makes the feedback explicit: undesirable output can impair the environmental resource base and reduce utility.

As with harvesting and growth, the comparison requires a common basis of measurement. The slide gives no units or detailed physical law and does not discuss the equality case \(W=A\).

It also does not establish that all waste below capacity is harmless in every setting. The diagram's positive and negative arrows represent its qualitative framework, not a universal empirical emissions rule.
sections.title: Waste and capacity

sections.html:
1. Compare harvest rate \(h\) and yield/growth \(y\) on the same basis and time interval. A per-year rate cannot be compared directly with a per-month rate; convert only if the relation is explicitly given.
  2. In the renewable branch \(h>y\) shows negative resource effect because removal outruns replenishment; \(h<y\) shows positive effect because replenishment exceeds removal. The source also displays a negative \(h>y\) exhaustible branch, without a full exhaustible-resource dynamic law.
  3. Compare waste \(W\) and assimilative capacity \(A\) on a common basis. \(W>A\) has negative resource feedback and a negative amenity effect on \(U\). \(W<A\) has a positive resource-return branch in this schematic model.
  4. These signs do not quantify stock changes or wellbeing. Do not infer that all waste below capacity is harmless in every setting.
  5. The source does not specify \(h=y\) or \(W=A\), a growth function, exact sustainable harvest, universal pollution threshold or time horizon. If equality or mismatched units occur, report the missing information rather than extending a sign rule.
sections.title: Connect the reasoning

sections.html:
instruction only. Hypothetical quantities on explicitly common annual bases: renewable harvest \(h=8\) and growth \(y=12\) resource-units/year; waste \(W=15\) and capacity \(A=10\) waste-units/year. What signs follow, and what if equality occurs?

Worked solution: Step 1: units/time bases match within each comparison; no comparison of resource units to waste units is needed.

Step 2: \(8<12\) implies \(h<y\), positive renewable-resource effect in the diagram. Step 3: \(15>10\) implies \(W>A\), negative resource and amenity/utility effects.

Step 4: effects can coexist; no sizes or net-welfare conclusion follow.

Step 5: at \(h=y\) or \(W=A\) the diagram supplies no equality prediction. No stock-growth amount is calculated from the differences.

A diagram can show what to investigate without answering a policy question. Locating resources, feedback and utility makes a proposal assessable, but an optimal instrument or climate mechanism requires material the introduction does not contain.

Terms and symbols are defined in the explanation below and exact cited sections. In network lessons \(P\) denotes production, \(C\) denotes consumption, \(U\) denotes utility, \(R\) denotes natural resources, \(\mathrm{ER}\) denotes exhaustible resources, \(\mathrm{RR}\) denotes renewable resources, \(h\) denotes harvest rate, \(y\) denotes yield/growth, \(W\) denotes waste, \(A\) denotes assimilative capacity. These are qualitative labels; units are supplied explicitly only in our hypothetical comparisons.

original_sections.html:
1. Locate resources beside resource branches, growth/sustainability above P and C, externality along feedback paths, regulation around P/waste, valuation beside amenity-to-U paths. These are topic placements, not derivations.
  2. Use the network to ask what resources support activity, whether use outruns replenishment, how waste compares with capacity, and which consumption/amenity paths affect wellbeing. The course’s economic, environmental and social impact aims motivate these questions; no numerical estimates are supplied.
  3. For a proposal, name the affected paths and what comparison/data would be needed. Avoid deriving an optimal tax, valuation formula, emissions threshold or growth model from labels.
  4. The finished orientation note says the uploaded introduction supplies environmental functions/network and course information. The separately linked physical climate lecture is advertised, including mitigation/adaptation/geoengineering and Kyoto-to-Paris history, but not explained in these notes. Later policy comparisons/modeling topics are outside current academic coverage. No policy outcome or current calendar is inferred from orientation alone.

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The economic questions placed on the network; fingerprint efb3d63bd3709f51261b845db081603746a89796298bbe89a4849ca6e0e84b23. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The economic questions placed on the network

The same network with the source's topic labels: resources, growth and sustainability, externality, regulation, and valuation. Reproduced from 00_Intro.pptx, slide 5. The placement connects each topic to the physical or utility relationships it concerns. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 5

Slide 5 overlays the course's economic questions on the physical network. Resources appears beside the resource branches. Growth and sustainability appears above the production-and-consumption relationship. Externality appears along feedback paths. Regulation appears around the production/waste part of the network. Valuation appears beside the amenity connections to utility. The overlay locates these topics but does not derive a policy instrument, an optimal pollution level, a valuation formula or a growth model. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 5

An explanatory synthesis is to use this network as a sequence of questions. What resources support economic activity? Does resource use outrun replenishment? How much waste reaches the environment relative to its capacity? Which pathways change wellbeing, and how should those changes be assessed? The source's regulation and valuation labels point toward these policy and assessment questions. Formal externality theory and instrument comparisons belong to later material and are not supplied by these introductory diagrams. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 4–6

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the introductory framework establishes; fingerprint efb3d63bd3709f51261b845db081603746a89796298bbe89a4849ca6e0e84b23. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What the introductory framework establishes

The economy depends on resources and wider environmental services, while production and consumption generate waste and feedback to the environment and utility. The crucial conditions in the source diagram compare harvest with growth and waste with assimilative capacity. These conditions make resource renewal and environmental capacity part of the analysis. The diagram offers a conceptual foundation for later policy assessment, while leaving quantitative models, measurements and climate science unspecified. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 2–5

The scope note identifies the separate climate-foundation lecture referenced on slide 1. The uploaded deck supplies the environment–economy introduction, rather than the physical climate mechanisms, mitigation/adaptation/geoengineering explanations, or Kyoto-to-Paris history advertised for that lecture.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Course Orientation and Week 1 Scope; fingerprint f0b080e8ef565e2c6f73bb37f1ab81239a904c63186fad7659685b96a87ba3a2. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Course Orientation and Week 1 Scope

What will Economics of Green Deal examine, and what does the first week's uploaded material actually explain? The course studies environmental problems and climate change through economics, including how optimal regulation is defined and how policies' economic, social and environmental impacts can be quantified. It gives special attention to decarbonisation scenarios and pathways, technology and social innovation. This note records that orientation and the assessment information, while identifying which Week 1 topics are supported by the supplied files. Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, English annotation and aim

Course navigation: Economics of Green Deal — Week 1. The Environment–Economy Nexus note explains the substantive introductory diagrams.

Course information in the supplied SIS export

The supplied SIS export identifies the course as Economics of Green Deal — JEB159. It lists the winter semester, 5 E-credits, English instruction, in-person delivery and a written examination. The prerequisite is JEB104. The course guarantor is Mgr. Milan Ščasný, Ph.D. These details come from the Czech part of the export; they are not a newly verified current timetable. The course folder remains Economics_of_Green_Deal within the existing vault structure. Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, course information

The export header states the academic year 2026/2027, but the English descriptions and syllabus give 29.09.2025 as their last modification date. The supplied lecture materials use dates such as September 29 and October 6, while slide 9 lists Monday teaching. These materials therefore cannot, without further confirmation, establish the calendar for 2026/2027. Dates recorded here are labels from the sources, rather than a newly constructed timetable. Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, header and modification date Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, syllabus 00_Intro.pptx, slides 6 and 9

The course's central question

The English annotation frames the European Green Deal as a policy to transform the EU into a carbon-neutral, resource-efficient and competitive economy. The transition involves technology, behaviour and lifestyle, and the course asks how to assess its impacts on the economy, environment and people. Environmental economics supplies the foundation, complemented by energy, transport and behavioural economics, energy-system modelling and environmental sciences. These are the course's stated aims and framing, rather than separately verified claims about current policy outcomes. Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1, English annotation

The introductory environment–economy framework explains why that assessment has several dimensions. Resources and environmental services support economic activity, waste feeds back into the environment, and both consumption and environmental amenities affect utility. Consequently, the course's stated environmental, economic and social impact questions share a common conceptual setting. This connection is a synthesis of the annotation and the introductory diagrams. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 2–5 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1

Week 1 content supplied and content only advertised

The Week 1 lecture is titled “Setting the Stage — Climate Change: Physical Foundation and Policy Implications”, attributed to Miroslav Havránek, CENIA and Charles University Environment Center. The source labels it September 29. The SIS syllabus advertises two strands: mitigation, adaptation, a global perspective and geoengineering solutions; and the historical context from Kyoto to Paris to the Green Deal. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 1 and 6 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, Week 1 syllabus

The uploaded 00_Intro.pptx contains ten slides. Slides 2–5 explain environmental functions and the environment–economy network. Slides 6–8 give the course schedule, and slides 9–10 give contacts, materials and assessment information. Slide 1 contains the climate-foundation lecture title and a hyperlink to a Prezi presentation; the climate-foundation presentation itself is not embedded in the uploaded file. No hidden slide or substantive speaker note supplies that missing content. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 1–10

Source limitation: the supplied files identify the climate-foundation topics but do not explain their physical mechanisms, evidence, history, or policy details. Those strands remain advertised topics, rather than completed teaching coverage. The linked Prezi was not accessed in this ingestion, and no explanation was invented from the title or syllabus bullets. An accessible copy of that lecture would be needed to ingest those strands in full. The uploaded introduction and Week 1 SIS information are covered here. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 1 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2

The SIS document also describes Weeks 2–12 and lists other downloadable materials. These regions were inspected to establish their scope, but their academic content is excluded from this Week 1 ingestion. In particular, this note does not cover the Week 2 readings, policy-instrument comparisons, later modelling lectures, or later distributional and behavioural topics. The schedule slides provide orientation only. 00_Intro.pptx, slides 6–8 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, Week 2–5 syllabus Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 3, Week 6–12 syllabus

Assessment and grading in the supplied materials

The deck and SIS export agree on three components. A writing test with a satisfactory grade carries 65 points, the written open-book examination carries 35 points, and active participation in lectures carries 10 points. The open-book exam is described as testing understanding and application rather than memorisation. The source qualifies permitted material as “all, but electronic,” which excludes electronic materials under its stated wording. It does not enumerate particular permitted paper resources. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 10 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, completion requirements

Points stated in the source Grade
91 and more A
81–90 B
71–80 C
61–70 D
51–60 E
50 and less Failed

These are point bands, not percentages. The three displayed component allocations sum to 110 points. The supplied materials do not explain whether participation is a bonus, whether the final result is capped, or how fractional point totals would be handled. Keep the source's allocations and thresholds without inventing a normalization or a bonus rule. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 10 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 2, grading

Contacts and materials recorded in the deck

Slide 9 names Milan Ščasný as coordinator and supplies milan.scasny@czp.cuni.cz. It gives lectures as Mondays, 15:30–16:50, room O206, and identifies SIS as the materials location. Offices are listed at the Institute of Economic Studies (#408) and the Environment Center (José Martího 2/407, #1617). Office hours require prior communication, by email or after lectures. These are the deck's administrative statements, subject to the calendar limitation above. The deck labels the course JEB159, with JEM335 in parentheses, and prints “5 ETS”; the SIS export separately states 5 E-kreditů. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 9 Předměty.pdf, physical PDF p. 1

The lecturer list associates Lukáš Rečka with energy-system modelling, Matěj Opatrný with distributional impacts, Vojtěch Máca with environmental policy and transportation, Vědunka Kopečná with CGE modelling and impact assessment, and Iñaki Alberto Veruete Villegas with IOA, CGE and inequality. It also lists Miroslav Havránek (environmental sciences, CENIA/CUNI), Richard Juřík (Ministry of the Environment), and Vladimír Kubeček (ČEPS/TSO, VŠE). These roles provide orientation; their later subject matter is outside this Week 1 coverage. 00_Intro.pptx, slide 9

Sources and page conventions

  • 00_Intro.pptx: all ten slides, hidden-slide flags, speaker notes, relationships and package contents inspected; diagrams rendered locally with LibreOffice. No hidden slides or embedded lecture objects were found.
  • Předměty.pdf: all four physical PDF pages extracted and visually inspected. Citations use physical PDF page numbers. The administrative navigation, file listing and historic enrollment statistics on pages 1, 3 and 4 supply no additional Week 1 teaching content.

original_sections.html:
O004-W1 v1, instruction only. Agent-created proposal: firms increase production using renewable biomass while visitors value a forest. Use the framework to organize an assessment without choosing a policy.

Worked solution: Step 1: resources label concerns biomass inputs; ask h versus y rather than assuming renewable use is maintained. Step 2: growth/sustainability concerns P/C and their resource pressures. Step 3: identify waste and feedback under externality, locate regulation around P/W, ask W versus A on comparable bases. Step 4: valuation concerns the amenity-to-U path; consumption also has a positive U path and excess waste a negative one. Step 5: this organizes economic/environmental/social questions without a net-welfare amount or optimal instrument. Physical climate mechanisms and Kyoto/Paris history require the missing lecture; names in orientation are not teaching coverage.

Every I and D task explicitly tests all indexed components: map_overlay_topics, frame_multidimensional_assessment, separate_supported_from_advertised_content. A missing keyed reason/limit is partial, even if labels or inequalities are right. Wrong mechanism, reversed sign, conflated arrow/service categories, unsupported equality/optimal-policy/universal-safety claim, or invented verified definition is a critical conceptual error and fails the relevant whole task. For O003, a lone transcription/comparison slip with a correct stated mechanism is partial rather than diagnosed conceptual failure; clarify once without providing the answer. Unknown help/exposure conditions do not produce independent pass evidence. General source-faithful alternatives are acceptable; unsupported alternatives trigger a plan issue instead of improvised grading.
original_sections.title: Rubric and independence

original_sections.html:
Sign: a topic label becomes an established optimal policy or an advertised title becomes a completed explanation. Tentative after one answer. Correction: separate a path, an assessment question and a solved model; cite the finished scope note’s missing-lecture boundary. Hint 1: ask where a formula/result appears. Hint 2: contrast a title with explained mechanisms.

Score the original answer first; use at most the two hints above, then explain the prepared missing step. Corrective feedback creates exposure.

O004-C1 v1, fresh correction, assistance allowed: Repair “more consumption settles wellbeing; the source already ranks policies and explains the climate lecture.” Map the five topic labels and frame resource, waste and amenity questions for an expansion with forest recreation; state the supported/advertised boundary.

Key: Resources R; growth/sustainability P/C; externality feedback; regulation P/W; valuation amenity-U. Ask harvest/growth, waste/capacity, positive C and amenities plus possible negative waste utility, so consumption alone does not settle wellbeing. Within the original Week1 case, functions/network are supplied but the separate linked climate lecture/policy-history strands are absent; that introduction supplies no policy ranking, valuation formula or welfare magnitude.

Rubric: the full keyed component set correct = correction pass; omitted reason/limit = partial; repeated critical mechanism error = fail. C1 is repair evidence and does not establish acquisition. If I1/I2 are already exposed or exhausted, stop and request new prepared variants from plan.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, frame economic assessment questions within source limits.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Place the five source topic labels on relevant network relationships, frame resource/waste/amenity questions for an hypothetical proposal
  • Distinguish the original Week1 uploaded introduction/SIS source set from its advertised absent linked Prezi and methods not supplied in that historical case.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Classify the four environmental functions
  • Trace material, waste and utility paths
  • Interpret harvest and waste capacity comparisons
Check the foundations

Solution: Compare harvest rate h with yield/growth y, and waste W with assimilative capacity A, using comparable quantities over a common time basis within each pair. Harvest versus replenishment and waste versus capacity determine which displayed strict branch can apply;

the category names alone do not make the comparisons. Equalities \(h=y\) and \(W=A\) are not specified by the source.

No growth function, universal safety threshold, stock-change amount or numerical utility model supplies a precise safe-use or net-welfare figure. The answer does not need an invented numeric case.

original_sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

original_sections.html: Start with the decision maker (supplier), affected receptor and real variable in utility or production. The effect must be omitted from that decision for this technological-externality framework. Physical changes, competitive price effects and deliberate reciprocal/altruistic relations must be distinguished; social/private benefits of transport do not erase an external wedge. Effects differ by sign, production/consumption origin, spatial reach (local or global), temporal reach (current or intergenerational), depletability and recipient structure. These dimensions require separately stated facts; location or activity alone does not imply a particular magnitude. Congestion shows an actor can also be a receptor. A strict Pareto improvement has at least one gain and no loss. Pareto efficiency says no feasible such improvement remains, not that distribution is uniquely fair. Kaldor accepts if winners could compensate afterwards; Hicks if initial losers could not compensate winners sufficiently to prevent the change. These potential tests do not require payment. Competitive welfare theorems are conditional and equity/merit arguments are separate; a remedy also incurs costs. The supplied risk opening distinguishes event probability/severity and defensive choices from compensating insurance, without a complete later model.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Identify the externality before proposing a remedy; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Identify the externality before proposing a remedy

The chapter's definition has two actors: a supplier whose action determines a real variable and a receptor whose utility or production function depends on it. The supplier does not account for that effect in choosing the action. Noise, contaminated water or air quality can be such real variables. An upstream factory that discharges waste, reduces dissolved oxygen and fish stocks, and harms downstream anglers illustrates the mechanism. If downstream welfare does not enter the factory's decision, the private return from production remains higher than its social return. The lecture also presents the uncompensated-welfare-loss wording of an external cost. The definition used in the chapter makes the neglected real relationship central; compensation and incentives require separate analysis. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 3,5–6 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,5

A physical environmental change without a utility or production consequence does not establish an economic externality. An unpriced relationship is also insufficient. Barter can exchange benefits implicitly, and altruism deliberately takes another person's pleasure into account. The chapter excludes deliberate violence, jealousy and promotion from its externality category as well. This is a classification of the argument for efficiency correction, not approval of harmful conduct or a claim that policy has no equity or other rationale. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 7–10 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 3

Pecuniary effects operate through prices in existing markets. A change in transport or input prices moves a consumer along a given demand/utility relationship rather than creating the technological shift represented by an externality. Under the competitive assumptions here, the market already transmits these effects. Greater consumer surplus from cheaper output can be valuable without being an external benefit. Employment and value added in related industries are likewise not evidence that excessive externality-generating activity should be encouraged. Infrastructure investment and the actual use of infrastructure need separate assessments. The transport note develops these distinctions. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 9–10,19 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5

Types and boundaries

Positive versus negative refers to the receptor's benefit or loss, while production versus consumption refers to the originating activity. Spatial neighbourhood, partial/global and intergenerational classifications identify the reach of the effect. The lecture also lists effects involving several interacting uses, such as fishing, boating and swimming, and marginal versus inframarginal effects. These classifications identify which relationships require measurement; the lecture supplies no separate formal model for every category. Lecture, physical PDF p. 12

A depletable effect differs from an undepletable effect in whether one receptor's consumption changes what is available to others. An undepletable externality has public-good or public-bad characteristics alongside the externality. The chapter reports that this distinction does not require different Pigouvian pricing rules by itself, but can make voluntary bargaining vulnerable to strategic behaviour and free riding. In congestion, an actor can simultaneously cause and receive effects; the appropriate individual-level incentive does not disappear merely because the harm stays inside the road-user sector. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,6–7 Lecture, physical PDF pp. 12,27

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What welfare criteria can establish; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What welfare criteria can establish

A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. A Pareto-efficient allocation leaves no feasible rearrangement that everyone weakly prefers, with somebody strictly preferring it. These criteria make relatively little use of interpersonal welfare comparisons, but they cannot rank alternative efficient allocations with different distributions. Verhoef contrasts them with potential Pareto or compensation criteria: the winners could compensate the losers so that a Pareto improvement becomes possible. The Kaldor criterion accepts the change if its winners could compensate its losers afterwards. The Hicks criterion accepts it if the initial losers could not compensate the winners sufficiently to prevent the change. These are differently directed compensation tests, not a requirement that a transfer actually occurs. Actual compensation is not required by the potential criterion. Therefore a positive aggregate net benefit can coexist with people who lose. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 2

Under the conditions of the first welfare theorem, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient; the second theorem relates alternative efficient allocations to appropriate endowment distributions. The chapter also relates maxima of Paretian, welfaristic social welfare functions to efficiency and, under concavity, the converse with suitable welfare weights. These are conditional results. Increasing returns, market power, external effects, public goods and imperfect information can prevent their usual competitive conclusion. Equity and merit-good arguments are additional rationales for intervention, distinct from a demonstration of market failure. A failure identifies a possible efficiency rationale; an intervention still needs gains exceeding its costs. The chapter calls a technological externality potentially Pareto relevant when correcting it costs less than the available welfare gain. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 2–3 Lecture, physical PDF pp. 4,22

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The next-chapter fragment included in the file; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The next-chapter fragment included in the file

Physical PDF p. 10 includes printed p. 215, the opening of “Endogenous environmental risk” by Crocker and Shogren. It defines risk through an event's likelihood and severity and explains how defensive choices can alter these, particularly when insurance/contingent-claims markets are incomplete. Examples include boiling contaminated drinking water, filtering water, changing outdoor activity and using sunscreen. Insurance compensates an insured loss; it does not by itself change the probability. Defining only contamination as a fixed state can hide the household's ability to change the risk of illness through boiling. This is an additional supplied fragment, not the full chapter, and contains no complete risk model or later argument to reconstruct. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 10

O005-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Given hypothetical cases: (a)factory discharge reduces an angler’s utility, explicitly omitted from the supplier’s decision; (b)cheaper production lowers a product price through ordinary competitive prices without an unpriced real effect; (c)a friend deliberately enjoys helping another friend, deliberately considered by the actor. Classify each using supplier/receptor/real-variable/neglected-effect criteria; explain why a physical change alone is insufficient and what depletable/public-bad and congestion distinctions mean. In three additional hypothetical omitted-effect cases, the household actions are consumption and the mine/farm/workshop/factory/plant/forest actions are production. Classify sign, origin and spatial/temporal reach from the declared effects: a factory’s smoke harms nearby households today; a household’s ornamental garden benefits a local neighbour in the next generation; a factory’s greenhouse emissions harm people worldwide in future generations. A separate money-valued policy gives winners \(20\), losers \(-10\); within this declared transferable-money illustration explain strict Pareto, Kaldor and Hicks acceptance directions and apply them without assuming actual compensation. State why market-failure and welfare-theorem conditions do not automatically justify any intervention. Distinguish defensive reduction of environmental illness risk from insurance compensation using the supplied next-chapter fragment, and limit the inference to that fragment.

Steps and interpretation: (a) is a technological externality: identify the supplier action, other person’s utility/production affected through the specified real variable, and its omission. (b) is a pecuniary market effect under the stated competitive boundary, not that externality; ordinary price transmission already enters decisions. (c) is an intentionally considered unpriced relation, so omission is absent; unpriced alone is not enough. The additional cases are respectively negative/production/local/current; positive/consumption/local/intergenerational; negative/production/global/intergenerational. Classification follows the declared origin and recipients/timing; it does not estimate magnitude or prove the effect exists in an actual case. A physical alteration without welfare effect does not meet the definition. Depletable/rival benefit can be used up; an undepletable public bad affects many simultaneously and creates coordination/free-rider problems. Congestion can be caused and received by the same road users but remains external to the individual actor. With gains \(20\) and loss \(10\), net \(10>0\) but losers remain: no strict Pareto improvement absent compensation. Kaldor accepts if winners could compensate afterwards; here \(20>10\). Hicks accepts if initial losers cannot compensate winners enough to prevent it; under this explicitly transferable-money example their \(10\) is insufficient against \(20\). Actual transfer is not required by these potential criteria and redistribution/equity remains separate. Conditional competitive welfare results can fail with externalities, public goods, market power, increasing returns or information limits; correction costs must be compared with possible gain, so identifying failure is not universal policy approval. Boiling contaminated water can change illness likelihood; risk includes likelihood and severity, while insurance compensates a loss without itself changing probability. The supplied page is only an opening fragment, not a complete risk model.

O005-I1

Prompt: Given hypothetical cases: (a)vehicle emissions harm another household’s health, explicitly omitted from the supplier’s decision; (b)faster paid delivery lowers traded-goods cost through ordinary competitive prices without an unpriced real effect; (c)a donor knowingly values a recipient’s wellbeing, deliberately considered by the actor. Classify each using supplier/receptor/real-variable/neglected-effect criteria; explain why a physical change alone is insufficient and what depletable/public-bad and congestion distinctions mean. In three additional hypothetical omitted-effect cases, the household actions are consumption and the mine/farm/workshop/factory/plant/forest actions are production. Classify sign, origin and spatial/temporal reach from the declared effects: a mine’s operations damage nearby crops now; a household’s shade tree benefits local neighbours in a later generation; a power plant’s emissions harm people globally in future generations. A separate money-valued policy gives winners \(40\), losers \(-15\); within this declared transferable-money illustration explain strict Pareto, Kaldor and Hicks acceptance directions and apply them without assuming actual compensation. State why market-failure and welfare-theorem conditions do not automatically justify any intervention. Distinguish defensive reduction of environmental illness risk from insurance compensation using the supplied next-chapter fragment, and limit the inference to that fragment.
interactions.solution_html: Key and essential rubric: (a) is a technological externality: identify the supplier action, other person’s utility/production affected through the specified real variable, and its omission. (b) is a pecuniary market effect under the stated competitive boundary, not that externality; ordinary price transmission already enters decisions. (c) is an intentionally considered unpriced relation, so omission is absent; unpriced alone is not enough. The additional cases are respectively negative/production/local/current; positive/consumption/local/intergenerational; negative/production/global/intergenerational. Classification follows the declared origin and recipients/timing; it does not estimate magnitude or prove the effect exists in an actual case. A physical alteration without welfare effect does not meet the definition. Depletable/rival benefit can be used up; an undepletable public bad affects many simultaneously and creates coordination/free-rider problems. Congestion can be caused and received by the same road users but remains external to the individual actor. With gains \(40\) and loss \(15\), net \(25>0\) but losers remain: no strict Pareto improvement absent compensation. Kaldor accepts if winners could compensate afterwards; here \(40>15\). Hicks accepts if initial losers cannot compensate winners enough to prevent it; under this explicitly transferable-money example their \(15\) is insufficient against \(40\). Actual transfer is not required by these potential criteria and redistribution/equity remains separate. Conditional competitive welfare results can fail with externalities, public goods, market power, increasing returns or information limits; correction costs must be compared with possible gain, so identifying failure is not universal policy approval. Boiling contaminated water can change illness likelihood; risk includes likelihood and severity, while insurance compensates a loss without itself changing probability. sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, identify economic externalities and apply conditional welfare criteria.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Classify a neglected real welfare relationship
  • Distinguish actual versus potential welfare improvement with stated boundaries.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Trace material, waste and utility paths
Check the foundations

Does a waste arrow alone prove another person loses welfare?

Reveal foundation explanation

No; trace exposure/utility and whether the actor considers it, rather than infer harm from physical movement alone. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Technological externality: A real welfare/production effect neglected in the actor’s decision under the stated definition.
  • Pecuniary effect: An effect transmitted through ordinary market prices under the competitive boundary.
  • Potential compensation: A welfare comparison about feasible compensation, distinct from an actual transfer.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The chapter's definition has two actors: a supplier whose action determines a real variable and a receptor whose utility or production function depends on it. The supplier does not account for that effect in choosing the action.

Noise, contaminated water or air quality can be such real variables. An upstream factory that discharges waste, reduces dissolved oxygen and fish stocks, and harms downstream anglers illustrates the mechanism.

If downstream welfare does not enter the factory's decision, the private return from production remains higher than its social return. The lecture also presents the uncompensated-welfare-loss wording of an external cost.

The definition used in the chapter makes the neglected real relationship central; compensation and incentives require separate analysis.

A physical environmental change without a utility or production consequence does not establish an economic externality. An unpriced relationship is also insufficient.

Barter can exchange benefits implicitly, and altruism deliberately takes another person's pleasure into account. The chapter excludes deliberate violence, jealousy and promotion from its externality category as well.

This is a classification of the argument for efficiency correction, not approval of harmful conduct or a claim that policy has no equity or other rationale.

Pecuniary effects operate through prices in existing markets. A change in transport or input prices moves a consumer along a given demand/utility relationship rather than creating the technological shift represented by an externality.

Under the competitive assumptions here, the market already transmits these effects. Greater consumer surplus from cheaper output can be valuable without being an external benefit.

Employment and value added in related industries are likewise not evidence that excessive externality-generating activity should be encouraged. Infrastructure investment and the actual use of infrastructure need separate assessments.

The transport note develops these distinctions.

4.1 Types and boundaries

Positive versus negative refers to the receptor's benefit or loss, while production versus consumption refers to the originating activity. Spatial neighbourhood, partial/global and intergenerational classifications identify the reach of the effect.

The lecture also lists effects involving several interacting uses, such as fishing, boating and swimming, and marginal versus inframarginal effects. These classifications identify which relationships require measurement;

the lecture supplies no separate formal model for every category.

A depletable effect differs from an undepletable effect in whether one receptor's consumption changes what is available to others. An undepletable externality has public-good or public-bad characteristics alongside the externality.

The chapter reports that this distinction does not require different Pigouvian pricing rules by itself, but can make voluntary bargaining vulnerable to strategic behaviour and free riding. In congestion, an actor can simultaneously cause and receive effects;

the appropriate individual-level incentive does not disappear merely because the harm stays inside the road-user sector.
sections.title: Identify the externality before proposing a remedy

sections.html:
A Pareto improvement makes at least one person better off without making anyone worse off. A Pareto-efficient allocation leaves no feasible rearrangement that everyone weakly prefers, with somebody strictly preferring it.

These criteria make relatively little use of interpersonal welfare comparisons, but they cannot rank alternative efficient allocations with different distributions. Verhoef contrasts them with potential Pareto or compensation criteria: the winners could compensate the losers so that a Pareto improvement becomes possible.

The Kaldor criterion accepts the change if its winners could compensate its losers afterwards. The Hicks criterion accepts it if the initial losers could not compensate the winners sufficiently to prevent the change.

These are differently directed compensation tests, not a requirement that a transfer actually occurs. Actual compensation is not required by the potential criterion.

Therefore a positive aggregate net benefit can coexist with people who lose.

Under the conditions of the first welfare theorem, a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient; the second theorem relates alternative efficient allocations to appropriate endowment distributions.

The chapter also relates maxima of Paretian, welfaristic social welfare functions to efficiency and, under concavity, the converse with suitable welfare weights. These are conditional results.

Increasing returns, market power, external effects, public goods and imperfect information can prevent their usual competitive conclusion. Equity and merit-good arguments are additional rationales for intervention, distinct from a demonstration of market failure.

A failure identifies a possible efficiency rationale; an intervention still needs gains exceeding its costs.

The chapter calls a technological externality potentially Pareto relevant when correcting it costs less than the available welfare gain.
sections.title: What welfare criteria can establish

sections.html:
Physical PDF p. 10 includes printed p. 215, the opening of “Endogenous environmental risk” by Crocker and Shogren. It defines risk through an event's likelihood and severity and explains how defensive choices can alter these, particularly when insurance/contingent-claims markets are incomplete.

Examples include boiling contaminated drinking water, filtering water, changing outdoor activity and using sunscreen. Insurance compensates an insured loss;

it does not by itself change the probability. Defining only contamination as a fixed state can hide the household's ability to change the risk of illness through boiling.
