original_sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

original_sections.html: Total welfare is the integral of marginal benefit minus all relevant marginal cost. With negative externality its derivative is \(\mathrm{MPB}-\mathrm{MPC}-\mathrm{MEC}\); an interior social maximum equates \(\mathrm{MPB}\) to \(\mathrm{MPC}+\mathrm{MEC}\), while private ignores \(\mathrm{MEC}\). A positive external benefit enters as \(\mathrm{MPB}+\mathrm{MEB}-\mathrm{MPC}\). Smoothness, interior feasibility and negative curvature matter: equality alone does not prove maximum. Marginal tax \(\mathrm{MEC}\) at the chosen social optimum can implement the harmful comparison in a first-best model, and marginal subsidy addresses the benefit wedge. Damage is an integral area in money while tax is money per unit activity; remaining damage can be positive because avoiding every last unit can sacrifice more benefit. A fall in private cost produces priced gains but need not remove \(\mathrm{MEC}\). Optimisation concerns the resulting welfare choice; compensation concerns transfers, regulation changes incentives, and narrow internalisation brings the effect into a market/common decision. They should not be treated as synonyms or universally equivalent under uncertainty/heterogeneity.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Derive the private and social activity levels; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Derive the private and social activity levels

Let \(Q\) denote an activity level over a given period, \(MPB(Q)\) marginal private benefit, \(MPC(Q)\) marginal private cost, \(MEC(Q)\) marginal external cost and \(MEB(Q)\) marginal external benefit. Marginal quantities are money or welfare equivalents per unit of \(Q\), measured on a common basis. In the source's smooth partial-equilibrium diagrams, private choice satisfies

\[MPB(Q^0)=MPC(Q^0).\]

Without external effects this also maximizes the area between the benefit and cost curves. With negative external effects,

\[MSC(Q)=MPC(Q)+MEC(Q),\qquad MPB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*)+MEC(Q^*).\]

An explanatory mathematical reconstruction of the diagram is

\[W(Q)=\int_0^Q\big[MPB(q)-MPC(q)-MEC(q)\big]dq,\]

so that \(W'(Q)=MPB(Q)-MPC(Q)-MEC(Q)\). The interior optimum sets this derivative to zero; a negative second derivative or suitable concavity is needed for a maximum. The source's increasing marginal external cost and decreasing net private benefit produce \(Q^*<Q^0\). This formula is a synthesis of the source's areas, rather than an extra empirical model. It excludes other distortions and any fixed costs absent from the diagram. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5,9 note7 Lecture, physical PDF pp. 14–15,20

Lecture physical PDF p. 15: the downward curve is marginal net private benefit (\(MNPB=MPB-MPC\)), the upward curve is MEC. At zero activity, the diagram normalizes welfare to zero. At unrestricted \(Q_{max}\), private net benefit is \(A+B+C\) and damage is \(B+C+D\), giving \(A-D\). At \(Q_{optimum}\), private net benefit is \(A+B\), damage is \(B\), and welfare is \(A\). The increase from restriction is \(D\), while \(B\) remains as optimal damage. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 15,25

The lettered areas in this lecture figure differ from those in Verhoef's Figure 13.1. In the chapter's negative-externality panel, \(A\) denotes optimal external damage and \(C\) the deadweight loss avoided by restricting activity. Area labels must always be read within their own figure. Optimization does not imply eliminating all external damage. Nor is reducing production necessarily a strict Pareto improvement: the supplier loses private returns and would need appropriate compensation to satisfy that stronger criterion. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5

For a positive externality, social benefit is \(MSB=MPB+MEB\) and the condition is

\[MPB(Q^*)+MEB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*).\]

The source's diagrams imply \(Q^*>Q^0\): the supplier otherwise omits part of the benefit. A correcting subsidy \(s^*=MEB(Q^*)\) can align the private choice, just as \(t^*=MEC(Q^*)\) can correct the negative externality in the simple setting. These are marginal, optimum-specific rates, not total damage divided arbitrarily by output. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 16–20 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5

Lecture p. 17: adding the external benefit raises MSB above MPB, moves the chosen output from \(Q^0\) toward \(Q^*\) and supplies the subsidy wedge \(s^*\). Lecture, physical PDF p. 17

The lecture p. 18 compares output below, at and above \(Q^*\) using coloured areas. Its line for \(Q^+>Q^*\) adds the pointwise expression \(MSB[q^+]-MPC[q^+]\) to areas \(A+B+C\). A marginal value and a total welfare area have different dimensions; that printed expression should not be used as a complete total-welfare identity. The reliable comparison follows the marginal curves: beyond their intersection the extra activity has negative marginal social surplus, so its accumulated welfare effect is the integral of that negative difference. This dimensional clarification is agent synthesis of the diagram and the chapter's area definition. Lecture, physical PDF p. 18 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3–5

Why a cost reduction is not a new external benefit

Verhoef physical p. 4, printed pp. 202–203, Figure 13.1: normal market choice, negative external cost, positive external benefit and pecuniary benefit. The original spread has been rotated for readability. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 4

In panel (d), a lower private cost curve lowers social cost too, assuming the external cost function is unchanged. The new efficient output can increase, and lower market prices increase consumer surplus through a movement along MPB. That price-mediated benefit is pecuniary. The external wedge remains: new unrestricted output still exceeds the new optimum. Calling the extra consumer surplus an external benefit would wrongly suggest another subsidy on top of the remaining correction. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 4–5 Lecture, physical PDF p. 19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Four different policy concepts; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Four different policy concepts

Optimization means choosing an effect level consistent with optimal allocation under the potential Pareto criterion. Compensation is a transfer covering the receptor's welfare effect. Internalization, in the chapter's narrow terminology, removes the external character by creating a market for the effect or gathering interests, for example by merging an upstream and a downstream firm. Regulation is direct government intervention, including taxes, standards or permits. The chapter explicitly notes that Pigouvian taxation is often called internalization in broader usage, although it does not create a market and thus fails its narrow definition. The lecture uses both regulation and market creation in explaining remedies. Preserve that terminology difference rather than equating all four operations. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 5,9 note9 Lecture, physical PDF p. 28

A transfer need not optimize behaviour. If receptors are automatically reimbursed for residual harm or protective spending, they may have less reason to choose efficient defensive measures. Conversely, a negotiated payment under well-defined rights can coexist with efficient choice because the bargain itself governs the effect. The abatement-and-defence model shows why incentives at both sides matter. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 5–6 Lecture, physical PDF p. 28

O006-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Hypothetical smooth monetary curves per unit Q: \(\mathrm{MPB}=100-10Q, \mathrm{MPC}=20\); harmful activity \(\mathrm{MEC}=5Q\). Separately a beneficial-activity illustration has the same MPB/MPC and \(\mathrm{MEB}=2Q\). All optima interior, \(Q\ge 0\) and displayed linear curvatures maintained. Derive private and each social first-order condition from integrated welfare; compute \(Q_0\), harmful \(Q^{*}\), optimal marginal tax and remaining total damage, and beneficial \(Q^{*}\). State the concavity and units checks, why zero harm is not the goal, and why a private-cost reduction or compensation alone is not a new technological benefit or a complete incentive correction.

Steps and interpretation: Private derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}-\mathrm{MPC}=0\) gives \(Q_0=(100-20)/10=8.000000\). Harmful welfare derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}-\mathrm{MPC}-\mathrm{MEC}=80-(10+5)Q=0\) gives \(Q^{*}=5.333333\), curvature \(-(10+5)<0\). Tax \(t^{*}=\mathrm{MEC}(Q^{*})=26.666667\) money/unit, rather than total damage. Damage integral \(\int_0^{Q^{*}}5Q\,dQ=71.111111\) money, positive at optimum. \(W\) counts area benefits less costs; derivatives are money per unit \(Q\). Beneficial derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}+\mathrm{MEB}-\mathrm{MPC}=80-(10-2)Q=0\) gives \(Q^{*}=10.000000\); the displayed demand slope \(10>2\) makes curvature negative. Benefit-side correction is marginal subsidy \(\mathrm{MEB}(Q^{*})\) under the same first-best conditions. Private-cost reduction changes a priced schedule; it can raise consumer surplus without removing the external wedge, so not automatically a new neglected external benefit. Compensation distributes money; without changing the marginal objective it need not optimise behaviour. Feasibility/boundaries and other distortions can invalidate this simple tax/subsidy comparison; no literal-area-letter mixing between diagrams.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, derive private and social activity optima and marginal corrective signals.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Derive and calculate smooth private/social choices for negative and positive external effects, keeping marginal incentives separate from total harm.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Identify economic externalities and apply conditional welfare criteria
Check the foundations

Does ordinary competitive price reduction alone add \(\mathrm{MEB}\)?

Reveal foundation explanation

No; distinguish priced consumer benefit from a neglected real welfare relation before adding an external marginal benefit. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Marginal external cost: Additional neglected harm from one more activity unit.
  • Social optimum: A feasible activity level maximizing the specified total benefit less social cost.
  • Corrective tax: A marginal signal equal to marginal external harm at the first-best optimum under stated conditions.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
Let \(Q\) denote an activity level over a given period, \(MPB(Q)\) marginal private benefit, \(MPC(Q)\) marginal private cost, \(MEC(Q)\) marginal external cost and \(MEB(Q)\) marginal external benefit. Marginal quantities are money or welfare equivalents per unit of \(Q\), measured on a common basis. In the source's smooth partial-equilibrium diagrams, private choice satisfies

\[MPB(Q^0)=MPC(Q^0).\]

Without external effects this also maximizes the area between the benefit and cost curves. With negative external effects,

\[MSC(Q)=MPC(Q)+MEC(Q),\qquad MPB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*)+MEC(Q^*).\]

An explanatory mathematical reconstruction of the diagram is

\[W(Q)=\int_0^Q\big[MPB(q)-MPC(q)-MEC(q)\big]dq,\]

so that \(W'(Q)=MPB(Q)-MPC(Q)-MEC(Q)\). The interior optimum sets this derivative to zero;

a negative second derivative or suitable concavity is needed for a maximum. The source's increasing marginal external cost and decreasing net private benefit produce \(Q^*<Q^0\).

This formula is a synthesis of the source's areas, rather than an extra empirical model. It excludes other distortions and any fixed costs absent from the diagram.

Lecture physical PDF p. 15: the downward curve is marginal net private benefit (\(MNPB=MPB-MPC\)), the upward curve is MEC. At zero activity, the diagram normalizes welfare to zero.

At unrestricted \(Q_{max}\), private net benefit is \(A+B+C\) and damage is \(B+C+D\), giving \(A-D\). At \(Q_{optimum}\), private net benefit is \(A+B\), damage is \(B\), and welfare is \(A\).

The increase from restriction is \(D\), while \(B\) remains as optimal damage.

The lettered areas in this lecture figure differ from those in Verhoef's Figure 13.1. In the chapter's negative-externality panel, \(A\) denotes optimal external damage and \(C\) the deadweight loss avoided by restricting activity.

Area labels must always be read within their own figure. Optimization does not imply eliminating all external damage.

Nor is reducing production necessarily a strict Pareto improvement: the supplier loses private returns and would need appropriate compensation to satisfy that stronger criterion.

For a positive externality, social benefit is \(MSB=MPB+MEB\) and the condition is

\[MPB(Q^*)+MEB(Q^*)=MPC(Q^*).\]

The source's diagrams imply \(Q^*>Q^0\): the supplier otherwise omits part of the benefit. A correcting subsidy \(s^*=MEB(Q^*)\) can align the private choice, just as \(t^*=MEC(Q^*)\) can correct the negative externality in the simple setting. These are marginal, optimum-specific rates, not total damage divided arbitrarily by output.

Lecture p. 17: adding the external benefit raises MSB above MPB, moves the chosen output from \(Q^0\) toward \(Q^*\) and supplies the subsidy wedge \(s^*\).

The lecture p. 18 compares output below, at and above \(Q^*\) using coloured areas. Its line for \(Q^+>Q^*\) adds the pointwise expression \(MSB[q^+]-MPC[q^+]\) to areas \(A+B+C\).

A marginal value and a total welfare area have different dimensions; that printed expression should not be used as a complete total-welfare identity.

The reliable comparison follows the marginal curves: beyond their intersection the extra activity has negative marginal social surplus, so its accumulated welfare effect is the integral of that negative difference. This dimensional clarification is Explanation of the diagram and the chapter's area definition.

4.1 Why a cost reduction is not a new external benefit

Verhoef , printed pp. 202–203, Figure 13.1: normal market choice, negative external cost, positive external benefit and pecuniary benefit. The original spread has been rotated for readability.

In panel (d), a lower private cost curve lowers social cost too, assuming the external cost function is unchanged. The new efficient output can increase, and lower market prices increase consumer surplus through a movement along MPB.

That price-mediated benefit is pecuniary. The external wedge remains: new unrestricted output still exceeds the new optimum.

Calling the extra consumer surplus an external benefit would wrongly suggest another subsidy on top of the remaining correction.
sections.title: Derive the private and social activity levels

sections.html:
Optimization means choosing an effect level consistent with optimal allocation under the potential Pareto criterion. Compensation is a transfer covering the receptor's welfare effect. Internalization, in the chapter's narrow terminology, removes the external character by creating a market for the effect or gathering interests, for example by merging an upstream and a downstream firm. Regulation is direct government intervention, including taxes, standards or permits. The chapter explicitly notes that Pigouvian taxation is often called internalization in broader usage, although it does not create a market and thus fails its narrow definition.

Use both regulation and market creation in explaining remedies. Preserve that terminology difference rather than equating all four operations.

A transfer need not optimize behaviour. If receptors are automatically reimbursed for residual harm or protective spending, they may have less reason to choose efficient defensive measures. Conversely, a negotiated payment under well-defined rights can coexist with efficient choice because the bargain itself governs the effect. The abatement-and-defence model shows why incentives at both sides matter.

Explanation: Private derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}-\mathrm{MPC}=0\) gives \(Q_0=(110-22)/11=8.000000\). Harmful welfare derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}-\mathrm{MPC}-\mathrm{MEC}=88-(11+5)Q=0\) gives \(Q^{*}=5.500000\), curvature \(-(11+5)<0\).

derivatives are money per unit \(Q\). Beneficial derivative \(\mathrm{MPB}+\mathrm{MEB}-\mathrm{MPC}=88-(11-3)Q=0\) gives \(Q^{*}=11.000000\);

original_sections.html: Figure 13.2 uses its own area letters. At \(Q^{*}\), integrate \(\mathrm{MNPB}\) to get \(A+B+C\) and \(\mathrm{MEC}\) to get \(C\); social sum \(A+B\). Tax rectangle \(Q^*t^*=B+C\) is a transfer, not extra damage. Extending from \(Q^{*}\) to private \(Q_0\) adds \(D\) private gain and \(D+E\) damage, lowering welfare by \(E\). A restriction leaves producer \(A+B+C\) and victim \(-C\); tax additionally moves \(B+C\) to regulator; compensation moves \(C\) to the victim. Ideal rights-based negotiation trades the benefit of reducing/allowing output. Producer right: reduction sacrifices \(D\) and avoids \(D+E\) harm, so transfer bounds from \(D\) to \(D+E\); maximum presumes truthful no-above-\(Q_0\) threat. Victim right: permitting \(Q^{*}\) costs victim \(C\) and is worth \(A+B+C\) to the producer, giving bounds from \(C\) to \(A+B+C\). Rights choose transfer direction and bargaining picks its size. Enforceability, feasible transfers and low transaction costs underpin the ideal efficiency result; many victims and free-riding break easy coordination. Intra/inter-sector and marginal/total cost questions differ. Income-dependent monetary valuations can change policy comparisons without settling ethical equity. Uncertainty/heterogeneity and actual institutions limit the simple equivalence.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Coasean bargaining and its limitations; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Coasean bargaining and its limitations

The lecture illustrates bargaining with radio stations whose broadcasts interfere. With enforceable rights, transferable money, feasible ways of avoiding the harm and no transaction costs, the station with the higher-valued use can compensate the other to obtain that use. In the usual Coasean argument, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome regardless of initial rights, under the stated ideal conditions and with the lecture's uniqueness qualification. Initial rights still govern who pays whom and how surplus is distributed. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 23–24 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 3,7–8

Transaction costs include finding and coordinating participants, negotiating, monitoring and enforcing agreements. The lecture's factory facing a thousand landowners illustrates why the two-person ideal becomes difficult: individual victims can wait for others to finance the improvement. Missing environmental-quality rights and undepletable public-bad effects add difficulties. With transaction costs, the attainable allocation can depend on initial rights. The lecture's “Second Coase theorem” recommends institutions that reduce reallocation costs, while admitting that governments cannot know the highest-valued use without cost. This title is the lecture's wording, not a reason to omit its qualifications. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 26–27 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 3

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Efficiency and equity lead to different comparisons; fingerprint 529d959710600922cf0919bc4bb77ccd698aa1e4c411e91dcc19de2023f47e39. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Efficiency and equity lead to different comparisons

An efficient tax sets the marginal incentive; it need not equal the total unpaid bill. For an increasing MEC curve, the rectangle \(Q^*t^*\) can exceed the area of total external damage. In the chapter's linear diagram it is twice the optimal external damage \(A\). With constant MEC, marginal and average damage coincide. Thus the polluter-pays principle is ambiguous until one specifies payment of total damage, marginal incentive, or both. Willingness to pay or accept also depends on income: the same physical exposure can receive a larger money valuation for a richer receptor. Locating pollution where measured money damage is low can therefore conflict with equity concerns. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 6

Table 13.1, physical p. 7, printed p. 208. The efficiency question needs marginal external cost, individual aggregation and both intra- and intersectoral harm. The unpaid-bill question needs total external cost plus defensive outlays, sectoral aggregation and costs shifted outside the sector. Footnotes retain the qualifications on insurance and taxes. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7

A fixed annual insurance premium or ownership tax has little direct effect on the next kilometre driven. It can nevertheless matter to unpaid-bill accounting, with the table's restrictions: insurance payments must be compared with costs imposed outside the sector; ownership taxes cover unpaid costs only above infrastructure expenditure; fuel taxes used as Pigouvian corrections need a differential above ordinary indirect taxation, apart from second-best taxation questions. Existing transfers should therefore be evaluated against the actual research question. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7

Figure 13.2, physical p. 7, printed p. 209. Its letters belong to this figure, separately from Figure 13.1 and the lecture diagram. Here \(MNPB=MPB-MPC\) is marginal net private benefit in money per unit of activity \(Q\), and \(MEC\) is marginal external cost in the same units. The private choice \(Q^0\) has \(MNPB=0\); the social choice \(Q^*\) has \(MNPB=MEC=t^*\). The labelled areas integrate these marginal quantities and therefore measure money, rather than money per unit. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 7

To read the letters, start left of \(Q^*\). Area \(A\) lies between \(MNPB\) and the horizontal tax level \(t^*\); \(B\) lies between \(t^*\) and \(MEC\); \(C\) is below \(MEC\). Thus net private benefit through \(Q^*\) is \(A+B+C\), damage is \(C\), the tax rectangle is \(B+C\), and social welfare is \(A+B\). Right of \(Q^*\), \(D\) is below \(MNPB\) between \(Q^*\) and \(Q^0\), while \(E\) is between \(MEC\) and \(MNPB\). Continuing to \(Q^0\) adds private benefit \(D\) and damage \(D+E\), lowering social welfare by \(E\). Unrestricted private benefit is consequently \(A+B+C+D\), damage is \(C+D+E\), and their difference is \(A+B-E\). This construction makes every transfer in Table 13.2 interpretable without borrowing another diagram's letters. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8

Table 13.2, physical p. 8, printed p. 210. It compares distribution under a single producer, a single victim unable to defend itself, and the Figure 13.2 area convention. Parentheses denote transfers between producer and victim; square brackets denote transfers to the regulator. In the simple model all optimizing schemes yield social welfare \(A+B\), while non-intervention yields \(A+B-E\). Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8

A quantity restriction leaves producer welfare \(A+B+C\) and victim welfare \(-C\). A Pigouvian tax transfers \(B+C\) to the regulator, leaving producer welfare \(A\), victim welfare \(-C\) and the same social total. Direct compensation transfers \(C\) to the victim, leaving it at zero and the producer at \(A+B\). A merger gathers the interests into the common total. If the producer owns the right, the victim pays to reduce production: the two extreme-bargainer cases transfer \(D\) or \(D+E\) and leave the producer above its unrestricted welfare in one case. If the victim owns the right, the producer pays between \(C\) and \(A+B+C\) in the table's extreme cases. The upper payment \(D+E\) assumes truthful bargaining: chapter note 12 excludes a producer threatening output above the private choice \(Q^0\) to extract a larger payment. Verhoef Externalities, physical p. 9, printed p. 213, note 12 These are alternative distributional bounds, not simultaneous payments. The chapter consequently explains why producer and victim rank schemes differently and why political support for standards can differ from support for taxes. Revenue allocation is assumed ignored by both actors in the table's tax row. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 7–8

The tax-versus-quantity equivalence here relies on a deliberately simple model. Chapter note 8 warns that uncertainty and heterogeneity can break it; tradable permits also introduce a market absent from a plain quantity restriction. The instrument note explains cost effectiveness and enforcement, while the taxation note adds pre-existing fiscal distortions. Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF pp. 9 notes8,11 Lecture, physical PDF pp. 31–54

O007-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Hypothetical Figure 13.2 area convention (distinct from earlier diagrams): \(A=B=C=D=10\) money and \(E=20\). A producer and one victim can bargain with enforceable rights. Define each area geometrically through \(Q^{*}\)/\(Q_0\), \(\mathrm{MNPB}\) and \(\mathrm{MEC}\); derive unrestricted/private/damage/social totals. Compute producer/victim/regulator welfare under restriction, Pigouvian tax and direct compensation at \(Q^{*}\). Derive min/max transfers and resulting welfare when producer owns the right and when victim owns it. Explain Coase conditions, producer-truthfulness upper-bound qualification, why equal efficiency need not mean equal equity, and marginal-tax versus total-unpaid-bill/valuation limits.

Steps and interpretation: Left of \(Q^{*}\): \(A\) between \(\mathrm{MNPB}\) and horizontal \(t^{*}\), \(B\) between \(t^{*}\) and \(\mathrm{MEC}\), \(C\) below \(\mathrm{MEC}\). From \(Q^{*}\) to \(Q_0\): \(D\) below \(\mathrm{MNPB}\), \(E\) between \(\mathrm{MEC}\) and \(\mathrm{MNPB}\). Private welfare at \(Q^{*}\) is \(A+B+C=30\); damage \(C=10\); social \(A+B=20\); tax rectangle \(B+C=20\). Unrestricted private welfare is \(A+B+C+D = 40\), damage \(C+D+E=40\), social \(A+B-E=0\). Restriction: producer \(30\), victim \(-10\); tax: producer \(A=10\), victim \(-10\), regulator \(B+C=20\); compensation transfer \(C=10\): producer \(20\), victim \(0\), same total \(20\). Producer owns the right: victim pays \(D=10\) minimum (producer’s lost private gain) through \(D+E=30\) maximum (victim’s avoided damage); at \(Q^{*}\) producer \(A+B+C+\text{transfer}\) ranges from \(40\) to \(60\), victim \(-C-\text{transfer}\) ranges from \(-20\) to \(-40\); total \(A+B=20\) always. Upper bound requires truthful producer not threatening above \(Q_0\). Victim owns the right: producer pays from \(C=10\) to \(A+B+C=30\), so producer welfare ranges from \(20\) to \(0\) and victim welfare ranges from \(0\) to \(20\). These are alternative bargaining extremes, not simultaneous payments. Coase needs enforceable rights, feasible money transfers and sufficiently low transaction/coordination costs; many victims/public-bad free riding can obstruct negotiation. Rights change transfers, not the ideal efficient \(Q^{*}\), but transaction costs can change attainable allocation. Efficiency does not determine fair distribution; marginal incentive and total damage differ (tax rectangle \(20\) versus total damage \(10\) here), while income-sensitive willingness-to-pay can conflict with equity. A fixed insurance/ownership payment may compensate but not price another kilometre; sector unpaid-bill accounting needs its own boundary and defence expenditures.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, compare bargaining and policy transfers without confusing efficiency and equity.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Derive local welfare areas
  • Compare conditional policy/bargaining distributions at an efficient allocation.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Derive private and social activity optima and marginal corrective signals
Check the foundations

At \(Q^{*}\) do private andsocial objectives have to give the same distribution?

Reveal foundation explanation

No. Social optimum fixes the conditional marginal balance; rights/taxes/compensation can distribute its aggregate surplus differently. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Bargaining range: Transfers acceptable to both sides under the declared rights and alternatives.
  • Efficiency: Maximizing the specified aggregate surplus.
  • Equity: The distribution of outcomes, not determined by equal total surplus.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The lecture illustrates bargaining with radio stations whose broadcasts interfere. With enforceable rights, transferable money, feasible ways of avoiding the harm and no transaction costs, the station with the higher-valued use can compensate the other to obtain that use.

In the usual Coasean argument, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome regardless of initial rights, under the stated ideal conditions and with the lecture's uniqueness qualification. Initial rights still govern who pays whom and how surplus is distributed.

Transaction costs include finding and coordinating participants, negotiating, monitoring and enforcing agreements. The lecture's factory facing a thousand landowners illustrates why the two-person ideal becomes difficult: individual victims can wait for others to finance the improvement.

Missing environmental-quality rights and undepletable public-bad effects add difficulties. With transaction costs, the attainable allocation can depend on initial rights.

The lecture's “Second Coase theorem” recommends institutions that reduce reallocation costs, while admitting that governments cannot know the highest-valued use without cost. This title is the lecture's wording, not a reason to omit its qualifications.
sections.title: Coasean bargaining and its limitations

sections.html:
An efficient tax sets the marginal incentive; it need not equal the total unpaid bill.

For an increasing MEC curve, the rectangle \(Q^*t^*\) can exceed the area of total external damage. In the chapter's linear diagram it is twice the optimal external damage \(A\).

With constant MEC, marginal and average damage coincide. Thus the polluter-pays principle is ambiguous until one specifies payment of total damage, marginal incentive, or both.

Willingness to pay or accept also depends on income: the same physical exposure can receive a larger money valuation for a richer receptor. Locating pollution where measured money damage is low can therefore conflict with equity concerns.

Table 13.1, , printed p. 208. The efficiency question needs marginal external cost, individual aggregation and both intra- and intersectoral harm. The unpaid-bill question needs total external cost plus defensive outlays, sectoral aggregation and costs shifted outside the sector. Footnotes retain the qualifications on insurance and taxes.

A fixed annual insurance premium or ownership tax has little direct effect on the next kilometre driven. It can nevertheless matter to unpaid-bill accounting, with the table's restrictions: insurance payments must be compared with costs imposed outside the sector;

ownership taxes cover unpaid costs only above infrastructure expenditure; fuel taxes used as Pigouvian corrections need a differential above ordinary indirect taxation, apart from second-best taxation questions.

Existing transfers should therefore be evaluated against the actual research question.

Figure 13.2, , printed p. 209. Its letters belong to this figure, separately from Figure 13.1 and the lecture diagram. Here \(MNPB=MPB-MPC\) is marginal net private benefit in money per unit of activity \(Q\), and \(MEC\) is marginal external cost in the same units.

The private choice \(Q^0\) has \(MNPB=0\); the social choice \(Q^*\) has \(MNPB=MEC=t^*\).

The labelled areas integrate these marginal quantities and therefore measure money, rather than money per unit.

To read the letters, start left of \(Q^*\). Area \(A\) lies between \(MNPB\) and the horizontal tax level \(t^*\); \(B\) lies between \(t^*\) and \(MEC\); \(C\) is below \(MEC\).

Thus net private benefit through \(Q^*\) is \(A+B+C\), damage is \(C\), the tax rectangle is \(B+C\), and social welfare is \(A+B\). Right of \(Q^*\), \(D\) is below \(MNPB\) between \(Q^*\) and \(Q^0\), while \(E\) is between \(MEC\) and \(MNPB\).

Continuing to \(Q^0\) adds private benefit \(D\) and damage \(D+E\), lowering social welfare by \(E\). Unrestricted private benefit is consequently \(A+B+C+D\), damage is \(C+D+E\), and their difference is \(A+B-E\).

This construction makes every transfer in Table 13.2 interpretable without borrowing another diagram's letters.

Table 13.2, , printed p. 210. It compares distribution under a single producer, a single victim unable to defend itself, and the Figure 13.2 area convention. Parentheses denote transfers between producer and victim; square brackets denote transfers to the regulator. In the simple model all optimizing schemes yield social welfare \(A+B\), while non-intervention yields \(A+B-E\).

A quantity restriction leaves producer welfare \(A+B+C\) and victim welfare \(-C\). A Pigouvian tax transfers \(B+C\) to the regulator, leaving producer welfare \(A\), victim welfare \(-C\) and the same social total.

Direct compensation transfers \(C\) to the victim, leaving it at zero and the producer at \(A+B\). A merger gathers the interests into the common total.

If the producer owns the right, the victim pays to reduce production: the two extreme-bargainer cases transfer \(D\) or \(D+E\) and leave the producer above its unrestricted welfare in one case. If the victim owns the right, the producer pays between \(C\) and \(A+B+C\) in the table's extreme cases.

The upper payment \(D+E\) assumes truthful bargaining: chapter note 12 excludes a producer threatening output above the private choice \(Q^0\) to extract a larger payment. These are alternative distributional bounds, not simultaneous payments.

The chapter consequently explains why producer and victim rank schemes differently and why political support for standards can differ from support for taxes. Revenue allocation is assumed ignored by both actors in the table's tax row.

The tax-versus-quantity equivalence here relies on a deliberately simple model. Chapter note 8 warns that uncertainty and heterogeneity can break it; tradable permits also introduce a market absent from a plain quantity restriction. The instrument note explains cost effectiveness and enforcement, while the taxation note adds pre-existing fiscal distortions.

Explanation: Left of \(Q^{*}\): \(A\) between \(\mathrm{MNPB}\) and horizontal \(t^{*}\), \(B\) between \(t^{*}\) and \(\mathrm{MEC}\), \(C\) below \(\mathrm{MEC}\). From \(Q^{*}\) to \(Q_0\): \(D\) below \(\mathrm{MNPB}\), \(E\) between \(\mathrm{MEC}\) and \(\mathrm{MNPB}\).

Private welfare at \(Q^{*}\) is \(A+B+C=105\); damage \(C=35\);

social \(A+B=70\); tax rectangle \(B+C=70\).

Unrestricted private welfare is \(A+B+C+D = 140\), damage \(C+D+E=140\), social \(A+B-E=0\). Restriction: producer \(105\), victim \(-35\);

tax: producer \(A=35\), victim \(-35\), regulator \(B+C=70\); compensation transfer \(C=35\): producer \(70\), victim \(0\), same total \(70\).

Producer owns the right: victim pays \(D=35\) minimum (producer’s lost private gain) through \(D+E=105\) maximum (victim’s avoided damage); at \(Q^{*}\) producer \(A+B+C+\text{transfer}\) ranges from \(140\) to \(210\), victim \(-C-\text{transfer}\) ranges from \(-70\) to \(-140\);

total \(A+B=70\) always. Upper bound requires truthful producer not threatening above \(Q_0\).

Victim owns the right: producer pays from \(C=35\) to \(A+B+C=105\), so producer welfare ranges from \(70\) to \(0\) and victim welfare ranges from \(0\) to \(70\). These are alternative bargaining extremes, not simultaneous payments.

Coase needs enforceable rights, feasible money transfers and sufficiently low transaction/coordination costs; many victims/public-bad free riding can obstruct negotiation.

Rights change transfers, not the ideal efficient \(Q^{*}\), but transaction costs can change attainable allocation. Efficiency does not determine fair distribution;

marginal incentive and total damage differ (tax rectangle \(70\) versus total damage \(35\) here), while income-sensitive willingness-to-pay can conflict with equity. A fixed insurance/ownership payment may compensate but not price another kilometre;

sector unpaid-bill accounting needs its own boundary and defence expenditures. All components are required.

original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Activity abatement and defence are jointly chosen

The basic output diagram makes harm depend only on \(Q\). The richer model allows the supplier to reduce damage through abatement (for example quieter/cleaner vehicles) and the receptor to reduce exposure through defensive measures (for example double glazing). Let \(Q\) be the externality-causing activity, \(A\) monetary abatement outlays by the supplier, \(D\) monetary defensive outlays by the victim, and \(EC\) the residual or net external cost after those measures:

\[EC=EC(Q,D,A).\]

The article sometimes writes the argument order \((Q,A,D)\); variable names consistently identify the same three inputs. With \(PC(Q)\) private production cost, the distinctions are

\[\begin{aligned} \text{gross private cost}&=PC(Q)+A,\\ \text{gross external cost}&=EC(Q,D,A)+D,\\ \text{social cost of the activity}&=PC(Q)+A+EC(Q,D,A)+D. \end{aligned}\]

Defensive expenditure consumes real resources even if it succeeds in reducing experienced harm. Ignoring it treats an externally induced expense as costless. Abatement is included on the supplier's side rather than being added automatically to the receptor's unpaid bill. The article cautions that this explicit supplier/victim split fits environmental nuisance better than congestion or accidents, where the same road user can be on both sides. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 6, equation1 and footnote5

Assumptions and derivative notation

A subscript denotes a partial derivative holding the other arguments fixed: \(EC_Q=\partial EC/\partial Q\), \(EC_{DD}=\partial^2 EC/\partial D^2\), and so forth. The paper assumes

\[EC_Q>0,\quad EC_{QQ}\geq0;\qquad EC_D<0,\quad EC_{DD}>0;\qquad EC_A<0,\quad EC_{AA}>0.\]

Activity raises residual damage at a nondecreasing marginal rate. Spending on defence or abatement reduces it, but each additional money unit has diminishing damage-reduction effectiveness. For smooth functions it also postulates

\[EC_{DQ}=EC_{QD}<0,\qquad EC_{AQ}=EC_{QA}<0,\qquad EC_{AD}=EC_{DA}>0.\]

More activity gives protective outlays more damage to reduce; protection lowers the damage added by extra activity. The positive cross derivative between \(A\) and \(D\) means greater protection on one side reduces the marginal effectiveness of the other side. These are assumed functional properties for the model's likely case, not measured transport coefficients. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7, equations2a–i

Let \(PB(Q)\) be private benefit and define net private benefit as \(NPB(Q)=PB(Q)-PC(Q)\). The displayed equation makes this a difference, although the source's adjacent prose mistakenly calls it a “sum”; the subtraction is also used in its welfare function. The assumption \(NPB_{QQ}<0\) means diminishing marginal net private benefit. Supplier welfare and victim welfare are

\[W^p=NPB(Q)-A,\qquad W^v=-EC(Q,D,A)-D.\]

Summing them gives

\[W=NPB(Q)-EC(Q,D,A)-A-D.\]

The monetary units of \(A\) and \(D\) are crucial: a one-unit increase directly costs one unit of welfare in this money-valued representation. The model's additive welfare measure abstracts from additional income effects or heterogeneous welfare weights. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7, equations3–6

Derive and interpret the efficient conditions

Differentiate the welfare expression with respect to each choice:

\[\begin{aligned} W_Q&=NPB_Q-EC_Q=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad NPB_Q=EC_Q,\\ W_A&=-EC_A-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_A=-1,\\ W_D&=-EC_D-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_D=-1. \end{aligned}\]

The first condition balances the benefit sacrificed by reducing activity against the avoided damage. The second and third say that a last money unit spent on either abatement or defence avoids one money unit of residual harm. Together, all three available ways of reducing external cost have the same marginal efficiency. They apply to an interior solution. Boundary constraints can instead prevent an equality, and the paper's footnote7 requires the relevant Hessian conditions for a welfare maximum; stationarity alone is insufficient. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 7–8, equations7a–c

Without a mechanism making residual damage enter the supplier's objective, it chooses \(Q\) to maximize \(NPB\) and has no benefit from \(A\) in \(W^p\), so the simple model predicts excessive activity and zero abatement. A victim who bears both damage and protective cost already faces the \(D\) tradeoff and can behave efficiently on that margin. Automatic compensation can alter this incentive. This motivates policies aimed first at reducing activity and inducing abatement, while examining what compensation does to defence. It is a result of the model's separation of objectives, not a universal prediction that every real driver makes no voluntary abatement investment. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 8

Minimizing the activity's social cost alone would select no activity and no outlays, whereas maximizing welfare balances costs against benefits. The paper contrasts this with a nuisance-based cost convention including foregone production: different definitions can make a “minimum social cost” statement mean a different optimization problem. Always identify the accounting boundary before using that phrase. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 8, footnote8

Prompt: Hypothetical supplier/victim model at an interior candidate: \(\mathrm{NPB}_{Q}=3\), \(\mathrm{EC}_{Q}=4\), \(\mathrm{EC}_{A}=-1.5\), \(\mathrm{EC}_{D}=-0.5\); money outlays \(A=5\) and \(D=4\), residual \(\mathrm{EC}=10\), private benefit \(\mathrm{PB}=50\) and private cost \(\mathrm{PC}=20\). Why is minimising activity cost alone not the same as welfare optimisation, and why does the supplier/victim split have limits for congestion/accidents?

Steps and interpretation: \(\mathrm{NPB}=\mathrm{PB}-\mathrm{PC}=30\). Supplier \(W=\mathrm{NPB}-A=25\); victim \(W=-\mathrm{EC}-D=-14\); aggregate \(W=\mathrm{NPB}-\mathrm{EC}-A-D=11\). Gross private \(\mathrm{PC}+A=25\), gross external \(\mathrm{EC}+D=14\), social cost \(\mathrm{PC}+A+\mathrm{EC}+D=39\). Interior FOCs:\(W_{Q}=\mathrm{NPB}_{Q}-\mathrm{EC}_{Q}=0, W_{A}=-\mathrm{EC}_{A}-1=0, W_{D}=-\mathrm{EC}_{D}-1=0\), hence \(NPB_Q=EC_Q\) and \(\mathrm{EC}_A=\mathrm{EC}_D=-1\). Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Abatement A: Supplier protection expenditure in the stated model.
  • Defence D: Victim expenditure reducing exposure or harm.
  • Residual external cost: Damage left after the stated activity/protection choices.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The basic output diagram makes harm depend only on \(Q\). The richer model allows the supplier to reduce damage through abatement (for example quieter/cleaner vehicles) and the receptor to reduce exposure through defensive measures (for example double glazing).

Let \(Q\) be the externality-causing activity, \(A\) monetary abatement outlays by the supplier, \(D\) monetary defensive outlays by the victim, and \(EC\) the residual or net external cost after those measures:

\[EC=EC(Q,D,A).\]

The article sometimes writes the argument order \((Q,A,D)\); variable names consistently identify the same three inputs. With \(PC(Q)\) private production cost, the distinctions are

\[\begin{aligned} \text{gross private cost}&=PC(Q)+A,\\ \text{gross external cost}&=EC(Q,D,A)+D,\\ \text{social cost of the activity}&=PC(Q)+A+EC(Q,D,A)+D. \end{aligned}\]

Defensive expenditure consumes real resources even if it succeeds in reducing experienced harm. Ignoring it treats an externally induced expense as costless.

Abatement is included on the supplier's side rather than being added automatically to the receptor's unpaid bill. The article cautions that this explicit supplier/victim split fits environmental nuisance better than congestion or accidents, where the same road user can be on both sides.

4.1 Assumptions and derivative notation

A subscript denotes a partial derivative holding the other arguments fixed: \(EC_Q=\partial EC/\partial Q\), \(EC_{DD}=\partial^2 EC/\partial D^2\), and so forth. The paper assumes

\[EC_Q>0,\quad EC_{QQ}\geq0;\qquad EC_D<0,\quad EC_{DD}>0;\qquad EC_A<0,\quad EC_{AA}>0.\]

Activity raises residual damage at a nondecreasing marginal rate. Spending on defence or abatement reduces it, but each additional money unit has diminishing damage-reduction effectiveness. For smooth functions it also postulates

\[EC_{DQ}=EC_{QD}<0,\qquad EC_{AQ}=EC_{QA}<0,\qquad EC_{AD}=EC_{DA}>0.\]

More activity gives protective outlays more damage to reduce; protection lowers the damage added by extra activity. The positive cross derivative between \(A\) and \(D\) means greater protection on one side reduces the marginal effectiveness of the other side. These are assumed functional properties for the model's likely case, not measured transport coefficients.

Let \(PB(Q)\) be private benefit and define net private benefit as \(NPB(Q)=PB(Q)-PC(Q)\). The displayed equation makes this a difference, although the source's adjacent prose mistakenly calls it a “sum”; the subtraction is also used in its welfare function. The assumption \(NPB_{QQ}<0\) means diminishing marginal net private benefit. Supplier welfare and victim welfare are

\[W^p=NPB(Q)-A,\qquad W^v=-EC(Q,D,A)-D.\]

Summing them gives

\[W=NPB(Q)-EC(Q,D,A)-A-D.\]

The monetary units of \(A\) and \(D\) are crucial: a one-unit increase directly costs one unit of welfare in this money-valued representation. The model's additive welfare measure abstracts from additional income effects or heterogeneous welfare weights.

4.2 Derive and interpret the efficient conditions

Differentiate the welfare expression with respect to each choice:

\[\begin{aligned} W_Q&=NPB_Q-EC_Q=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad NPB_Q=EC_Q,\\ W_A&=-EC_A-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_A=-1,\\ W_D&=-EC_D-1=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad EC_D=-1. \end{aligned}\]

The first condition balances the benefit sacrificed by reducing activity against the avoided damage. The second and third say that a last money unit spent on either abatement or defence avoids one money unit of residual harm.

Together, all three available ways of reducing external cost have the same marginal efficiency. They apply to an interior solution.

Boundary constraints can instead prevent an equality, and the paper's footnote7 requires the relevant Hessian conditions for a welfare maximum; stationarity alone is insufficient.

Without a mechanism making residual damage enter the supplier's objective, it chooses \(Q\) to maximize \(NPB\) and has no benefit from \(A\) in \(W^p\), so the simple model predicts excessive activity and zero abatement. A victim who bears both damage and protective cost already faces the \(D\) tradeoff and can behave efficiently on that margin.

Automatic compensation can alter this incentive. This motivates policies aimed first at reducing activity and inducing abatement, while examining what compensation does to defence.

It is a result of the model's separation of objectives, not a universal prediction that every real driver makes no voluntary abatement investment.

Minimizing the activity's social cost alone would select no activity and no outlays, whereas maximizing welfare balances costs against benefits. The paper contrasts this with a nuisance-based cost convention including foregone production: different definitions can make a “minimum social cost” statement mean a different optimization problem. Always identify the accounting boundary before using that phrase.

original_sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

original_sections.html: Define who causes/receives effects and whether the boundary is the individual, sector or whole society. Residual damage \(\mathrm{EC}\) excludes receptor protection D; gross burden \(\mathrm{EC}+D\) includes both, while abatement A is on the supplier side. Congestion and accidents can be external to an individual but inside the sector. Efficient pricing asks for marginal cost at a time/place; the unpaid bill asks for a consistently bounded total. Damage×market price methods and behavioural valuation (surrogate markets or hypothetical survey) measure different components and uncertainty; higher WTP is not automatically verified complete harm. Complementarity needs nonoverlap. Investment stocks require annualisation before comparison with annual GDP. Historical noise/pollution/accident tables vary in years, currency, standards and valuation; preserve attribution and limitations rather than memorising old amounts. Accident risk valuation/insurance boundaries matter; transport usefulness/infrastructure development does not remove a trip’s external wedge.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Transport benefits and external benefits are different; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Transport benefits and external benefits are different

The article requires a real variable in a receptor's utility/profit function whose value depends on a supplier's behaviour and is omitted from that supplier's decision. Ordinary economic dependencies through prices are excluded from this definition. In the paper's simple Figure 1, external costs push unrestricted activity beyond its efficient level, while external benefits would justify encouragement. A downward private-cost shift can increase consumer surplus while leaving the external-cost wedge intact. Thus useful transport and technological external benefit are different propositions. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 2–3

The author finds no significant external benefits of individual road transport activities, apart from a possible car-spotter example. Cheaper production, wider product choice and faster delivery generally enter market transactions; associated employment and value added do not justify transport above its optimum. Visits to friends can reflect reciprocal exchange or deliberate altruism. Infrastructure's contribution to accessibility and regional development belongs to the investment appraisal, rather than being credited as an external benefit of each extra trip. Better emergency access also depends on infrastructure; more traffic may instead obstruct it through congestion. These conclusions are the author's classifications under the stated market framework, including the assumption of no distortions elsewhere when tracing market benefits to final consumers. They do not say transport has no private or social benefit. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 4–6

Classify the harm and its incidence

Figure 2, physical PDF p. 4 (printed p. 276), also reproduced in lecture p. 11. Rows separate intra-sectoral harm among road users from ecological and social environmental harm; columns separate moving traffic, stationary vehicles and infrastructure-associated effects. Shading represents first-order incidence. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 4

Congestion lies largely within the sector; noise affects social surroundings; air, water and soil pollution reach ecological surroundings; accidents have several incidences, including fellow road users and people outside the sector, and hazardous-material accidents can harm ecosystems. Parking consumes public space and can create parking congestion. Infrastructure can sever biotopes, create visual annoyance or impose barriers within communities. The article displays this broad typology but explicitly excludes environmental effects caused by the mere presence of infrastructure from its later analysis. A second-order effect can connect categories: congestion increases emissions per vehicle-kilometre. Severity is sensitive to time and place. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 4, footnote2

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures

One question asks for optimal marginal choices or road prices. The other asks what total burden transport shifts to other people. The second requires \(EC+D\), rather than residual damage alone. Average gross burden indicates an optimal marginal rate only under additional conditions such as constant marginal external cost; total harm divided by total kilometres generally does not supply a time-and-place-specific optimal price. There is no single aggregate optimal road-transport quantity independent of location and time. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 8

The level of aggregation matters too. Harm imposed by one motorist on another is external to the first motorist but remains inside the motorist sector. Adding that harm to environmental damage can be appropriate for some social-cost questions, but it cannot be labelled without qualification as the sector's unpaid bill to the rest of society. This distinction becomes especially important in accident accounting. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 8–9

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Accidents: risk valuation and aggregation; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Accidents: risk valuation and aggregation

Accident costs can include vehicle/property/environmental damage, legal/police/emergency costs, medical/funeral costs, pain and suffering and lost production. Responsibility can be shared in a chain collision; a responsible driver's own injury can impose further losses on relatives and society. Some published studies define social accident costs as total costs less insurance coverage, which differs from the article's earlier total private-plus-external social-cost definition. Fixed yearly insurance premiums can compensate losses without pricing the marginal kilometre, so compensation does not establish optimized accident risk. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 12–13, footnote12

Valuing life solely through expected net production can give negative values for elderly or jobless people. The author instead favours ex ante valuation of changes in physical risk. Historical estimates differ substantially by concept: the paper cites ECU 12,280 for gross earnings in Portugal, ECU 1,667,246 for social willingness to pay in Switzerland, and an even lower Netherlands friction-cost estimate of DFL 2,400 (about ECU 1,000). These are evidence of incompatible valuation concepts rather than comparable prices of a human being. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 13–14

Table 3, PDF p. 13, printed p. 285. The original source clips some text at the right margin; the legible numerical columns and method distinctions are retained. These are social accident costs with varied boundaries, not one consistently defined environmental external-cost series. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 13

The Swiss Neuenschwander et al. (1991) rows give SF 5,379 million / 1.70% GDP in social costs, SF 1,488 million / 0.47% GDP in external cost at individual level, and SF 789 million / 0.25% GDP at mode level. The footnote on PDF p. 12 likewise contrasts individual and mode aggregation for car traffic and reports a larger proportional reduction for rail traffic. Changing the analytical boundary changes what is external. The paper therefore warns against adding these accident totals to noise and air-pollution external costs and calling the result transport's external burden. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 12 footnote11,13–14

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Topic map of the paper; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Topic map of the paper

The diagram follows sections 2–6 and the qualifications in the original, physical PDF pp. 1–14 (printed pp. 273–286). Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 1–14

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Why noise and air-pollution estimates can undercount; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Why noise and air-pollution estimates can undercount

The paper evaluates the studies in Tables 1 and 2 as mostly unpaid-bill studies, not estimations of the welfare-maximizing activity. A recurring problem is estimating one component of gross external cost instead of \(EC+D\). Actual protective expenditure measures part of \(D\) while omitting remaining damage. A valuation of experienced harm measures part of \(EC\) while omitting induced protective expenditure. Studies using abatement expenditure \(A\) measure a different component again. The paper's exceptions combining prevention and residual damage try to assess an optimal rather than actual situation, and their choice of optimum is unclear. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 9–10

Shortcuts and choice of a standard

Using observed protection outlays as the entire loss assumes away the harm that remains after rational protection. Usually victims stop protection while another reduction in nuisance would still have value, because additional spending competes with other consumption. Using the hypothetical cost of a programme that reduces nuisance to a supposedly reasonable level has three further problems: it omits remaining damage, replaces the value of the damage reduction with the programme cost, and selects the standard before the cost/benefit balance that should determine it. The IRT France estimates vary by a factor of six with the noise standard; the Dutch Van der Meijs estimates differ by factors of nine for noise and twelve for pollution. These illustrate dependence on an imposed norm, not precision about the underlying welfare loss. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 10–11, footnotes9–10

What valuation techniques measure

Nonbehavioural linkage methods start with a damage or dose-response relationship and multiply physical impacts by market prices: building deterioration, agricultural damage or cost of illness are examples. They do not directly recover the receptor's utility loss and can omit non-use values. Behavioural linkage methods infer valuation from choices in a surrogate market, such as hedonic house prices, travel costs or household protection, or from a hypothetical market, such as a contingent-valuation willingness-to-pay survey. Surrogate markets may be absent or regulated; hypothetical responses have methodological uncertainty. The author prefers utility-linked valuation conceptually but does not rank one method as universally best. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 11–12

Some methods can be complementary if they measure genuinely different components. The example is psychological willingness to pay combined with costs, such as paid sick leave, that may not enter an individual's optimization. This is a conditional argument for assessing omitted components, not permission to add overlapping valuations blindly. The article notes that both behavioural and nonbehavioural estimates can still capture only net damage. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 12

Read the historical tables

Table 1, PDF p. 9, printed p. 281. Columns retain authors/year/country, original monetary units, GDP shares and measurement methods. The footnote identifies GDP data from IMF (1991) and estimates quoted through Quinet (1989). Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 9

The road-noise row for Dogs et al. (1991), Germany, reports DM 0.84 billion / 0.03% GDP for avoidance cost versus DM 12.8 billion / 0.52% GDP for willingness to pay. This is about fifteen times as large, but the comparison concerns distinct methods rather than two independently comparable estimates of identical complete costs. The UK Sharp estimate of 11.18% GDP is particularly high because the study did not spread outlays over their useful years; a stock of investment should not be compared unadjusted with annual GDP. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 9,11–12

Table 2, PDF p. 10, printed p. 282. The source retains the distinct damage, programme-cost and WTP approaches and warns that some rows include noise or all transport modes. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 10

Dogs et al.'s road-pollution rows report DM 12.1 billion / 0.49% GDP for damage cost and DM 22.3 billion / 0.91% GDP for WTP. Shulz's table contrasts DM 3–6 billion / 0.15–0.30% GDP for damage with DM 5–16 billion / 0.25–0.79% GDP for willingness to pay; each is attributed to 30% of the corresponding total air-pollution burden/value. Higher survey figures can indicate understatement by other methods or difficulties in contingent valuation. The article does not establish the larger figure as the true complete loss. Its review of hedonic noise studies reports house-price reductions of 0.15–1.3% per extra decibel, dependent on the zero-annoyance baseline and study setting. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 10,12

The conclusion challenges frequently cited OECD-country figures of 0.1% GDP for noise and 0.4% for air pollution. It suggests possible multipliers of eight for noise and two or three for air pollution if hypothetical valuations are trusted. The author also identifies omitted effects, including then-unestimated CO₂ emissions and other Figure 2 categories. These are the 1994 review's criticism and conditional numerical comparisons; they are not present-day GDP shares, statistical confidence intervals or a new aggregate estimate. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF p. 14

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the review establishes; fingerprint cc396e42c7c4541affc1793168ef6857bb6cf76f1e847ce27f397ae86f77b0fd. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What the review establishes

Transport's value to users and markets does not cancel a technological externality. A consistent assessment must specify the activity, who causes/receives effects, the aggregation boundary, and whether it measures residual damage, protective resources or both. Efficiency requires a joint marginal analysis; an unpaid-bill calculation needs the correctly bounded total. The survey's strongest conclusion is the conceptual incompleteness and noncomparability of many historical estimates, with contingent-valuation uncertainty and accident-specific complications retained. Verhoef 1994, physical PDF pp. 6–14

O009-W1 / item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Hypothetical survey of noise and road use: measured residual harm \(\mathrm{EC}=20\), induced receptor defence \(D=5\), supplier abatement \(A=4\), of \(\mathrm{EC}\) an identified 6 is borne by fellow road users within the sector. Separately a historical row reports protection investment stock 100 against annual GDP 1000. Derive a consistently bounded outside-sector unpaid bill given all D is borne outside; contrast residual-only, defence-only and abatement-only measures. Explain why that total / traffic is not automatically optimal marginal tax, how transport benefits/typology differ, and why stock/annual flow and survey valuation methods and overlap make historical tables noncomparable. Include accident risk versus production-value and insurance/aggregation qualifications; does an old GDP share prove current physical damage?

Steps and interpretation: Outside residual \(\mathrm{EC}=20-6=14\); all D outside gives bill \(\mathrm{EC}_{out}+D=19\). Residual-only omits defence, defence-only omits remaining harm, and A is supplier real cost, not automatically the victim’s unpaid bill. Whole individual harm \(\mathrm{EC}+D=25\) has another aggregation boundary; social cost may include \(\mathrm{PC}+A\) as well. Total/traffic is an average; optimal rate uses marginal time/place harm under defined conditions, not generally the average. Ordinary priced transport benefits/employment do not cancel a technological external wedge; infrastructure access benefits are investment appraisal, not automatic trip \(\mathrm{MEB}\). Typology separates intra-sector/environment and moving/stationary/infrastructure; the later paper excludes mere infrastructure presence. The stock-to-annual-GDP ratio is \(\frac{100\ \mathrm{currency\ units}}{1000\ \mathrm{currency\ units/year}}=0.1\ \mathrm{years}\): a stock-to-annual-flow ratio with time units, rather than an annual GDP cost share. An annual cost comparison requires annualisation (useful-life/assumptions absent). Dose-response×market price may omit utility/nonuse; surrogate hedonic/travel/defence and hypothetical WTP each have availability/bias/boundaries. Add methods only for genuinely nonoverlapping components; preset noise-standard programme cost is neither full harm nor an optimal standard. Ex-ante risk-change WTP differs from net earnings-life valuation, which can misrepresent elderly/jobless; fixed insurance compensation does not necessarily price marginal risk. Accident individual/sector aggregation changes externality classification, so adding all accident totals to noise/pollution can mix boundaries. Historically dated currencies and GDP shares do not establish present physical damage or current values.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: AddingA automatically to the unpaid bill; ignoringD; sector-internal harm labelled as outside-sector bill; average called marginal tax; adding overlapping valuations; stock treated as annual flow; old estimates treated as current.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.
