sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, audit transport cost estimates by welfare component, valuation and aggregation.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Audit a supplied transport estimate for omitted cost components and incompatible valuation/aggregation rather than treating historical tables as current totals.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Derive joint activity, abatement and defence conditions in the transport model
Check the foundations

Ifresidual EC10 and defence D3, is gross receptor burden10?

Reveal foundation explanation

No:\(\mathrm{EC}+D=13\) with a matched boundary, because defence consumes resources. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Unpaid external bill: The specified outside residual harm plus outside defence expenditure.
  • Marginal damage: The harm from an additional activity unit at its relevant time/place.
  • Stock-to-flow ratio: A ratio carrying time units when a stock is divided by an annual flow.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The article requires a real variable in a receptor's utility/profit function whose value depends on a supplier's behaviour and is omitted from that supplier's decision. Ordinary economic dependencies through prices are excluded from this definition.

In the paper's simple Figure 1, external costs push unrestricted activity beyond its efficient level, while external benefits would justify encouragement. A downward private-cost shift can increase consumer surplus while leaving the external-cost wedge intact.

Thus useful transport and technological external benefit are different propositions.

The author finds no significant external benefits of individual road transport activities, apart from a possible car-spotter example. Cheaper production, wider product choice and faster delivery generally enter market transactions;

associated employment and value added do not justify transport above its optimum. Visits to friends can reflect reciprocal exchange or deliberate altruism.

Infrastructure's contribution to accessibility and regional development belongs to the investment appraisal, rather than being credited as an external benefit of each extra trip. Better emergency access also depends on infrastructure;

more traffic may instead obstruct it through congestion. These conclusions are the author's classifications under the stated market framework, including the assumption of no distortions elsewhere when tracing market benefits to final consumers.

They do not say transport has no private or social benefit.

4.1 Classify the harm and its incidence

Figure 2, physical PDF p. 4 (printed p. 276), also reproduced in lecture p. 11. Rows separate intra-sectoral harm among road users from ecological and social environmental harm; columns separate moving traffic, stationary vehicles and infrastructure-associated effects. Shading represents first-order incidence.

Congestion lies largely within the sector; noise affects social surroundings;

air, water and soil pollution reach ecological surroundings; accidents have several incidences, including fellow road users and people outside the sector, and hazardous-material accidents can harm ecosystems.

Parking consumes public space and can create parking congestion. Infrastructure can sever biotopes, create visual annoyance or impose barriers within communities.

The article displays this broad typology but explicitly excludes environmental effects caused by the mere presence of infrastructure from its later analysis. A second-order effect can connect categories: congestion increases emissions per vehicle-kilometre.

Severity is sensitive to time and place.
sections.title: Transport benefits and external benefits are different

sections.html:
One question asks for optimal marginal choices or road prices. The other asks what total burden transport shifts to other people.

The second requires \(EC+D\), rather than residual damage alone. Average gross burden indicates an optimal marginal rate only under additional conditions such as constant marginal external cost;

total harm divided by total kilometres generally does not supply a time-and-place-specific optimal price. There is no single aggregate optimal road-transport quantity independent of location and time.

The level of aggregation matters too. Harm imposed by one motorist on another is external to the first motorist but remains inside the motorist sector. Adding that harm to environmental damage can be appropriate for some social-cost questions, but it cannot be labelled without qualification as the sector's unpaid bill to the rest of society. This distinction becomes especially important in accident accounting.
sections.title: Efficiency and the unpaid bill require different measures

sections.html:
Accident costs can include vehicle/property/environmental damage, legal/police/emergency costs, medical/funeral costs, pain and suffering and lost production. Responsibility can be shared in a chain collision;

a responsible driver's own injury can impose further losses on relatives and society. Some published studies define social accident costs as total costs less insurance coverage, which differs from the article's earlier total private-plus-external social-cost definition.

Fixed yearly insurance premiums can compensate losses without pricing the marginal kilometre, so compensation does not establish optimized accident risk.

Valuing life solely through expected net production can give negative values for elderly or jobless people. The author instead favours ex ante valuation of changes in physical risk.

Historical estimates differ substantially by concept: the paper cites ECU 12,280 for gross earnings in Portugal, ECU 1,667,246 for social willingness to pay in Switzerland, and an even lower Netherlands friction-cost estimate of DFL 2,400 (about ECU 1,000). These are evidence of incompatible valuation concepts rather than comparable prices of a human being.

Table 3, PDF p. 13, printed p. 285. The original source clips some text at the right margin; the legible numerical columns and method distinctions are retained. These are social accident costs with varied boundaries, not one consistently defined environmental external-cost series.

The Swiss Neuenschwander et al. (1991) rows give SF 5,379 million / 1.70% GDP in social costs, SF 1,488 million / 0.47% GDP in external cost at individual level, and SF 789 million / 0.25% GDP at mode level. The footnote on PDF p. 12 likewise contrasts individual and mode aggregation for car traffic and reports a larger proportional reduction for rail traffic.

Changing the analytical boundary changes what is external. The paper therefore warns against adding these accident totals to noise and air-pollution external costs and calling the result transport's external burden.
sections.title: Accidents: risk valuation and aggregation

sections.html: The diagram follows sections 2–6 and the qualifications in the original, physical PDF pp. 1–14 (printed pp. 273–286).
sections.title: Topic map of the paper

sections.html:
The paper evaluates the studies in Tables 1 and 2 as mostly unpaid-bill studies, not estimations of the welfare-maximizing activity. A recurring problem is estimating one component of gross external cost instead of \(EC+D\).

Actual protective expenditure measures part of \(D\) while omitting remaining damage. A valuation of experienced harm measures part of \(EC\) while omitting induced protective expenditure.

Studies using abatement expenditure \(A\) measure a different component again. The paper's exceptions combining prevention and residual damage try to assess an optimal rather than actual situation, and their choice of optimum is unclear.

8.1 Shortcuts and choice of a standard

Using observed protection outlays as the entire loss assumes away the harm that remains after rational protection. Usually victims stop protection while another reduction in nuisance would still have value, because additional spending competes with other consumption.

Using the hypothetical cost of a programme that reduces nuisance to a supposedly reasonable level has three further problems: it omits remaining damage, replaces the value of the damage reduction with the programme cost, and selects the standard before the cost/benefit balance that should determine it. The IRT France estimates vary by a factor of six with the noise standard;

the Dutch Van der Meijs estimates differ by factors of nine for noise and twelve for pollution. These illustrate dependence on an imposed norm, not precision about the underlying welfare loss.

8.2 What valuation techniques measure

Nonbehavioural linkage methods start with a damage or dose-response relationship and multiply physical impacts by market prices: building deterioration, agricultural damage or cost of illness are examples. They do not directly recover the receptor's utility loss and can omit non-use values.

Behavioural linkage methods infer valuation from choices in a surrogate market, such as hedonic house prices, travel costs or household protection, or from a hypothetical market, such as a contingent-valuation willingness-to-pay survey. Surrogate markets may be absent or regulated;

hypothetical responses have methodological uncertainty. The author prefers utility-linked valuation conceptually but does not rank one method as universally best.

Some methods can be complementary if they measure genuinely different components. The example is psychological willingness to pay combined with costs, such as paid sick leave, that may not enter an individual's optimization.

This is a conditional argument for assessing omitted components, not permission to add overlapping valuations blindly. The article notes that both behavioural and nonbehavioural estimates can still capture only net damage.

8.3 Read the historical tables

Table 1, PDF p. 9, printed p. 281. Columns retain authors/year/country, original monetary units, GDP shares and measurement methods. The footnote identifies GDP data from IMF (1991) and estimates quoted through Quinet (1989).

The road-noise row for Dogs et al. (1991), Germany, reports DM 0.84 billion / 0.03% GDP for avoidance cost versus DM 12.8 billion / 0.52% GDP for willingness to pay. This is about fifteen times as large, but the comparison concerns distinct methods rather than two independently comparable estimates of identical complete costs.

The UK Sharp estimate of 11.18% GDP is particularly high because the study did not spread outlays over their useful years; a stock of investment should not be compared unadjusted with annual GDP.

Table 2, PDF p. 10, printed p. 282. The source retains the distinct damage, programme-cost and WTP approaches and warns that some rows include noise or all transport modes.

Dogs et al.'s road-pollution rows report DM 12.1 billion / 0.49% GDP for damage cost and DM 22.3 billion / 0.91% GDP for WTP. Shulz's table contrasts DM 3–6 billion / 0.15–0.30% GDP for damage with DM 5–16 billion / 0.25–0.79% GDP for willingness to pay;

each is attributed to 30% of the corresponding total air-pollution burden/value. Higher survey figures can indicate understatement by other methods or difficulties in contingent valuation.

The article does not establish the larger figure as the true complete loss. Its review of hedonic noise studies reports house-price reductions of 0.15–1.3% per extra decibel, dependent on the zero-annoyance baseline and study setting.

The conclusion challenges frequently cited OECD-country figures of 0.1% GDP for noise and 0.4% for air pollution. It suggests possible multipliers of eight for noise and two or three for air pollution if hypothetical valuations are trusted.

The author also identifies omitted effects, including then-unestimated CO₂ emissions and other Figure 2 categories. These are the 1994 review's criticism and conditional numerical comparisons;

they are not present-day GDP shares, statistical confidence intervals or a new aggregate estimate.
sections.title: Why noise and air-pollution estimates can undercount

sections.html:
Transport's value to users and markets does not cancel a technological externality. A consistent assessment must specify the activity, who causes/receives effects, the aggregation boundary, and whether it measures residual damage, protective resources or both.

Efficiency requires a joint marginal analysis; an unpaid-bill calculation needs the correctly bounded total.

The survey's strongest conclusion is the conceptual incompleteness and noncomparability of many historical estimates, with contingent-valuation uncertainty and accident-specific complications retained.
sections.title: What the review establishes

sections.html:
Prompt: Hypothetical survey of noise and road use: measured residual harm \(\mathrm{EC}=20\), induced receptor defence \(D=5\), supplier abatement \(A=4\), of \(\mathrm{EC}\) an identified 6 is borne by fellow road users within the sector. Separately a historical row reports protection investment stock 100 against annual GDP 1000.

Derive a consistently bounded outside-sector unpaid bill given all D is borne outside; contrast residual-only, defence-only and abatement-only measures.

Explain why that total / traffic is not automatically optimal marginal tax, how transport benefits/typology differ, and why stock/annual flow and survey valuation methods and overlap make historical tables noncomparable. Include accident risk versus production-value and insurance/aggregation qualifications;

does an old GDP share prove current physical damage?

Steps and interpretation: Outside residual \(\mathrm{EC}=20-6=14\); all D outside gives bill \(\mathrm{EC}_{out}+D=19\).

Residual-only omits defence, defence-only omits remaining harm, and A is supplier real cost, not automatically the victim’s unpaid bill. Whole individual harm \(\mathrm{EC}+D=25\) has another aggregation boundary;

social cost may include \(\mathrm{PC}+A\) as well. Total/traffic is an average;

optimal rate uses marginal time/place harm under defined conditions, not generally the average. Ordinary priced transport benefits/employment do not cancel a technological external wedge;

infrastructure access benefits are investment appraisal, not automatic trip \(\mathrm{MEB}\). Typology separates intra-sector/environment and moving/stationary/infrastructure;

the later paper excludes mere infrastructure presence. The stock-to-annual-GDP ratio is \(\frac{100\ \mathrm{currency\ units}}{1000\ \mathrm{currency\ units/year}}=0.1\ \mathrm{years}\): a stock-to-annual-flow ratio with time units, rather than an annual GDP cost share.

An annual cost comparison requires annualisation (useful-life/assumptions absent). Dose-response×market price may omit utility/nonuse;

surrogate hedonic/travel/defence and hypothetical WTP each have availability/bias/boundaries. Add methods only for genuinely nonoverlapping components;

preset noise-standard programme cost is neither full harm nor an optimal standard. Ex-ante risk-change WTP differs from net earnings-life valuation, which can misrepresent elderly/jobless;

fixed insurance compensation does not necessarily price marginal risk. Accident individual/sector aggregation changes externality classification, so adding all accident totals to noise/pollution can mix boundaries.

Historically dated currencies and GDP shares do not establish present physical damage or current values.

original_sections.html: For these numerical examples \(C_1(0)=C_2(0)=0\); a marginal-cost curve alone would leave each additive cost constant unspecified. For a fixed total abatement, minimise the sum of each firm’s cost with \(\sum_i a_i=\text{target}\). At a smooth interior choice, every \(\mathrm{MAC}_i=\lambda\), the constraint’s marginal cost. Otherwise shifting a small amount from the higher marginal cost to the lower one reduces cost at unchanged total. A tax creates savings of \(t\) per emission avoided; a tradable right creates opportunity value \(p\), even if received free. Thus interior \(\mathrm{MAC}_i=t\) or \(\mathrm{MAC}_i=p\). This is cost effectiveness; welfare efficiency also requires the target’s social tradeoff. Quantity and price instruments fix different variables, with coverage/enforcement defining their reach. Flexibility across time and space needs defined rights and can change receptor exposure; emissions are not automatically interchangeable. Innovation can change costs unevenly. Historical graphics compare dimensions with different units, dates and missing values; they do not establish current legal rules or causal welfare performance.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Four instrument families; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Four instrument families

Lecture physical PDF p. 31, based on Böchler (2012). Direct regulation, market based, cooperative and informational instruments are separate families; the attached OECD pointer is not an additional ingested source. Lecture, physical PDF p. 31

Direct regulation includes emission/technical standards, bans on toxic substances and land-planning measures. Price based instruments include taxes, direct subsidies, feed-in tariffs and bonus/malus systems; quantity based instruments include tradable permits and green certificates. Cooperative approaches include voluntary agreements, roundtables, mediation and forest certification. Information instruments include ecolabelling, communication campaigns and education. The classification describes how policy acts; it does not demonstrate that all entries have equal enforceability or welfare effects. Lecture, physical PDF p. 31

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Tradable rights and flexibility; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Tradable rights and flexibility

A firm with allowances above its emissions can sell its surplus to another firm that lacks them. A market price makes saving an allowance valuable even when it was originally allocated free: abatement permits a sale or avoids a purchase. A cap-and-trade system sets an aggregate quota; a baseline-and-credit system issues emission-reduction credits relative to a baseline. The lecture also lists minimum-limit-and-trade arrangements, averaging across similar products (cars/engines), and transferable use/abstraction rights such as fishing quotas. These forms require different baselines and definitions of the tradable right; the source supplies their classification rather than detailed design rules. Lecture, physical PDF p. 34

Flexibility across time

Budgeting emissions or abstractions over a period allows transfers within that period. Banking moves a currently valid permit to a later period; borrowing uses a permit from a future period early. Differentiating ordinary operation from short pollution peaks is another listed form of timing flexibility. These arrangements change when compliance occurs, so a total over several years and a short-term peak constraint are different requirements. This distinction is explanatory synthesis of the listed forms; the lecture does not specify discount rates, borrowing limits or safeguards. Lecture, physical PDF p. 32

Flexibility across space

An emission bubble sets a total emissions ceiling for a designated territory with several sources. A deposition bubble instead covers sources contributing deposition to a target area. Offsets transfer between bubbles while adjusting their ceilings, possibly with weights. Netting is a bubble-like arrangement within an industrial facility. The distinction between emitted quantity and deposition at a receptor matters because equal quantities from different locations need not have identical consequences. The source lists the forms but supplies no numerical transport/deposition coefficients. Lecture, physical PDF p. 33

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Why common marginal costs minimize total abatement costs; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Why common marginal costs minimize total abatement costs

Let \(a_i\) be firm \(i\)'s abatement, \(C_i(a_i)\) its abatement cost and \(MAC_i=C_i'(a_i)\) its marginal abatement cost, expressed as money per avoided emission unit. For a fixed total abatement requirement \(\bar a\), an explanatory derivation of the lecture's least-cost condition is

\[\min_{a_1,\ldots,a_n}\sum_i C_i(a_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_i a_i=\bar a.\]

At a smooth interior optimum, \(MAC_i(a_i)=\lambda\) for every firm, where \(\lambda\) is the common marginal cost of meeting the target. If one firm instead has higher MAC, shifting a small amount of abatement from it to a lower-MAC firm keeps the total unchanged and lowers cost. This argument assumes comparable emission/abatement units and a target that allows the transfer. Location-specific damage, constraints and transaction costs can restrict it; the lecture does not establish that unrestricted trading of every pollutant is harmless. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 33–34,44

Under a tax \(t\) per emitted unit, a firm saves \(t\) by avoiding one unit and, at an interior choice, abates until \(MAC_i=t\). With an allowance price \(p\), it abates and sells/avoids buying an allowance when \(MAC_i<p\), while emitting and buying is cheaper when \(MAC_i>p\); the equilibrium margin is \(MAC_i=p\). A common price thus equalizes marginal costs across unconstrained firms. This is cost effectiveness for a given target. It establishes full welfare efficiency only if the target/price also reflects social benefits and damages under the conditions in the optimum model. Lecture, physical PDF p. 44 Lecture, physical PDF p. 20

Lecture p. 46 compares a tax shifting the private supply schedule toward social cost with a permit quantity that fixes the relevant quantity and allows a price to emerge. It is a simple known-curve illustration, not an uncertainty model. Lecture, physical PDF p. 46

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Innovation and environmental effectiveness; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Innovation and environmental effectiveness

Pricing each emission unit gives a continuing reason to seek cheaper avoidance. The lecture illustrates innovation as a shift from \(MAC_1\) to \(MAC_2\), with greater abatement at the same tax and a reduction in compliance cost. But innovation need not lower MAC at every margin: a technology can lower some parts of the curve while raising others. The source distinguishes this from commonly assumed reductions in average cost at all margins. The welfare or firm gain must therefore follow the actual curves, rather than treating every innovation as a parallel downward shift. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 44–45

Lecture p. 45: the horizontal Pigouvian tax intersects \(MAC_1\) at \(A_1\) and \(MAC_2\) at \(A_2\). The slide discusses the area between marginal curves but also qualifies the commonly used downward-shift picture. Lecture, physical PDF p. 45

A monitored/enforced ban or direct quantity requirement specifies a target. A tax specifies a rate and leaves the response—and therefore the achieved emission quantity—dependent on behaviour, exemptions and costs. A tradable quantity constraint fixes the covered quantity while leaving its price to the market. Voluntary and information instruments are difficult to enforce or give uncertain responses. These are the lecture's ideal effectiveness comparisons. Clear targets require monitoring, enforcement and appropriate coverage; a cap on covered sources is not by itself proof of an economy-wide emission outcome. The lecture mentions minimizing control mistakes under price-versus-quantity instruments but does not derive an uncertainty-based ranking. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 44,47

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Historical policy examples and chart interpretation; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Historical policy examples and chart interpretation

The lecture reports that the US Acid Rain Program followed the 1990 Clean Air Act amendment, began SO₂ trading in 1995 and expanded in 2000. It attributes practicality to relatively few easily monitored polluters and reports emissions more than 50% lower in 2007, three years before the statutory deadline, with compliance costs about one quarter of original predictions. The slide does not state the reference year for that percentage or an identification method separating trading from other influences. Treat these as the supplied lecture's historical descriptive claims, not a new causal estimate or current performance measure. Lecture, physical PDF p. 36

Different ETS metrics answer different questions

Lecture p. 38 reproduces an ICAP Status Report 2024 map, labelled as January 2024. Blue indicates systems in force; green indicates development; light green/question marks indicate consideration. Layered borders indicate multiple systems or an additional system under development. Lecture, physical PDF p. 38

The text says 36 systems were in force and 14 under development. It says 12 jurisdictions were considering ETS, while the legend labels 8 under consideration; the displayed discrepancy/counting-unit distinction is not resolved by the slide and should not be collapsed into one count. The map shows that deployment spans several jurisdictions and administrative layers, without establishing effectiveness or comparable system coverage. The preceding lecture claim that permits are somewhat preferred to carbon taxation is motivated by temperature targets and carbon budgets, not proven by this map. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 37–38

Lecture p. 39, ICAP 2024: rows show jurisdiction-emission coverage (%), 2023 average price (USD per metric tonne CO₂e), auction share of the 2023 cap (%), and maximum offset share of a compliance entity's obligation (%). NA is unavailable, not zero. Circle sizes represent the values within their respective dimensions. Lecture, physical PDF p. 39

The EU ETS column gives 38% coverage, USD 90/tCO₂e, 57% auction share and 0% offsets. China's national ETS gives 40%, USD 10, 0% and 5%, respectively. A larger circle for coverage cannot be interpreted as a higher price or a larger absolute volume: the rows have different units and scales. Washington's offset footnote distinguishes up to 5% plus another 3% from projects on federally recognized tribal land. The 100% figures for Tokyo and Saitama retain quantitative restrictions on credits from outside those areas; the China coverage footnote is CO₂ emissions. These qualifications limit direct comparisons. Lecture, physical PDF p. 39

Lecture p. 40, ICAP 2024: stacked bars show annual revenues in million USD from 2007–2023, with annotations on additional systems; the pie separates 2023 revenue by system. It reports almost USD 303 billion cumulative revenue and almost USD 74 billion in 2023. Lecture, physical PDF p. 40

The 2023 EU ETS component is USD 47,098.0 million, Germany USD 11,560.0 million and UK USD 5,223.9 million. A revenue increase can reflect price, auctioned amount or new systems; it is not an emission-reduction series or a direct welfare gain. Footnotes state that some Canadian data stop in 2020 or 2022 and that New Brunswick/Ontario data were unavailable, and qualify the Nova Scotia last auctions. Therefore even the plotted historical totals have coverage limitations. Revenue use connects to the recycling and double-dividend discussion. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 40,49–53

Climate agreements and EU targets as recorded in the lecture

The source lists UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto adopted in 1997/in force 2005, Kyoto II commitments through 2020 for 61 countries, and international trading among three flexible mechanisms; it reports a Czech sale to Japan of about CZK 20 billion. It presents the Paris 2015 objective as well below 2°C while pursuing 1.5°C and describes NDC revision every five years. Its shorthand “not formally binding” refers to the slide's characterization of NDCs and should not be used as a complete statement of all obligations under the treaty. The lecture first records the EU's older 40% 2030 ambition, then p. 42 records a 55% GHG reduction relative to 1990, 42.5% renewable share and 11.7% energy-efficiency improvement relative to projected 2030 use under the 2020 reference scenario. These have different denominators and the two emissions ambitions are historical versus later source figures, not one percentage applied to the same baseline. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 41–42

The p. 42 line “EU 2040 climate target” contains no target value. No number can be recovered from that title. All policy figures and system descriptions above are bounded to this October 2025 lecture and its 2024 graphics; this ingestion does not verify the present legal or policy situation. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 1,38–42

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What to retain; fingerprint 9e2f739fb2dec5a81d11a4afc2b62308b70ad5ab27a0310d07f641df4eb7d87a. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What to retain

Equalizing marginal abatement costs economizes on compliance resources, while selecting the social target and achieving it require additional reasoning and enforcement. A price incentive can promote innovation, but the technology response is not mechanically uniform. Interpret ETS quantity, price, coverage, auctions, offsets and revenue as separate metrics with their source dates and units. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 44–47,38–40

original_sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Pass requires every listed component, all requested outputs and essential keyed reasoning without a critical conceptual error. Algebraically equivalent formulas, explicitly defined opposite cash-flow signs and equivalent plain-language reasoning are accepted. Partial means a missing component or a correct method with an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip; fail means the central mechanism or condition is wrong. Unscorable means the response or help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown conditions never certify independence. Arithmetic slips require independent correction before a pass. No numerical grade is invented.

Critical errors: Equal target split always cheapest; free allowance has no incentive; equal \(\mathrm{MAC}\) proves optimal social target; revenue/coverage proves welfare; cap automatically controls all emissions; missing count/target invented.

Acquisition requires two distinct unassisted passes from I1/I2/D1/D2 using the exact six routes in metadata. Each full prompt and key covers every component; any pair therefore covers the whole outcome twice. A fresh D item used for acquisition cannot later certify delayed retention. Worked/support/prerequisite items and the narrow C1 correction cannot substitute for a full check. The finite bank must not be reused after exposure; request a plan_issue when fewer than two fresh full items remain.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, allocate a fixed abatement target and compare instrument boundaries.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Derive least-cost abatement
  • Compare what price/quantity instruments establish under explicit coverage and enforcement conditions.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Derive private and social activity optima and marginal corrective signals
Check the foundations

Does equal \(\mathrm{MAC}\) alone prove the emissions target optimal?

Reveal foundation explanation

No; it minimises comparable compliance cost for a given feasible target; social benefit/damage selects the target. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Marginal abatement cost: The extra cost of one more unit of emissions reduction.
  • Cost-effective allocation: A feasible allocation minimizing cost for a fixed total target.
  • Allowance opportunity cost: The forgone sale or avoided-purchase value of using an allowance, even if received free.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
Lecture physical PDF p. 31, based on Böchler (2012). Direct regulation, market based, cooperative and informational instruments are separate families; the attached OECD pointer is not an additional ingested source.

Direct regulation includes emission/technical standards, bans on toxic substances and land-planning measures. Price based instruments include taxes, direct subsidies, feed-in tariffs and bonus/malus systems;

quantity based instruments include tradable permits and green certificates. Cooperative approaches include voluntary agreements, roundtables, mediation and forest certification.

Information instruments include ecolabelling, communication campaigns and education. The classification describes how policy acts;

it does not demonstrate that all entries have equal enforceability or welfare effects.
sections.title: Four instrument families

sections.html:
A firm with allowances above its emissions can sell its surplus to another firm that lacks them. A market price makes saving an allowance valuable even when it was originally allocated free: abatement permits a sale or avoids a purchase.

A cap-and-trade system sets an aggregate quota; a baseline-and-credit system issues emission-reduction credits relative to a baseline.

The lecture also lists minimum-limit-and-trade arrangements, averaging across similar products (cars/engines), and transferable use/abstraction rights such as fishing quotas. These forms require different baselines and definitions of the tradable right;

the source supplies their classification rather than detailed design rules.

5.1 Flexibility across time

Budgeting emissions or abstractions over a period allows transfers within that period. Banking moves a currently valid permit to a later period; borrowing uses a permit from a future period early. Differentiating ordinary operation from short pollution peaks is another listed form of timing flexibility.

These arrangements change when compliance occurs, so a total over several years and a short-term peak constraint are different requirements. This distinction is explanatory synthesis of the listed forms;

the lecture does not specify discount rates, borrowing limits or safeguards.

5.2 Flexibility across space

An emission bubble sets a total emissions ceiling for a designated territory with several sources. A deposition bubble instead covers sources contributing deposition to a target area. Offsets transfer between bubbles while adjusting their ceilings, possibly with weights. Netting is a bubble-like arrangement within an industrial facility.

The distinction between emitted quantity and deposition at a receptor matters because equal quantities from different locations need not have identical consequences. The source lists the forms but supplies no numerical transport/deposition coefficients.
sections.title: Tradable rights and flexibility

sections.html:
Let \(a_i\) be firm \(i\)'s abatement, \(C_i(a_i)\) its abatement cost and \(MAC_i=C_i'(a_i)\) its marginal abatement cost, expressed as money per avoided emission unit. For a fixed total abatement requirement \(\bar a\), an explanatory derivation of the lecture's least-cost condition is

\[\min_{a_1,\ldots,a_n}\sum_i C_i(a_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_i a_i=\bar a.\]

At a smooth interior optimum, \(MAC_i(a_i)=\lambda\) for every firm, where \(\lambda\) is the common marginal cost of meeting the target. If one firm instead has higher MAC, shifting a small amount of abatement from it to a lower-MAC firm keeps the total unchanged and lowers cost.

This argument assumes comparable emission/abatement units and a target that allows the transfer. Location-specific damage, constraints and transaction costs can restrict it;

the lecture does not establish that unrestricted trading of every pollutant is harmless.

Under a tax \(t\) per emitted unit, a firm saves \(t\) by avoiding one unit and, at an interior choice, abates until \(MAC_i=t\). With an allowance price \(p\), it abates and sells/avoids buying an allowance when \(MAC_i<p\), while emitting and buying is cheaper when \(MAC_i>p\);

the equilibrium margin is \(MAC_i=p\). A common price thus equalizes marginal costs across unconstrained firms.

This is cost effectiveness for a given target. It establishes full welfare efficiency only if the target/price also reflects social benefits and damages under the conditions in the optimum model.

Lecture p. 46 compares a tax shifting the private supply schedule toward social cost with a permit quantity that fixes the relevant quantity and allows a price to emerge. It is a simple known-curve illustration, not an uncertainty model.
sections.title: Why common marginal costs minimize total abatement costs

sections.html:
Pricing each emission unit gives a continuing reason to seek cheaper avoidance. The lecture illustrates innovation as a shift from \(MAC_1\) to \(MAC_2\), with greater abatement at the same tax and a reduction in compliance cost.

But innovation need not lower MAC at every margin: a technology can lower some parts of the curve while raising others. The source distinguishes this from commonly assumed reductions in average cost at all margins.

The welfare or firm gain must therefore follow the actual curves, rather than treating every innovation as a parallel downward shift.

Lecture p. 45: the horizontal Pigouvian tax intersects \(MAC_1\) at \(A_1\) and \(MAC_2\) at \(A_2\). The slide discusses the area between marginal curves but also qualifies the commonly used downward-shift picture.

A monitored/enforced ban or direct quantity requirement specifies a target. A tax specifies a rate and leaves the response—and therefore the achieved emission quantity—dependent on behaviour, exemptions and costs.

A tradable quantity constraint fixes the covered quantity while leaving its price to the market. Voluntary and information instruments are difficult to enforce or give uncertain responses.

These are the lecture's ideal effectiveness comparisons. Clear targets require monitoring, enforcement and appropriate coverage;

a cap on covered sources is not by itself proof of an economy-wide emission outcome. The lecture mentions minimizing control mistakes under price-versus-quantity instruments but does not derive an uncertainty-based ranking.
sections.title: Innovation and environmental effectiveness

sections.html:
The lecture reports that the US Acid Rain Program followed the 1990 Clean Air Act amendment, began SO₂ trading in 1995 and expanded in 2000. It attributes practicality to relatively few easily monitored polluters and reports emissions more than 50% lower in 2007, three years before the statutory deadline, with compliance costs about one quarter of original predictions.

The slide does not state the reference year for that percentage or an identification method separating trading from other influences. Treat these as the supplied lecture's historical descriptive claims, not a new causal estimate or current performance measure.

8.1 Different ETS metrics answer different questions

Lecture p. 38 reproduces an ICAP Status Report 2024 map, labelled as January 2024. Blue indicates systems in force; green indicates development; light green/question marks indicate consideration. Layered borders indicate multiple systems or an additional system under development.

The text says 36 systems were in force and 14 under development. It says 12 jurisdictions were considering ETS, while the legend labels 8 under consideration;

the displayed discrepancy/counting-unit distinction is not resolved by the slide and should not be collapsed into one count. The map shows that deployment spans several jurisdictions and administrative layers, without establishing effectiveness or comparable system coverage.

The preceding lecture claim that permits are somewhat preferred to carbon taxation is motivated by temperature targets and carbon budgets, not proven by this map.

Lecture p. 39, ICAP 2024: rows show jurisdiction-emission coverage (%), 2023 average price (USD per metric tonne CO₂e), auction share of the 2023 cap (%), and maximum offset share of a compliance entity's obligation (%). NA is unavailable, not zero. Circle sizes represent the values within their respective dimensions.

The EU ETS column gives 38% coverage, USD 90/tCO₂e, 57% auction share and 0% offsets. China's national ETS gives 40%, USD 10, 0% and 5%, respectively.

A larger circle for coverage cannot be interpreted as a higher price or a larger absolute volume: the rows have different units and scales. Washington's offset footnote distinguishes up to 5% plus another 3% from projects on federally recognized tribal land.

The 100% figures for Tokyo and Saitama retain quantitative restrictions on credits from outside those areas; the China coverage footnote is CO₂ emissions.

These qualifications limit direct comparisons.

Lecture p. 40, ICAP 2024: stacked bars show annual revenues in million USD from 2007–2023, with annotations on additional systems; the pie separates 2023 revenue by system. It reports almost USD 303 billion cumulative revenue and almost USD 74 billion in 2023.

The 2023 EU ETS component is USD 47,098.0 million, Germany USD 11,560.0 million and UK USD 5,223.9 million. A revenue increase can reflect price, auctioned amount or new systems;

it is not an emission-reduction series or a direct welfare gain. Footnotes state that some Canadian data stop in 2020 or 2022 and that New Brunswick/Ontario data were unavailable, and qualify the Nova Scotia last auctions.

Therefore even the plotted historical totals have coverage limitations. Revenue use connects to the recycling and double-dividend discussion.

8.2 Climate agreements and EU targets as recorded in the lecture

The source lists UNFCCC (1992), Kyoto adopted in 1997/in force 2005, Kyoto II commitments through 2020 for 61 countries, and international trading among three flexible mechanisms; it reports a Czech sale to Japan of about CZK 20 billion.

It presents the Paris 2015 objective as well below 2°C while pursuing 1.5°C and describes NDC revision every five years. Its shorthand “not formally binding” refers to the slide's characterization of NDCs and should not be used as a complete statement of all obligations under the treaty.

The lecture first records the EU's older 40% 2030 ambition, then p. 42 records a 55% GHG reduction relative to 1990, 42.5% renewable share and 11.7% energy-efficiency improvement relative to projected 2030 use under the 2020 reference scenario. These have different denominators and the two emissions ambitions are historical versus later source figures, not one percentage applied to the same baseline.

The p. 42 line “EU 2040 climate target” contains no target value. No number can be recovered from that title. All policy figures and system descriptions above are bounded to this October 2025 lecture and its 2024 graphics; this ingestion does not verify the present legal or policy situation.
sections.title: Historical policy examples and chart interpretation

sections.html: Equalizing marginal abatement costs economizes on compliance resources, while selecting the social target and achieving it require additional reasoning and enforcement. A price incentive can promote innovation, but the technology response is not mechanically uniform. Interpret ETS quantity, price, coverage, auctions, offsets and revenue as separate metrics with their source dates and units.

original_sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

original_sections.html: A first-best marginal correction uses external cost at the optimum. Government also needs revenue and existing distortionary taxes change behaviour. The displayed dirty-commodity expression combines Ramsey \(R\) and Pigou \(P\) with \(\eta=1/\mathrm{MCPF}\). Substitution gives weights \((1-1/\mathrm{MCPF})\) and \(1/\mathrm{MCPF}\); \(\mathrm{MCPF}=1\) yields \(P\). That supported algebra does not define the missing expanded utility symbols or tax base. Ramsey’s inverse-elasticity statement is a conditional simplified revenue rule, not a universal tax recommendation. Revenue is a transfer, while excess burden is the additional distortion. Lump-sum independence removes substitution incentives but not every income effect. The commodity formula excludes labour tax; later labour discussion separates environmental gain, revenue recycling and interaction loss. Weak dividend compares recycling versus lump-sum use of the same environmental revenue. Strong dividend claims an additional overall nonenvironmental efficiency improvement and depends on initial distortions/substitution/mobility etc. A toy accounting can illustrate the distinction, never establish a calibrated model or prove the final terse separability qualifications.
original_sections.title: Motivation and explanation

original_sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Three goals of an environmental tax; fingerprint 8da1915b95877f0ba4297c03056ee3110e77fd0d03c58aa602d424cb8c391b1b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Three goals of an environmental tax

The lecture separates getting prices right, changing behaviour and raising funds for public goods. Corrective pricing in the simple model uses the marginal external cost at the optimum, rather than total historical damage. Behavioural incentives can induce resource saving and lower emissions. Revenue is an additional consequence whose use matters: the same gross collection can finance spending, be returned as a lump sum or reduce another tax. Revenue is a transfer to government, not automatically an extra social benefit equal to the cash amount. The last distinction is explanatory synthesis consistent with the source's separate recycling and interaction effects. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 49,52

For a given revenue requirement, optimal-tax theory seeks to minimize excess burden: the welfare loss caused by tax-induced distortions beyond the revenue transferred. The source contrasts a first-best lump-sum tax with second-best commodity taxation, where uniform rates are rarely optimal in the general setting. A lump-sum tax is independent of the taxed agent's behaviour and induces no substitution effect, but may still have an income effect. Lecture, physical PDF p. 49 Verhoef Externalities, physical PDF p. 9 note3

The lecture's Ramsey inverse-elasticity rule associates larger rates with less elastic demand: when quantity responds less strongly, a rate can raise revenue with less distortion on that margin. This is the source's simplified rule, not a general prescription ignoring cross-price responses, distribution or other constraints. The lecture does not derive its full demand-system assumptions. Lecture, physical PDF p. 49

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Sandmo decomposition and the cost of public funds; fingerprint 8da1915b95877f0ba4297c03056ee3110e77fd0d03c58aa602d424cb8c391b1b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Sandmo decomposition and the cost of public funds

In the lecture's Sandmo (1975) commodity-tax setting, clean goods follow a Ramsey component and the dirty-good tax combines Ramsey and Pigouvian components. The source explicitly excludes labour taxation from this displayed commodity-tax model. It writes

\[\theta_D=(1-\eta)R+\eta P.\]

Here \(\theta_D\) is its optimal dirty-commodity tax expression, \(R\) denotes the Ramsey component and \(P\) the Pigouvian component. The weight \(\eta=\lambda/\mu\) compares the marginal utility of income (\(\lambda\)) with the effect of a larger revenue requirement on social utility (\(\mu\)), as defined on the slide. \(R\) is unfortunately also used elsewhere for revenue requirement; the context is needed to distinguish the meanings. This expression says the tax combines revenue and correction considerations, with a model-dependent weight. It is not enough to compute a numerical rate without their values and a fully specified tax base. Lecture, physical PDF p. 50

The next slide introduces the marginal cost of public funds, \(MCPF=1/\eta\), and writes \(MCPF=-\Delta W/\Delta R\) for social welfare lost in raising an additional revenue amount. In that ratio \(\Delta R\) means additional public revenue, not the Ramsey component. Substituting \(\eta=1/MCPF\) gives

\[\theta_D=\left(1-\frac1{MCPF}\right)R+\frac1{MCPF}P.\]

The displayed slide then expands its components as

\[\theta_D=\left(1-\frac1{MCPF}\right)\left(-\frac1{\varepsilon_{DD}}\right) +\frac1{MCPF}\left(-N\frac{u_{ND}}{u_D}\right).\]

Lecture PDF p. 51. The formula has been checked visually: the Pigou term is \(-N u_{ND}/u_D\), with \(ND\) as a subscript on \(u\) and \(D\) as a subscript in the denominator. Lecture, physical PDF p. 51

The connection to the preceding inverse-elasticity slide identifies the first bracket as the Ramsey part. However, the lecture does not define \(N\), \(u_{ND}\) or \(u_D\), state the utility function from which they come, or specify whether \(\theta_D\) is a normalized/ad valorem or per-unit measure. It also does not provide a derivation of the full expansion. These symbols are retained rather than assigned guessed meanings. Only the weighted decomposition and its conditional algebraic case are self-contained from the supplied material. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 49–51

If \(MCPF=1\), the Ramsey weight becomes zero and the Pigouvian weight one, so \(\theta_D=P\). The source describes this as indifference between public and private consumption. For any other value the weighting differs; the source does not supply empirical MCPF values or prove their sign/range. The decomposition should therefore not be treated as a universally calibrated environmental-tax rule. Lecture, physical PDF p. 51

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Revenue recycling and the double dividend; fingerprint 8da1915b95877f0ba4297c03056ee3110e77fd0d03c58aa602d424cb8c391b1b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Revenue recycling and the double dividend

The first or green dividend is an environmental improvement. A proposed second or blue dividend is higher employment or economic efficiency. Three effects must be separated. The primary welfare gain is the environmental improvement correcting the pollution market. The revenue-recycling effect can reduce distortions if proceeds cut existing distortionary taxes. The tax-interaction effect can increase distortions elsewhere: higher pollution-inclusive prices reduce real wages and can lower labour supply, depending on how leisure and dirty goods substitute or complement each other. Reduced labour-tax receipts and falling environmental-tax receipts as avoidance improves can also require other revenue sources. The labour-supply discussion here extends beyond the commodity-only model used for the Sandmo display; its effects cannot simply be inferred from that formula alone. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 52–53

Weak double dividend compares two uses of a given environmental-tax revenue: reducing distortionary taxes versus returning a lump sum. The lecture says recycling through distortionary-tax cuts generally improves efficiency relative to the lump-sum option. This comparison does not itself say the entire reform raises nonenvironmental welfare relative to no environmental tax. Strong double dividend makes that larger claim: overall economic efficiency rises in addition to the environmental gain. The lecture says theory is inconclusive and lists initial tax structure, substitutability, factor mobility and rigid wages as determinants. A revenue-recycling gain can coexist with a larger tax-interaction loss. Lecture, physical PDF p. 53

The final slide's qualifications

Lecture p. 54 is image-based and adds qualifications absent from native text extraction. Lecture, physical PDF p. 54

The slide says the weak form has theoretical and simulation support but conditions its claim on there being only one distortionary tax. It then says it holds without restrictions under a first-best setting only, relates tax convergence to Ramsey's inverse-elasticity argument and states that weak separability requires equal commodity-tax rates. These terse claims are not accompanied by a model, a definition of the separability relation, or a derivation. They coexist with p. 49's general statement that uniform commodity taxes are rarely optimal. Read the equal-rate claim as a differently conditioned source statement; the supplied slides do not permit a complete theorem reconciling all of these assertions or a universal weak-double-dividend guarantee. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 49,53–54

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What can be applied and what needs further source material; fingerprint 8da1915b95877f0ba4297c03056ee3110e77fd0d03c58aa602d424cb8c391b1b. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What can be applied and what needs further source material

The supplied material supports distinguishing marginal correction from revenue raising, explaining the weighted Ramsey/Pigou expression, evaluating its \(MCPF=1\) algebraic case and separating weak/strong double dividend from tax interaction. Numerical application of the expanded Sandmo formula and a proof of the p. 54 conditions require defined tax normalization, missing utility notation and full model assumptions. Those strands remain source gaps, while the mechanism and conditional comparisons above are usable. Lecture, physical PDF pp. 49–54

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, separate corrective taxation, revenue use and double-dividend claims.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Explain the supported symbolic tax decomposition
  • Distinguish revenue-use comparisons from an additional overall economic gain.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Derive private and social activity optima and marginal corrective signals
Check the foundations

Does collecting tax revenue automatically add the same amount to social welfare?

Reveal foundation explanation

No; the payer/government transfer cancels; behavioural/environmental and resource-distortion effects need separate accounting. Otherwise
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Excess burden: Distortionary welfare cost beyond a pure revenue transfer.
  • Revenue recycling: Using environmental-tax revenue, such as reducing another distortionary tax.
  • Strong double dividend: A nonenvironmental efficiency gain in addition to the environmental benefit, under the specified comparison.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
The lecture separates getting prices right, changing behaviour and raising funds for public goods. Corrective pricing in the simple model uses the marginal external cost at the optimum, rather than total historical damage.

Behavioural incentives can induce resource saving and lower emissions. Revenue is an additional consequence whose use matters: the same gross collection can finance spending, be returned as a lump sum or reduce another tax.

Revenue is a transfer to government, not automatically an extra social benefit equal to the cash amount. The last distinction is explanatory synthesis consistent with the source's separate recycling and interaction effects.

For a given revenue requirement, optimal-tax theory seeks to minimize excess burden: the welfare loss caused by tax-induced distortions beyond the revenue transferred. The source contrasts a first-best lump-sum tax with second-best commodity taxation, where uniform rates are rarely optimal in the general setting.

A lump-sum tax is independent of the taxed agent's behaviour and induces no substitution effect, but may still have an income effect.

The lecture's Ramsey inverse-elasticity rule associates larger rates with less elastic demand: when quantity responds less strongly, a rate can raise revenue with less distortion on that margin. This is the source's simplified rule, not a general prescription ignoring cross-price responses, distribution or other constraints. The lecture does not derive its full demand-system assumptions.
sections.title: Three goals of an environmental tax

sections.html:
In the lecture's Sandmo (1975) commodity-tax setting, clean goods follow a Ramsey component and the dirty-good tax combines Ramsey and Pigouvian components. The source explicitly excludes labour taxation from this displayed commodity-tax model. It writes

\[\theta_D=(1-\eta)R+\eta P.\]

Here \(\theta_D\) is its optimal dirty-commodity tax expression, \(R\) denotes the Ramsey component and \(P\) the Pigouvian component. The weight \(\eta=\lambda/\mu\) compares the marginal utility of income (\(\lambda\)) with the effect of a larger revenue requirement on social utility (\(\mu\)), as defined on the slide. \(R\) is unfortunately also used elsewhere for revenue requirement;

the context is needed to distinguish the meanings. This expression says the tax combines revenue and correction considerations, with a model-dependent weight.

It is not enough to compute a numerical rate without their values and a fully specified tax base.

The next slide introduces the marginal cost of public funds, \(MCPF=1/\eta\), and writes \(MCPF=-\Delta W/\Delta R\) for social welfare lost in raising an additional revenue amount. In that ratio \(\Delta R\) means additional public revenue, not the Ramsey component. Substituting \(\eta=1/MCPF\) gives

\[\theta_D=\left(1-\frac1{MCPF}\right)R+\frac1{MCPF}P.\]

The displayed slide then expands its components as

\[\theta_D=\left(1-\frac1{MCPF}\right)\left(-\frac1{\varepsilon_{DD}}\right) +\frac1{MCPF}\left(-N\frac{u_{ND}}{u_D}\right).\]

Lecture PDF p. 51. The formula has been checked visually: the Pigou term is \(-N u_{ND}/u_D\), with \(ND\) as a subscript on \(u\) and \(D\) as a subscript in the denominator.

The connection to the preceding inverse-elasticity slide identifies the first bracket as the Ramsey part. However, the lecture does not define \(N\), \(u_{ND}\) or \(u_D\), state the utility function from which they come, or specify whether \(\theta_D\) is a normalized/ad valorem or per-unit measure.

It also does not provide a derivation of the full expansion. These symbols are retained rather than assigned guessed meanings.

Only the weighted decomposition and its conditional algebraic case are self-contained from the supplied material.

If \(MCPF=1\), the Ramsey weight becomes zero and the Pigouvian weight one, so \(\theta_D=P\). The source describes this as indifference between public and private consumption. For any other value the weighting differs; the source does not supply empirical MCPF values or prove their sign/range. The decomposition should therefore not be treated as a universally calibrated environmental-tax rule.
sections.title: Sandmo decomposition and the cost of public funds

sections.html:
The first or green dividend is an environmental improvement. A proposed second or blue dividend is higher employment or economic efficiency.

Three effects must be separated. The primary welfare gain is the environmental improvement correcting the pollution market.

The revenue-recycling effect can reduce distortions if proceeds cut existing distortionary taxes. The tax-interaction effect can increase distortions elsewhere: higher pollution-inclusive prices reduce real wages and can lower labour supply, depending on how leisure and dirty goods substitute or complement each other.

Reduced labour-tax receipts and falling environmental-tax receipts as avoidance improves can also require other revenue sources. The labour-supply discussion here extends beyond the commodity-only model used for the Sandmo display;

its effects cannot simply be inferred from that formula alone.

Weak double dividend compares two uses of a given environmental-tax revenue: reducing distortionary taxes versus returning a lump sum. The lecture says recycling through distortionary-tax cuts generally improves efficiency relative to the lump-sum option.

This comparison does not itself say the entire reform raises nonenvironmental welfare relative to no environmental tax. Strong double dividend makes that larger claim: overall economic efficiency rises in addition to the environmental gain. The lecture says theory is inconclusive and lists initial tax structure, substitutability, factor mobility and rigid wages as determinants.

A revenue-recycling gain can coexist with a larger tax-interaction loss.

6.1 The final slide's qualifications

Lecture p. 54 is image-based and adds qualifications absent from native text extraction.

The slide says the weak form has theoretical and simulation support but conditions its claim on there being only one distortionary tax. It then says it holds without restrictions under a first-best setting only, relates tax convergence to Ramsey's inverse-elasticity argument and states that weak separability requires equal commodity-tax rates.

These terse claims are not accompanied by a model, a definition of the separability relation, or a derivation. They coexist with p. 49's general statement that uniform commodity taxes are rarely optimal.

Read the equal-rate claim as a differently conditioned source statement; the supplied slides do not permit a complete theorem reconciling all of these assertions or a universal weak-double-dividend guarantee.
sections.title: Revenue recycling and the double dividend

sections.html:
The supplied material supports distinguishing marginal correction from revenue raising, explaining the weighted Ramsey/Pigou expression, evaluating its \(MCPF=1\) algebraic case and separating weak/strong double dividend from tax interaction. Numerical application of the expanded Sandmo formula and a proof of the p. 54 conditions require defined tax normalization, missing utility notation and full model assumptions.

Those strands remain source gaps, while the mechanism and conditional comparisons above are usable.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources

Required components: complete_accounting_and_discount_units, uncertainty_distribution_and_public_goods, jurisdiction_cooperation_and_evidence_limits. original_sections.html: Use a counterfactual, not a policy label or repeal count. The seven principles link market failures to intervention rationale, complete discounted social accounting and uncertainty/distribution, then governance matched to physical spillovers and international cooperation. A saved cost can be smaller than forgone benefits. Discount \(B_t/(1+r)^t\) with explicit horizon; rates affect early/late costs too, so avoid universal net-benefit direction. Energy damages require energy rather than power units: \(\mathrm{ton}/\mathrm{MWh}\times\mathrm{USD}/\mathrm{ton}\) converts to \(\mathrm{USD}/\mathrm{MWh}\), then \(\text{cents}/\mathrm{kWh}\) by dividing \(10\). This instantiates the finished note’s source-unit repair. Uncertain harm is not automatically zero and cumulative exposures can matter. Local heterogeneity/information can favour decentralisation; cross-border effects/free riding can favour coordination. R&D/data have shared benefits and capacity effects; programme-specific historical returns do not prove every project worthwhile. The source is a dated conceptual critique with cited cases and evolving actions, not an original national treatment-effect estimate. Keep direct-production/lifecycle, legal protection/physical harm and proposal/final action distinctions.
