sections.html:
Prompt: Hypothetical appraisal has aggregate gain \(30-10\); one group gains \(30\), another loses \(10\), no compensation stated.

A completed report considers one preferred option late, with some benefits unmonetised and uncertainty unstated; the decision proceeds unchanged.

Officials use the report to consult stakeholders. In a declared historical-style funding arrangement, positive social NPV justifies a project but negative financial NPV can support cofinancing;

applicant supplies the information. A narrow board reviews business costs only.

Distinguish normative CBA/Pareto, use/quality/influence, all four possible motives and stage/capacity effects. Explain principal-agent incentives versus accidental forecast error, and propose source-supported process safeguards with their limits.

Interpret historical case/table associations without current, representative or causal claims; does explaining political divergence justify it?

Steps and interpretation: Aggregate \(\text{gain}=20>0\) passes the simplified aggregate criterion under given valuation, but actual loser remains; no strict Pareto improvement/actual compensation is established.

The chapter’s simplified sum omits discounting for illustration, not a full project manual. Completed report shows use;

omitted benefits/uncertainty/options can limit quality; unchanged decision indicates no observed decision influence, although absence of all influence requires fuller evidence.

Late timing narrows alternatives compared with early design/agenda input. Instrumental use informs choice, political use controls/delays/emphasises interests, communicative use enables consultation, perfunctory use ticks an obligation;

motives can coexist and stated facts do not prove all dishonesty. Capacity/expertise and institutional support/motives differ.

Funding authority (principal) relies on applicant (agent); rewarding socially positive/financially negative creates incentive to inflate the social case and depress the financial case under declared historical arrangement.

Error could also reflect uncertainty/uncontrolled events, so not automatic cheating or current funding rule. Safeguards: clear guidelines/capacity, transparent objectives/baselines/options/uncertainty, independent scrutiny with adequate remit/information/capacity, cofinancing to bear inefficiency and credible fair ex-post review/accountability.

A narrow business remit cannot guarantee full social appraisal; costly detection, political incentives and sanctions for uncontrollable error limit effectiveness.

Historical report length/monetary use, six motive cases, return associations and resubmission series are bounded evidence, not representative rates, causal institutional effects or current quality. Economic appraisal informs, not settles every objective;

explaining actual divergence does not justify poor appraisal or prove CBA useless.

Show a hint

Pause before calculating or choosing an explanation:

  • What quantities, actors or outcomes are being compared? Write their roles, units and dates beside them.
  • Which condition decides whether the relationship applies? Check the relevant definition before using a formula or classifying the case.
  • What would have to remain fixed for your comparison to be meaningful? Work through one link in the reasoning at a time.
  • How could you check the direction, boundary case or alternative explanation before stating your conclusion?

Fresh narrow check: report exists, omits uncertainty, chosen option unchanged.

Solve the following:

  1. Name three distinct questions.
interactions.solution_html: Use: yes, report exists. Quality: uncertainty omission is a concern. Influence: no observed change in stated facts; assess further effects before claiming none. These dimensions cannot be collapsed.

sections.html: Choose one answer per question. Check individual answers or check the whole quiz. Each option includes feedback on the reasoning, and everything works offline.

choices: High quality because a report exists.
Use is evident; quality and observed decision influence are separate questions.
No use because the decision did not change.
feedback: Completion does not establish completeness or soundness. Distinguish report production, analytical quality and decision influence.
Broader influence needs more evidence than an unchanged final choice. Distinguish report production, analytical quality and decision influence.
Distinguish report production, analytical quality and decision influence.
A completed appraisal can be used without changing the decision. Distinguish report production, analytical quality and decision influence.
interactions.prompt_html:
7.1 Question 1

A completed report omits major benefits and leaves a decision unchanged. What is established?
interactions.solution_html: Distinguish report production, analytical quality and decision influence.

choices: A political choice against it is economically justified by definition.
Positive aggregate welfare under the stated valuation, without actual compensation or strict Pareto improvement.
feedback: Explaining motives does not justify poor appraisal. Separate the benchmark, distribution and actual decision.
Separate the benchmark, distribution and actual decision.
Aggregate gain does not remove individual losses. Separate the benchmark, distribution and actual decision.
Losses can coexist with positive net gain. Separate the benchmark, distribution and actual decision.
interactions.prompt_html:
7.2 Question 2

A project has aggregate gain 20 but some actual losers. What follows?
interactions.solution_html: Separate the benchmark, distribution and actual decision.

choices: Strategic incentives may matter, but optimism alone does not prove cheating.
Every forecast error is deliberate deception.
Independent scrutiny guarantees truth regardless of remit/capacity.
Late appraisal always has the same design influence as early appraisal.
feedback: Analyze principal-agent incentives while preserving uncertainty and safeguards’ limits.
Uncertainty and uncontrollable events can also cause error. Analyze principal-agent incentives while preserving uncertainty and safeguards’ limits.
Review quality depends on information and resources. Analyze principal-agent incentives while preserving uncertainty and safeguards’ limits.
Timing changes the available alternatives. Analyze principal-agent incentives while preserving uncertainty and safeguards’ limits.

sections.title: Check your reasoning: an offline quiz

sections.html:
If a document is called influential, ask which option/design changed. If forecast error is called fraud, separate information/incentives from unforeseeable events and inspect evidence.

  • Diagnose how an appraisal enters a decision
  • Distinguish quality/incentive failures from an automatic justification of political outcomes.

Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, Impact pathways, health valuation and standing, fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Impact pathways, health valuation and standing

Why can the same tonne of pollution cause different damages in different places? Emissions are only the beginning of the causal chain. An impact-pathway assessment follows a specified activity through dispersion, exposure and physical effects, then values those effects for an explicitly chosen population. This connects Week 2 externality and benefit-cost concepts to a practical damage estimate. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 1–5, 19

This map follows physical pp. 2–13 and 19. Its central distinction is between a pressure, an exposure, an impact and a money value; each arrow needs different evidence. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 2–13, 19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Top-down allocation versus bottom-up pathways; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Top-down allocation versus bottom-up pathways

The top-down diagram starts from a national damage estimate and a pollutant/activity allocation, then assigns a fraction of damage to the activity. It can be useful at an aggregate level but does not itself trace where a particular source's emissions travel. The bottom-up side begins with resource use (electricity production), follows SO2 emissions and atmospheric concentrations, ecosystem acidification/disruption, damage to forest production/non-production functions, and market/non-market valuation. Moving from a national average to a specific plant requires those physical and receptor distinctions. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 2

The lecture describes ExternE (Externalities of Energy) as an EU research series launched in 1991, initially concerned with airborne pollution from power plants and later transport, industry and other activities. It connects the method to DPSIR: driving forces, pressures, state, impacts and responses. Its note that “I” is monetized impacts describes the valuation endpoint of this application; one must still calculate physical impacts before money values can be attached. Damage depends on technology, operation, location, time, the included fuel-cycle boundary and population preferences. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 3–4

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage From concentration to a receptor-specific impact; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

From concentration to a receptor-specific impact

The Lauffen/Stuttgart example maps changes in sulfate concentration due to a plant's SO2 emissions across Europe. The pressure-map legend is in ng/m³. A separate receptor map shows where potentially exposed people live. The mortality/life-year-loss map combines exposure changes and population response: a high concentration change in a sparsely populated area need not create the largest health loss. Transboundary transport explains why damages need not stay within the emitting jurisdiction. The maps' different units and colour breaks must not be equated. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5–8

The source diagram moves from emissions through transport/chemistry to human/material/crop effects and only then money. Treating an emission quantity itself as a welfare loss would skip the receptor and valuation steps. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5

An exposure/dose/concentration-response function connects a specified exposure change with a specified outcome. Physical p. 9 gives the illustrative equation

\[\text{additional years of life lost}=3.9\times10^{-5}\,\Delta\text{Sulfate}\times\text{Population}.\]

The coefficient embodies a response per concentration unit and exposed person, so concentration units, population definition and exposure period must match its calibration. The slide does not supply those calibration units/time details; the ng/m³ map is not permission to assume the equation uses ng/m³. This formula supports the pathway logic, but not a reproducible numerical health estimate without that missing context. Its graph contrasts linear, nonlinear, threshold/limited and initially beneficial (“fertilizing”) shapes; choosing a straight line is a substantive response assumption, not an automatic property of every pollutant. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 9

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Endpoints and the source response-value table; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Endpoints and the source response-value table

The source includes particulate matter, SO2/NOx/NH3/VOC, CO2, heavy metals, noise and odour as burdens, with health, buildings/materials, crops, climate, landscape, visibility and cultural heritage as impact categories. Its p. 11 embedded comment adds respiratory admissions, restricted activity, congestive heart failure, nonfatal cancer, bronchitis and asthma; material ageing/soiling across metals, paint and stone; and crop-yield changes for barley, oats, potato, rye, sugar beet, wheat, sunflower, rice and tobacco. The category list does not assert that every burden affects every endpoint equally. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 11

Physical p. 10's complete table retains its endpoint units and numerical entries. Long-term PM2.5 adult mortality is expressed per year of life lost (YOLL), while infant mortality and bronchitis rows are per case. Short-term PM2.5/PM10/O3 rows distinguish restricted/work days, respiratory/cardiovascular admissions, asthma symptoms and mortality. A value per day cannot be multiplied by a number of people without specifying days per person; a value per YOLL is not a value per death. The CRF column is calibrated per 10 µg/m³, whereas the noise rows use weighted day-evening-night level \(L_{den}\) in dB and separate quadratic annoyance functions. The table alone does not supply baseline disease frequencies, age structure or valid concentration/noise ranges; do not extrapolate its curves outside their study context. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 10

A CRF such as 1.019 per 10 µg/m³ is a relative risk: for that concentration increment, the respiratory-admission rate is multiplied by 1.019, a 1.9% relative increase. It is not 1.019 extra admissions per person, and it is not a YOLL conversion. As an explicitly simplified calculation for a 10 µg/m³ increase from a reference exposure, if the baseline admission rate is \(r_0\) cases per person per year and the exposed population is \(N\), then

\[\Delta\text{cases}\approx N r_0(1.019-1).\]

For an illustrative baseline of 0.01 admissions per person per year and 100,000 exposed people, the reference count is 1,000 admissions per year and the increase is 19 per year. These invented round inputs teach the calculation; they are not an estimate for the lecture's plant. Other increments require the study's specified response function, and reductions from an already exposed observed baseline require the corresponding attributable-fraction calculation rather than silently reusing the same baseline. The baseline incidence, exposed population, period and endpoint must match. Mortality-to-YOLL estimation additionally needs life-expectancy/age information; a relative-risk coefficient alone cannot produce life years. This expands the source's pathway reasoning, supported by the manuscript's Methods/Table 1. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 10

Bounded reference verification: Máca, Melichar, Ščasný and Braun Kohlová (2017), “Valuing environmental health for informed policy-making,” Reviews on Environmental Health 32(1–2), 171–175, author manuscript physical pp. 3–5 (Methods/Table 1/perspectives), confirms that background population and incidence enter the assessment, and identifies the values as euro 2014. It also distinguishes physical modeling uncertainty from economic standing/value choices. Consulted author manuscript. This verifies interpretation of the supplied table, rather than importing its whole case study as assigned scope.

original_sections.html:
O014-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: A hypothetical bottom-up assessment studies a 10 \(\mu\mathrm{g/m^3}\) increase from a reference exposure. For this explicitly matched endpoint/population/year the supplied relative risk is \(RR=1.019\), baseline respiratory admissions are \(r_0=0.01\) cases/person/year and exposed population \(N=100000\). Trace activity through emissions/chemistry, concentrations, receptor population, physical impacts and valuation, and contrast a national top-down allocation. Interpret RR and derive the baseline count and additional annual admissions. Explain why the emissions map alone cannot rank damages, why these are admissions rather than YOLL, and why the lecture sulfate coefficient \(3.9\times10^{-5}\) cannot produce a calibrated plant estimate from its map without missing units/time. State the boundary for other increments or reductions from an already exposed baseline.

Complete solution and essential rubric: Bottom-up analysis specifies technology/operation/location/time, follows emissions through transport and chemistry to concentration changes at receptors, combines exposure with population/baseline response, then attaches matching values. Top-down allocation divides an aggregate damage estimate by activity/pollutant shares without tracing this plant’s spatial pathway. \(RR=1.019\) multiplies the admission rate for the supplied reference-to-exposed increment, a relative increase of \(1.900000\%\), not 1.019 extra cases/person. Reference admissions are \(Nr_0=100000(0.01)=1000.000000\) cases/year; additional admissions are \(\Delta I=Nr_0(RR-1)=19.000000\) cases/year. These are illustrative expected counts, not identified actual persons or a plant result. Population distribution can reverse the ranking of concentration changes and health impacts. Per-case counts cannot be treated as years of life lost; mortality-to-YOLL requires age/life-expectancy information, and values per day/case/YOLL must match endpoints. The source sulfate coefficient lacks calibration concentration/time details, so the map’s ng/m³ label is not permission to insert it. Other increments need the study’s response function; a reduction from an observed exposed baseline needs the corresponding attributable-fraction calculation, not an unqualified reuse of the reference-baseline formula. Linear, nonlinear and threshold shapes are substantive response assumptions. original_sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Required components: pathway_and_top_down_contrast, relative_risk_baseline_population_and_endpoint_units, calibration_boundary_and_uncertainty. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: RR interpreted as extra cases/person; concentration/map legend substituted for missing calibration; cases/deaths/YOLL interchanged; emissions directly declared a monetary damage.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. Every I/D form covers all components; W1, S1, the prerequisite and C1 are forbidden substitutes. A D form used for acquisition cannot later be counted again as delayed success. No teach-generated item may replace a named full check; additional verified explanation/practice is allowed under the unchanged method and may not fabricate evidence. Endpoint/period/reference must match and other increments need the stated response law. Pass requires all keyed reasoning; partial for a missing part; fail for the conflicting mechanism. This repairs a common inference only; it cannot substitute for a full numerical/capability check.

\[\text{additional years of life lost}=3.9\times10^{-5}\,\Delta\text{Sulfate}\times\text{Population}.\]

The category list does not assert that every burden affects every endpoint equally. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 11, 11

Physical p. 10's complete table retains its endpoint units and numerical entries. Long-term PM2.5 adult mortality is expressed per year of life lost (YOLL), while infant mortality and bronchitis rows are per case. Short-term PM2.5/PM10/O3 rows distinguish restricted/work days, respiratory/cardiovascular admissions, asthma symptoms and mortality. A value per day cannot be multiplied by a number of people without specifying days per person; a value per YOLL is not a value per death. The CRF column is calibrated per 10 µg/m³, whereas the noise rows use weighted day-evening-night level \(L_{den}\) in dB and separate quadratic annoyance functions. \[\Delta\text{cases}\approx N r_0(1.019-1).\]

Market prices can inform crop losses, material repair and medical-resource costs. Non-market values address pain, premature mortality risk, recreation, aesthetic and landscape losses that have no complete market transaction. Physical p. 14 decomposes Czech plant external costs in Kč/kWh into health, crops, buildings, biodiversity and climate. Read the bars within this source's price year and configuration labels; do not combine them with a current market tariff. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 15

The 2021 Danish illustration attributes about 74% (roughly 3,000 premature deaths) to foreign sources and 26% (roughly 1,000) to Danish sources. These rounded modeled source contributions are not additive exact counts of identified persons. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 16

Retain the differing year/boundary labels instead of treating the figures as one exact estimate. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 18

Standing chooses whose impacts enter the benefit-cost account: residents of the emitting country, EU residents, or people worldwide. Perspective Receptors whose health impacts count Values applied to matching endpoints
Czech narrow Czech population only Czech values: EU unit values adjusted by the Czech/EU GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, about 0.82 for 2014.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, trace impact pathways and convert matched relative risks into cases.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Trace a specified source through concentration/receptors to health impacts
  • Derive a matched reference-baseline risk-to-cases illustration
  • Identify missing calibration before monetization.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Identify economic externalities and apply conditional welfare criteria
  • Audit transport cost estimates by welfare component, valuation and aggregation
Check the foundations

Why does an uncounted emissions pressure need a receptor utility/production effect to be an economic externality? Is observed defensive spending automatically total external cost?

Reveal foundation explanation

An economic externality requires the neglected real effect on a receptor, not pressure alone. Defensive spending can omit residual harm; the correctly bounded total may need both.

Prompt: A hypothetical bottom-up assessment studies a 10 \(\mu\mathrm{g/m^3}\) increase from a reference exposure. For this explicitly matched endpoint/population/year the supplied relative risk is \(RR=1.019\), baseline respiratory admissions are \(r_0=0.01\) cases/person/year and exposed population \(N=100000\).

Trace activity through emissions/chemistry, concentrations, receptor population, physical impacts and valuation, and contrast a national top-down allocation. Interpret RR and derive the baseline count and additional annual admissions.

Explain why the emissions map alone cannot rank damages, why these are admissions rather than YOLL, and why the lecture sulfate coefficient \(3.9\times10^{-5}\) cannot produce a calibrated plant estimate from its map without missing units/time. State the boundary for other increments or reductions from an already exposed baseline.

original_sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Monetizing the change in health and welfare; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Monetizing the change in health and welfare

Market prices can inform crop losses, material repair and medical-resource costs. Non-market values address pain, premature mortality risk, recreation, aesthetic and landscape losses that have no complete market transaction. Willingness to pay (WTP) asks what someone would give up to avoid an adverse change or obtain an improvement. It is preference-based valuation of the change, not a statement that a person's intrinsic worth equals an invoice. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 12–13

For mortality, the source emphasizes WTP for a reduction in the risk of dying and the difficulty of eliciting life-expectancy changes. Quality-adjusted/disability-based values depend on context and cause; the lecture does not supply a universal price per QALY/DALY. For morbidity, cost of illness includes medical treatment and lost earnings, while pain/inconvenience require a separate welfare component. Development/fertility examples include risks of very low birth weight, birth defects, conception and IQ, plus IVF/training/earnings costs. Mental-health impacts can also be elicited through WTP studies. These components must be consistently defined to avoid counting the same loss twice. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 13

A useful agent synthesis of the pathway is

\[D=\sum_{r}\sum_{j}\Delta I_{rj}\,v_{rj},\]

where \(\Delta I_{rj}\) is the modeled change in endpoint \(j\) for receptor region \(r\) and \(v_{rj}\) is a value per matching endpoint unit, in a specified currency/year. This is not a new estimated response law: it states how checked physical changes and unit values combine. Changing receptor coverage or monetary weights changes \(D\) even if emissions are unchanged. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 5, 10, 12–13, 19

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the electricity comparisons show; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

What the electricity comparisons show

Physical p. 14 decomposes Czech plant external costs in Kč/kWh into health, crops, buildings, biodiversity and climate. Its plant totals differ, with the largest displayed bars around 3 Kč/kWh and smaller ones below 1; health is a major component. Physical p. 15 instead groups fuel/technology examples and explicitly states 2008 prices: displayed examples range from about 0.2–0.4 for some gas configurations to 3.5 Kč/kWh for a biomass example; brown-coal examples include 1.2, 2.1, 2.9 and other values, and biogas examples 0.4, 0.5, 0.9. Different technologies and operating/location assumptions matter: the diagram is not proof that every biomass plant is more damaging than every coal plant. These are historical external-cost assessments, not current electricity prices or full private generation costs. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 14–15

The full fuel/technology graphic retains every category and displayed number. Its six-component legend includes heavy metals as well as health/biodiversity/climate/materials/crops. Read the bars within this source's price year and configuration labels; do not combine them with a current market tariff. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 15

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Denmark and local versus imported pollution; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Denmark and local versus imported pollution

The 2021 Danish illustration attributes about 74% (roughly 3,000 premature deaths) to foreign sources and 26% (roughly 1,000) to Danish sources. Within the domestic pie it shows agriculture 22%, road traffic 21%, other mobile 7%, energy industries 7%, nonindustrial combustion 36%, others 7%; annotations include about 220 traffic deaths, about 70 each for other mobile/energy industries and about 330 household/SNAP2 deaths (about 240 from wood stoves). Danish contributions to deaths abroad, about 2,300, are a different receptor total. These rounded modeled source contributions are not additive exact counts of identified persons. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 16

The 2019–2021 EVA v7.1 table gives approximately 427 short-exposure and 3,460 long-exposure premature deaths, total about 3,890. Its rounded pollutant totals are SO2~25, O3~85, NO2 ~30 and PM2.5 ~3,740. PM2.5 includes primary particles and secondary material formed in the atmosphere. The slide lists “NH4” among emitted precursor gases; ammonia is NH3, while ammonium NH4+ occurs in particle salts. EEA's “Sources and emissions of air pollutants in Europe,” pollutant definitions/secondary-PM passage, verifies ammonia's precursor role: EEA source. The table's rounded rows/columns need not reconcile exactly, and blank cells should not be silently interpreted as exact zero. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 17

On p. 18 the narrative local shares (including unexplained Copenhagen 12%, 5%, 9%) and the table are different presentations: the table explicitly concerns 2030 Nordic capital-city contributions, giving city/country/abroad shares Copenhagen 15/23/63, Stockholm 35/18/47, Helsinki 25/21/53 and Reykjavík 43/27/30 percent. Rounding explains sums such as 101%; it does not resolve the unlabeled Copenhagen narrative figures. The common lesson is that local measures address only part of exposure, with traffic and wood stoves identified as large local sources. Retain the differing year/boundary labels instead of treating the figures as one exact estimate. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 18

Origin: reused complete checked passage Economic standing: whose loss counts?; fingerprint df3400bedc26d3001c8239c118b327ba73e7fd2889154e49a8fb01fc0337016f. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Economic standing: whose loss counts?

Standing chooses whose impacts enter the benefit-cost account: residents of the emitting country, EU residents, or people worldwide. Valuation then chooses Czech unit values, uniform EU values, or country-specific WTP. These are separate decisions. Physical p. 19's four perspectives—Czech narrow, Czech broad, EU and independent observer—produce different stacked cost totals and geographical shares for the same mining-limit variants. Narrow standing excludes much of the transboundary harm; broader standing includes it. The figure is therefore about ethical/policy boundaries and monetary weights as well as atmospheric science. The source article's Methods/perspectives verifies this distinction. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 19

The four perspectives use these distinct rules in the cited mining case:

Perspective Receptors whose health impacts count Values applied to matching endpoints
Czech narrow Czech population only Czech values: EU unit values adjusted by the Czech/EU GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, about 0.82 for 2014.
Czech broad All populations covered by the model, including foreign receptors The same Czech values for every included country.
EU policy maker All modelled populations; the case also includes affected non-EU receptors Uniform EU unit values for every included country.
Independent observer All modelled populations Country-specific values, adjusting EU values by each country's relative GDP per person at purchasing-power parity.

Thus Czech narrow versus broad changes the receptor boundary while holding the value rule fixed; Czech broad versus EU changes monetary weights with the modelled receptor boundary held fixed. The independent-observer calculation adds country-specific weights. “All modelled” is the study's finite geographical coverage, not proof that every global effect was measured. These are appraisal conventions, not claims that a person's intrinsic worth depends on GDP. The bounded manuscript's Methods/perspectives explains the rules. Máca et al. 2017, manuscript physical pp. 3–5.

The figure's variants 1–4 are alternative territorial mining limits: 1 keeps the existing limits; 2 revokes them at Bílina only; 3 revokes them at Bílina and partly at ČSA; 4 revokes them at both mines. They alter the coal-extraction/use path over the case's 2015–2050 horizon. Within a variant, changing perspective changes whose damages and which values enter; comparing variants within one perspective changes the mining scenario. The graph should not be read as four different pollutants or four valuation rules alone. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 19

Location-specific exposure/response and explicit standing are core because they explain why “one tonne = one universal damage price” fails. The historical plant/Danish/Nordic examples are supporting applications; their exact vintage, units and caveats remain part of their meaning. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 4–19

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, value matched health endpoints under explicit economic standing.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Compute a declared hypothetical endpoint valuation under all four checked standing rules
  • Distinguish population inclusion, monetary weights and historical scenario interpretation.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Trace impact pathways and convert matched relative risks into cases
  • Compare bargaining and policy transfers without confusing efficiency and equity
  • Apply complete social accounting and governance principles to bounded policy cases
Check the foundations

Why are physical cases needed before a per-case money value is applied? Does a potential Pareto gain ensure actual compensation, and does complete social accounting mean only domestic market costs?

Reveal foundation explanation

Cases times a matching value/case yields money; mixing cases with YOLL/day values is invalid. Potential compensation does not imply transfers occur. Complete accounting needs the stated receptor/market/nonmarket/future boundary and distribution. Require all three;
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Receptor boundary: The affected populations included in an appraisal.
  • Value convention: The per-endpoint monetary values assigned under the chosen standing.
  • Double counting: Adding overlapping valuations of the same welfare loss.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
Market prices can inform crop losses, material repair and medical-resource costs. Non-market values address pain, premature mortality risk, recreation, aesthetic and landscape losses that have no complete market transaction. Willingness to pay (WTP) asks what someone would give up to avoid an adverse change or obtain an improvement.

It is preference-based valuation of the change, not a statement that a person's intrinsic worth equals an invoice.

For mortality, the source emphasizes WTP for a reduction in the risk of dying and the difficulty of eliciting life-expectancy changes. Quality-adjusted/disability-based values depend on context and cause;

the lecture does not supply a universal price per QALY/DALY. For morbidity, cost of illness includes medical treatment and lost earnings, while pain/inconvenience require a separate welfare component.

Development/fertility examples include risks of very low birth weight, birth defects, conception and IQ, plus IVF/training/earnings costs. Mental-health impacts can also be elicited through WTP studies.

These components must be consistently defined to avoid counting the same loss twice.

A useful Explanation of the pathway is

\[D=\sum_{r}\sum_{j}\Delta I_{rj}\,v_{rj},\]

where \(\Delta I_{rj}\) is the modeled change in endpoint \(j\) for receptor region \(r\) and \(v_{rj}\) is a value per matching endpoint unit, in a specified currency/year. This is not a new estimated response law: it states how checked physical changes and unit values combine. Changing receptor coverage or monetary weights changes \(D\) even if emissions are unchanged.
sections.title: Monetizing the change in health and welfare

sections.html:
decomposes Czech plant external costs in Kč/kWh into health, crops, buildings, biodiversity and climate. Its plant totals differ, with the largest displayed bars around 3 Kč/kWh and smaller ones below 1;

health is a major component. instead groups fuel/technology examples and explicitly states 2008 prices: displayed examples range from about 0.2–0.4 for some gas configurations to 3.5 Kč/kWh for a biomass example; brown-coal examples include 1.2, 2.1, 2.9 and other values, and biogas examples 0.4, 0.5, 0.9.

Different technologies and operating/location assumptions matter: the diagram is not proof that every biomass plant is more damaging than every coal plant. These are historical external-cost assessments, not current electricity prices or full private generation costs.

The full fuel/technology graphic retains every category and displayed number. Its six-component legend includes heavy metals as well as health/biodiversity/climate/materials/crops. Read the bars within this source's price year and configuration labels; do not combine them with a current market tariff.
sections.title: What the electricity comparisons show

sections.html:
The 2021 Danish illustration attributes about 74% (roughly 3,000 premature deaths) to foreign sources and 26% (roughly 1,000) to Danish sources. Within the domestic pie it shows agriculture 22%, road traffic 21%, other mobile 7%, energy industries 7%, nonindustrial combustion 36%, others 7%;

annotations include about 220 traffic deaths, about 70 each for other mobile/energy industries and about 330 household/SNAP2 deaths (about 240 from wood stoves). Danish contributions to deaths abroad, about 2,300, are a different receptor total.

These rounded modeled source contributions are not additive exact counts of identified persons.

The 2019–2021 EVA v7.1 table gives approximately 427 short-exposure and 3,460 long-exposure premature deaths, total about 3,890. Its rounded pollutant totals are SO2~25, O3~85, NO2 ~30 and PM2.5 ~3,740.

PM2.5 includes primary particles and secondary material formed in the atmosphere. The slide lists “NH4” among emitted precursor gases; ammonia is NH3, while ammonium NH4+ occurs in particle salts.

EEA's “Sources and emissions of air pollutants in Europe,” pollutant definitions/secondary-PM passage, verifies ammonia's precursor role: EEA source. The table's rounded rows/columns need not reconcile exactly, and blank cells should not be silently interpreted as exact zero.

On p. 18 the narrative local shares (including unexplained Copenhagen 12%, 5%, 9%) and the table are different presentations: the table explicitly concerns 2030 Nordic capital-city contributions, giving city/country/abroad shares Copenhagen 15/23/63, Stockholm 35/18/47, Helsinki 25/21/53 and Reykjavík 43/27/30 percent. Rounding explains sums such as 101%;

it does not resolve the unlabeled Copenhagen narrative figures. The common lesson is that local measures address only part of exposure, with traffic and wood stoves identified as large local sources.

Retain the differing year/boundary labels instead of treating the figures as one exact estimate.
sections.title: Denmark and local versus imported pollution

sections.html:
Standing chooses whose impacts enter the benefit-cost account: residents of the emitting country, EU residents, or people worldwide. Valuation then chooses Czech unit values, uniform EU values, or country-specific WTP.

These are separate decisions. 's four perspectives—Czech narrow, Czech broad, EU and independent observer—produce different stacked cost totals and geographical shares for the same mining-limit variants. Narrow standing excludes much of the transboundary harm;

broader standing includes it. The figure is therefore about ethical/policy boundaries and monetary weights as well as atmospheric science.

The source article's Methods/perspectives verifies this distinction.

The four perspectives use these distinct rules in the cited mining case:

Perspective Receptors whose health impacts count Values applied to matching endpoints
Czech narrow Czech population only Czech values: EU unit values adjusted by the Czech/EU GDP per person at purchasing-power parity, about 0.82 for 2014.
Czech broad All populations covered by the model, including foreign receptors The same Czech values for every included country.
EU policy maker All modelled populations; the case also includes affected non-EU receptors Uniform EU unit values for every included country.
Independent observer All modelled populations Country-specific values, adjusting EU values by each country's relative GDP per person at purchasing-power parity.

Thus Czech narrow versus broad changes the receptor boundary while holding the value rule fixed; Czech broad versus EU changes monetary weights with the modelled receptor boundary held fixed.

The independent-observer calculation adds country-specific weights. “All modelled” is the study's finite geographical coverage, not proof that every global effect was measured.

These are appraisal conventions, not claims that a person's intrinsic worth depends on GDP. The bounded manuscript's Methods/perspectives explains the rules. Máca et al. 2017, manuscript .

The figure's variants 1–4 are alternative territorial mining limits: 1 keeps the existing limits; 2 revokes them at Bílina only; 3 revokes them at Bílina and partly at ČSA; 4 revokes them at both mines. They alter the coal-extraction/use path over the case's 2015–2050 horizon.

Within a variant, changing perspective changes whose damages and which values enter; comparing variants within one perspective changes the mining scenario.

The graph should not be read as four different pollutants or four valuation rules alone.

Location-specific exposure/response and explicit standing are core because they explain why “one tonne = one universal damage price” fails. The historical plant/Danish/Nordic examples are supporting applications; their exact vintage, units and caveats remain part of their meaning.

original_sections.html:
Origin: reused complete note introduction before its first subsection, Greenhouse effect, CO2 and Earth's energy, fingerprint 0e546eb44a26562a6831079998cde23dd5004f51769540e9057950e69279b643. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Greenhouse effect, CO2 and Earth's energy

Why does increasing atmospheric greenhouse-gas abundance alter climate, and where does the extra energy go? The lecture links radiation, concentrations and Earth's heat inventory. A temperature change is one consequence of an energy imbalance; ocean heating and ice change are also part of that response. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 20–39

This source-derived map follows physical pp. 21–39 and distinguishes a radiative mechanism, its evidence and a separate chemical effect of CO2. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 21–39

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage The radiative mechanism and its limits as an analogy; fingerprint 0e546eb44a26562a6831079998cde23dd5004f51769540e9057950e69279b643. Heading depth alone is adapted.

The radiative mechanism and its limits as an analogy

The Czech schematic on p. 22 shows incoming sunlight, some reflection by Earth's surface/atmosphere, absorption at the surface and outgoing longwave heat radiation. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit part of that infrared radiation, including downward emission. “Sluneční záření” is solar radiation, “Země” Earth and “atmosféra” atmosphere. The source's text describes this as absorption and “reflection” by greenhouse-gas molecules; the physical mechanism is absorption and re-emission, not a literal infrared mirror. The embedded comment likewise contrasts reflected sunlight and thermal radiation. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22, 24–25

The p. 23 historical teaching diagram gives absorbed sunlight \(235\,\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\), split into \(67\) atmospheric and \(168\) surface absorption. Thermal loss to space is \(195+40=235\,\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\); its larger internal downward/upward flows (including \(324\) downward and \(350\) absorbed greenhouse radiation) do not create energy but redistribute it within the surface–atmosphere system. These are the figure's illustrative older-budget values, not a current measurement of every energy flux. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 23

Natural greenhouse warming makes the surface warmer than it would be without this radiative effect. Change in greenhouse-gas abundance enhances that natural effect and changes the balance; a natural greenhouse effect by itself is not synonymous with ongoing human-caused climate change. CO2 is a central long-lived greenhouse gas, not the only one: methane, nitrous oxide and halogenated gases also matter. The source's description of CO2 as “most important” is read in its long-lived anthropogenic context rather than ignoring water-vapour/cloud feedback. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25

The lecture says CO2 supplied about two-thirds of the total human-produced greenhouse-gas heating influence in 2021. Keep its year and denominator; a share of total forcing and a share of the increase since 1990 are different statistics. Its list includes “black carbon” among gases on pp. 25/48; that is a category error. Black carbon is an aerosol/soot component, not a greenhouse gas. The European Commission JRC glossary explicitly defines it as an aerosol species: consulted definition. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25, 48

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Energy imbalance and the heat inventory; fingerprint 0e546eb44a26562a6831079998cde23dd5004f51769540e9057950e69279b643. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Energy imbalance and the heat inventory

Incoming energy minus outgoing radiation is the net energy flux. A positive imbalance means energy accumulates in Earth's system. The source's von Schuckmann et al. 2020 figure estimates \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) total heat gain over 1971–2018 (\(1\,\mathrm{ZJ}=10^{21}\text{ joules}\)), equivalent to mean \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\). Its 2010–2018 estimate is \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\). These different periods must remain attached to the values. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 36–37

For 1971–2018, the diagram partitions heat uptake into ocean 89%, land 6%, cryosphere 4% and atmosphere 1%. Parentheses give 2010–2018 values 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%. Ocean layers account for 52% upper 0–700 m, 28% at 700–2000 m and 9% below 2000 m in the longer period, versus 52/30/8% in the later period. The ocean dominates: surface-air temperature alone does not measure all the accumulated energy. Reference verification: the cited original's §6 and Figure 8/caption reproduce the periods/partition and clarify the conditional calculation: von Schuckmann et al.2020. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37

The figure's “\((-57\pm8)\ \mathrm{ppm}\)” is the paper's modeled CO2 reduction from an approximately 410 ppm reference needed to counter its estimated 2010–2018 imbalance under its radiative assumptions. It is neither an observed concentration decline nor an unconditional present-day policy target. The paper also notes other greenhouse-gas changes affect that calculation. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37

Physical p. 38 shows ocean-heat-content anomalies relative to 2005–2017 for 0–300, 0–700, 0–2000 and 700–2000 m layers, with ensemble 2σ shading. Some depth bands overlap, so adding all curves would double count heat. The caption specifies the ocean area 60°S–60°N and bathymetry restrictions for the contributing products; do not generalize its per-area axis into an unqualified global total. Rising curves and uncertainty bands support ocean warming within that study coverage. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 38

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage CO2 also changes ocean chemistry; fingerprint 0e546eb44a26562a6831079998cde23dd5004f51769540e9057950e69279b643. Heading depth alone is adapted.

CO2 also changes ocean chemistry

\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) dissolving into seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. Physical p. 39 reports surface-ocean pH falling from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\) since industrialization and contrasts an intact shell with one exposed to more corrosive conditions. “Acidification” means decreasing pH; it does not mean the average seawater has already become acidic in the everyday \(\mathrm{pH}<7\) sense. The shell comparison illustrates a biological consequence but supplies no full experiment protocol for estimating an effect size. This chemical pathway is distinct from the radiative-heating pathway even though both start with increased \(\mathrm{CO}_2\). 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 39

The core foundations are radiation/energy conservation, concentration-versus-emission units and period/reference baselines, because those distinctions keep every graph interpretable. Historical temperatures and the shell image support these mechanisms without becoming current datasets or independent causal estimates. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22–39

original_sections.html:
O016-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: In a hypothetical short energy budget, absorbed incoming energy is \(240\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\) and outgoing radiation is \(238\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\); internal downward infrared flux is larger than either external flow. Compute the net flux and explain the radiative greenhouse mechanism and conservation. For a separate hypothetical heat inventory of \(100\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) over a specified study period, assume ocean share \(89.0\%\) and compute ocean heat; interpret why atmospheric temperature alone is incomplete. Contrast these invented inputs with the source’s historical \(235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\) budget and 1971–2018 versus 2010–2018 heat estimates. Explain the conditional \(410\to353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) calculation, overlapping ocean-depth curves, black-carbon category and pH \(8.21\to8.10\) meaning.

Complete solution and essential rubric: Net external flux is \(240-238=2.000000\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\): positive, so energy accumulates. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared, including downward emission; this is not a literal mirror or creation of energy. Large internal gross exchanges redistribute energy and do not add independently to the external budget. Natural greenhouse warming and increased abundance enhancing it are different statements. Hypothetical ocean heat is \(100(0.89)=89.000000\ \mathrm{ZJ}\); ocean/land/ice/air together form the inventory. The source older budget balances \(67+168=195+40=235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\). Its measured-study estimates are \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) and \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 1971–2018, and \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 2010–2018, with ocean shares \(89\%\) versus \(90\%\); periods are not interchangeable. The paper’s about \(410-57=353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) is a conditional modeled reduction under its estimated imbalance/radiative assumptions and other-gas context, not an observed decline or unconditional current target. Overlapping \(0\text{–}300\), \(0\text{–}700\), \(0\text{–}2000\) and \(700\text{–}2000\) m bands cannot all be summed; region/baseline/\(2\sigma\) qualifications remain. Black carbon is an aerosol, not a greenhouse gas. \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) also alters seawater chemistry: pH declines by \(0.11\) from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\), still above \(7\); acidification is a decrease in pH, a separate pathway from radiative warming. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

interactions.prompt_html:
O016-I1

O016-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: In a hypothetical short energy budget, absorbed incoming energy is \(250\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\) and outgoing radiation is \(247\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\); internal downward infrared flux is larger than either external flow. Compute the net flux and explain the radiative greenhouse mechanism and conservation. For a separate hypothetical heat inventory of \(300\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) over a specified study period, assume ocean share \(89.0\%\) and compute ocean heat; interpret why atmospheric temperature alone is incomplete. Contrast these invented inputs with the source’s historical \(235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\) budget and 1971–2018 versus 2010–2018 heat estimates. Explain the conditional \(410\to353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) calculation, overlapping ocean-depth curves, black-carbon category and pH \(8.21\to8.10\) meaning.
interactions.solution_html:
Complete solution and essential rubric: Net external flux is \(250-247=3.000000\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\): positive, so energy accumulates. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared, including downward emission; this is not a literal mirror or creation of energy. Large internal gross exchanges redistribute energy and do not add independently to the external budget. Natural greenhouse warming and increased abundance enhancing it are different statements. Hypothetical ocean heat is \(300(0.89)=267.000000\ \mathrm{ZJ}\); ocean/land/ice/air together form the inventory. The source older budget balances \(67+168=195+40=235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\). Its measured-study estimates are \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) and \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 1971–2018, and \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 2010–2018, with ocean shares \(89\%\) versus \(90\%\); periods are not interchangeable. The paper’s about \(410-57=353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) is a conditional modeled reduction under its estimated imbalance/radiative assumptions and other-gas context, not an observed decline or unconditional current target. Overlapping \(0\text{–}300\), \(0\text{–}700\), \(0\text{–}2000\) and \(700\text{–}2000\) m bands cannot all be summed; region/baseline/\(2\sigma\) qualifications remain. Black carbon is an aerosol, not a greenhouse gas. \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) also alters seawater chemistry: pH declines by \(0.11\) from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\), still above \(7\); acidification is a decrease in pH, a separate pathway from radiative warming. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

I1/I2 are immediate checks; D1/D2 are distinct parallel variants reserved where possible for delayed checks. A delayed success requires an unused form before recap, no help/solution access, and at least 24 actual elapsed hours after acquisition and the most recent relevant teaching/solution exposure. Record intervening exposure. A calendar-date change alone is insufficient; an early D attempt is immediate evidence only.

original_sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

original_sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

Why does increasing atmospheric greenhouse-gas abundance alter climate, and where does the extra energy go? The lecture links radiation, concentrations and Earth's heat inventory. A temperature change is one consequence of an energy imbalance; ocean heating and ice change are also part of that response. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 20–39

This source-derived map follows physical pp. 21–39 and distinguishes a radiative mechanism, its evidence and a separate chemical effect of CO2. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 21–39

The radiative mechanism and its limits as an analogy

The Czech schematic on p. 22 shows incoming sunlight, some reflection by Earth's surface/atmosphere, absorption at the surface and outgoing longwave heat radiation. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit part of that infrared radiation, including downward emission. “Sluneční záření” is solar radiation, “Země” Earth and “atmosféra” atmosphere. The source's text describes this as absorption and “reflection” by greenhouse-gas molecules; the physical mechanism is absorption and re-emission, not a literal infrared mirror. The embedded comment likewise contrasts reflected sunlight and thermal radiation. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22, 24–25

The p. 23 historical teaching diagram gives absorbed sunlight \(235\,\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\), split into \(67\) atmospheric and \(168\) surface absorption. Thermal loss to space is \(195+40=235\,\mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\); its larger internal downward/upward flows (including \(324\) downward and \(350\) absorbed greenhouse radiation) do not create energy but redistribute it within the surface–atmosphere system. These are the figure's illustrative older-budget values, not a current measurement of every energy flux. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 23

Natural greenhouse warming makes the surface warmer than it would be without this radiative effect. Change in greenhouse-gas abundance enhances that natural effect and changes the balance; a natural greenhouse effect by itself is not synonymous with ongoing human-caused climate change. CO2 is a central long-lived greenhouse gas, not the only one: methane, nitrous oxide and halogenated gases also matter. The source's description of CO2 as “most important” is read in its long-lived anthropogenic context rather than ignoring water-vapour/cloud feedback. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25

The lecture says CO2 supplied about two-thirds of the total human-produced greenhouse-gas heating influence in 2021. Keep its year and denominator; a share of total forcing and a share of the increase since 1990 are different statistics. Its list includes “black carbon” among gases on pp. 25/48; that is a category error. Black carbon is an aerosol/soot component, not a greenhouse gas. The European Commission JRC glossary explicitly defines it as an aerosol species: consulted definition. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 24–25, 48

Concentration is not a global daily average by default

A concentration in ppm measures a fraction of atmospheric molecules; Mauna Loa is a particular station, a daily/monthly average is not an annual average, and a global marine-surface estimate is not a station reading. The seasonal cycle on the Mauna Loa graphs reflects Northern Hemisphere vegetation uptake/decay over the year, superimposed on a long-term human-driven rise. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 27–29

The source reports global \(419.3\ \mathrm{ppm}\) in 2023, global \(422.7\ \mathrm{ppm}\) in 2024, and a Mauna Loa daily \(425.68\ \mathrm{ppm}\) on 1 November 2025; the last is a source-reported dated station value, not independently reconstructed daily data. Its 2024 “increase over 2023” \(3.75\ \mathrm{ppm}\) is not the arithmetic difference of the displayed annual means (\(422.7-419.3=3.4\)). These statements mix vintages and annual-average versus within-year growth conventions. Reference check: NOAA's archived 21 May 2025 article reports global 2024 annual \(422.8\ \mathrm{ppm}\), within-2024 increase \(3.75\ \mathrm{ppm}\) and Mauna Loa annual \(424.61\ \mathrm{ppm}\). This explains why year/series/averaging definition must accompany a number; the source \(422.7\) differs from that reference and from its own p. 30 figure \(422.8\). NOAA, “Carbon dioxide levels in 2024”. These are documented historical comparisons, not live 2026 concentrations. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 28–30

Physical p. 30 compares an 800,000-year ice-core record (below about 300 ppm in that displayed record) with a modern dot. Its graphic labels 2024 average 422.8 ppm, while the caption still says 2022. The observed lesson is the large, rapid recent rise relative to those glacial/interglacial variations; the inconsistent caption year is retained explicitly rather than relabeling the figure silently. The source attributes the underlying reconstruction to Lüthi et al. 2008/NOAA NCEI. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 30

Reading the temperature evidence

Physical p. 32 is a deep-time reconstructed-temperature composite with nonuniform time scales: millions, then thousands of years, with geological periods and human-evolution labels. It illustrates long-run climate variation; straight visual slopes across scale changes do not measure comparable rates. Physical p. 33's heading mentions a “hockey stick dispute,” but its actual graph compares several historical temperature series over roughly 1840–2000. It is not, by itself, a millennium reconstruction or a resolution of every attribution dispute. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 32–33

Physical p. 34 is explicitly a one-day average 2 m temperature field for 25 February 2018 from GFS/ClimateReanalyzer. It shows spatial weather variation, not a global multi-decade trend or an anomaly with a stated climatology. Physical p. 35 instead gives a global land/sea temperature anomaly relative to 1961–1990, with an 1850–2023 plotted record and grey 95% confidence bounds. An anomaly is a difference from that reference mean, not the absolute surface temperature. It cannot be directly equated with a warming target relative to a different preindustrial baseline. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 34–35

Energy imbalance and the heat inventory

Incoming energy minus outgoing radiation is the net energy flux. A positive imbalance means energy accumulates in Earth's system. The source's von Schuckmann et al. 2020 figure estimates \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) total heat gain over 1971–2018 (\(1\,\mathrm{ZJ}=10^{21}\text{ joules}\)), equivalent to mean \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\). Its 2010–2018 estimate is \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\). These different periods must remain attached to the values. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 36–37

For 1971–2018, the diagram partitions heat uptake into ocean 89%, land 6%, cryosphere 4% and atmosphere 1%. Parentheses give 2010–2018 values 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%. Ocean layers account for 52% upper 0–700 m, 28% at 700–2000 m and 9% below 2000 m in the longer period, versus 52/30/8% in the later period. The ocean dominates: surface-air temperature alone does not measure all the accumulated energy. Reference verification: the cited original's §6 and Figure 8/caption reproduce the periods/partition and clarify the conditional calculation: von Schuckmann et al.2020. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37

The figure's “\((-57\pm8)\ \mathrm{ppm}\)” is the paper's modeled CO2 reduction from an approximately 410 ppm reference needed to counter its estimated 2010–2018 imbalance under its radiative assumptions. It is neither an observed concentration decline nor an unconditional present-day policy target. The paper also notes other greenhouse-gas changes affect that calculation. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 37

Physical p. 38 shows ocean-heat-content anomalies relative to 2005–2017 for 0–300, 0–700, 0–2000 and 700–2000 m layers, with ensemble 2σ shading. Some depth bands overlap, so adding all curves would double count heat. The caption specifies the ocean area 60°S–60°N and bathymetry restrictions for the contributing products; do not generalize its per-area axis into an unqualified global total. Rising curves and uncertainty bands support ocean warming within that study coverage. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 38

CO2 also changes ocean chemistry

\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) dissolving into seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. Physical p. 39 reports surface-ocean pH falling from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\) since industrialization and contrasts an intact shell with one exposed to more corrosive conditions. “Acidification” means decreasing pH; it does not mean the average seawater has already become acidic in the everyday \(\mathrm{pH}<7\) sense. The shell comparison illustrates a biological consequence but supplies no full experiment protocol for estimating an effect size. This chemical pathway is distinct from the radiative-heating pathway even though both start with increased \(\mathrm{CO}_2\). 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 39

The core foundations are radiation/energy conservation, concentration-versus-emission units and period/reference baselines, because those distinctions keep every graph interpretable. Historical temperatures and the shell image support these mechanisms without becoming current datasets or independent causal estimates. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 22–39

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, explain radiative balance, heat storage and ocean chemistry.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Explain infrared absorption/emission and external energy balance
  • Calculate a declared illustrative heat partition and preserve period/coverage/conditionality and ocean-chemistry distinctions.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Classify the four environmental functions
  • Trace material, waste and utility paths
Check the foundations

Which environmental function includes climate support, and why can the wider environmental system change wellbeing beyond the firms/households consumption loop?

Reveal foundation explanation

Climate belongs to global biospheric life-supporting services; resources/amenities/waste feedbacks affect wellbeing beyond consumption. Require the correct function and at least one explicit physical/utility path;
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Radiative imbalance: Absorbed incoming energy minus outgoing energy at the external boundary.
  • Heat inventory: Accumulated energy across ocean, land, ice and atmosphere over a stated period.
  • Ocean acidification: A decline in seawater pH, which can occur while pH remains above7.

its larger internal downward/upward flows (including \(324\) downward and \(350\) absorbed greenhouse radiation) do not create energy but redistribute it within the surface–atmosphere system. These are the figure's illustrative older-budget values, not a current measurement of every energy flux.

Natural greenhouse warming makes the surface warmer than it would be without this radiative effect. Change in greenhouse-gas abundance enhances that natural effect and changes the balance; a natural greenhouse effect by itself is not synonymous with ongoing human-caused climate change.

CO2 is a central long-lived greenhouse gas, not the only one: methane, nitrous oxide and halogenated gases also matter. The source's description of CO2 as “most important” is read in its long-lived anthropogenic context rather than ignoring water-vapour/cloud feedback.

The lecture says CO2 supplied about two-thirds of the total human-produced greenhouse-gas heating influence in 2021. Keep its year and denominator;

a share of total forcing and a share of the increase since 1990 are different statistics. Its list includes “black carbon” among gases on pp. 25/48;

that is a category error. Black carbon is an aerosol/soot component, not a greenhouse gas.

The European Commission JRC glossary explicitly defines it as an aerosol species: consulted definition.

Concentration is not a global daily average by default

A concentration in ppm measures a fraction of atmospheric molecules; Mauna Loa is a particular station, a daily/monthly average is not an annual average, and a global marine-surface estimate is not a station reading. The seasonal cycle on the Mauna Loa graphs reflects Northern Hemisphere vegetation uptake/decay over the year, superimposed on a long-term human-driven rise.

The source reports global \(419.3\ \mathrm{ppm}\) in 2023, global \(422.7\ \mathrm{ppm}\) in 2024, and a Mauna Loa daily \(425.68\ \mathrm{ppm}\) on 1 November 2025; the last is a source-reported dated station value, not independently reconstructed daily data.

Its 2024 “increase over 2023” \(3.75\ \mathrm{ppm}\) is not the arithmetic difference of the displayed annual means (\(422.7-419.3=3.4\)). These statements mix vintages and annual-average versus within-year growth conventions. Reference check: NOAA's archived 21 May 2025 article reports global 2024 annual \(422.8\ \mathrm{ppm}\), within-2024 increase \(3.75\ \mathrm{ppm}\) and Mauna Loa annual \(424.61\ \mathrm{ppm}\).

This explains why year/series/averaging definition must accompany a number; the source \(422.7\) differs from that reference and from its own p. 30 figure \(422.8\). NOAA, “Carbon dioxide levels in 2024”.

These are documented historical comparisons, not live 2026 concentrations.

compares an 800,000-year ice-core record (below about 300 ppm in that displayed record) with a modern dot. Its graphic labels 2024 average 422.8 ppm, while the caption still says 2022.

The observed lesson is the large, rapid recent rise relative to those glacial/interglacial variations; the inconsistent caption year is retained explicitly rather than relabeling the figure silently.

The source attributes the underlying reconstruction to Lüthi et al. 2008/NOAA NCEI.

Reading the temperature evidence

is a deep-time reconstructed-temperature composite with nonuniform time scales: millions, then thousands of years, with geological periods and human-evolution labels. It illustrates long-run climate variation;

straight visual slopes across scale changes do not measure comparable rates. 's heading mentions a “hockey stick dispute,” but its actual graph compares several historical temperature series over roughly 1840–2000. It is not, by itself, a millennium reconstruction or a resolution of every attribution dispute.

is explicitly a one-day average 2 m temperature field for 25 February 2018 from GFS/ClimateReanalyzer. It shows spatial weather variation, not a global multi-decade trend or an anomaly with a stated climatology. instead gives a global land/sea temperature anomaly relative to 1961–1990, with an 1850–2023 plotted record and grey 95% confidence bounds.

An anomaly is a difference from that reference mean, not the absolute surface temperature. It cannot be directly equated with a warming target relative to a different preindustrial baseline.

Energy imbalance and the heat inventory

Incoming energy minus outgoing radiation is the net energy flux. A positive imbalance means energy accumulates in Earth's system.

The source's von Schuckmann et al. 2020 figure estimates \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) total heat gain over 1971–2018 (\(1\,\mathrm{ZJ}=10^{21}\text{ joules}\)), equivalent to mean \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\). Its 2010–2018 estimate is \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\).

These different periods must remain attached to the values.

For 1971–2018, the diagram partitions heat uptake into ocean 89%, land 6%, cryosphere 4% and atmosphere 1%. Parentheses give 2010–2018 values 90%, 5%, 3%, 2%.

Ocean layers account for 52% upper 0–700 m, 28% at 700–2000 m and 9% below 2000 m in the longer period, versus 52/30/8% in the later period. The ocean dominates: surface-air temperature alone does not measure all the accumulated energy. Reference verification: the cited original's §6 and Figure 8/caption reproduce the periods/partition and clarify the conditional calculation: von Schuckmann et al.2020.

The figure's “\((-57\pm8)\ \mathrm{ppm}\)” is the paper's modeled CO2 reduction from an approximately 410 ppm reference needed to counter its estimated 2010–2018 imbalance under its radiative assumptions. It is neither an observed concentration decline nor an unconditional present-day policy target. The paper also notes other greenhouse-gas changes affect that calculation.

shows ocean-heat-content anomalies relative to 2005–2017 for 0–300, 0–700, 0–2000 and 700–2000 m layers, with ensemble 2σ shading. Some depth bands overlap, so adding all curves would double count heat.

The caption specifies the ocean area 60°S–60°N and bathymetry restrictions for the contributing products; do not generalize its per-area axis into an unqualified global total.

Rising curves and uncertainty bands support ocean warming within that study coverage.

CO2 also changes ocean chemistry

\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) dissolving into seawater changes carbonate chemistry and lowers pH. reports surface-ocean pH falling from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\) since industrialization and contrasts an intact shell with one exposed to more corrosive conditions. “Acidification” means decreasing pH;

it does not mean the average seawater has already become acidic in the everyday \(\mathrm{pH}<7\) sense. The shell comparison illustrates a biological consequence but supplies no full experiment protocol for estimating an effect size.

This chemical pathway is distinct from the radiative-heating pathway even though both start with increased \(\mathrm{CO}_2\).

The core foundations are radiation/energy conservation, concentration-versus-emission units and period/reference baselines, because those distinctions keep every graph interpretable. Historical temperatures and the shell image support these mechanisms without becoming current datasets or independent causal estimates.

sections.html:
Prompt: In a hypothetical short energy budget, absorbed incoming energy is \(240\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\) and outgoing radiation is \(238\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\); internal downward infrared flux is larger than either external flow.

Compute the net flux and explain the radiative greenhouse mechanism and conservation. For a separate hypothetical heat inventory of \(100\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) over a specified study period, assume ocean share \(89.0\%\) and compute ocean heat;

interpret why atmospheric temperature alone is incomplete. Contrast these invented inputs with the source’s historical \(235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\) budget and 1971–2018 versus 2010–2018 heat estimates.

Explain the conditional \(410\to353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) calculation, overlapping ocean-depth curves, black-carbon category and pH \(8.21\to8.10\) meaning.

Solution: Net external flux is \(240-238=2.000000\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\): positive, so energy accumulates. Greenhouse gases/clouds absorb and emit thermal infrared, including downward emission;

this is not a literal mirror or creation of energy. Large internal gross exchanges redistribute energy and do not add independently to the external budget.

Natural greenhouse warming and increased abundance enhancing it are different statements. Hypothetical ocean heat is \(100(0.89)=89.000000\ \mathrm{ZJ}\);

ocean/land/ice/air together form the inventory. The source older budget balances \(67+168=195+40=235\ \mathrm{W/m^{2}}\).

Its measured-study estimates are \(358\pm37\ \mathrm{ZJ}\) and \(0.47\pm0.10\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 1971–2018, and \(0.87\pm0.12\ \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{m}^{2}\) for 2010–2018, with ocean shares \(89\%\) versus \(90\%\); periods are not interchangeable.

The paper’s about \(410-57=353\ \mathrm{ppm}\) is a conditional modeled reduction under its estimated imbalance/radiative assumptions and other-gas context, not an observed decline or unconditional current target. Overlapping \(0\text{–}300\), \(0\text{–}700\), \(0\text{–}2000\) and \(700\text{–}2000\) m bands cannot all be summed;

region/baseline/\(2\sigma\) qualifications remain. Black carbon is an aerosol, not a greenhouse gas. \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) also alters seawater chemistry: pH declines by \(0.11\) from \(8.21\) to \(8.10\), still above \(7\);

acidification is a decrease in pH, a separate pathway from radiative warming.

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, interpret concentration and temperature records with dates and baselines.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Compare supplied concentration/temperature records using actual series, averaging, reference periods and uncertainty, without relabeling historical observations as current data.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Explain radiative balance, heat storage and ocean chemistry
Check the foundations

What does positive net energy flux imply for stored heat, and is a local one-day field the same object as a whole-system long-period heat inventory?

Reveal foundation explanation

Positive net flux accumulates heat; a location/day field and a multicomponent long-period inventory have different spatial/time/variable definitions.

• Concentration: An atmospheric mixing ratio for a specified gas, location and averaging period.

A concentration in ppm measures a fraction of atmospheric molecules; Mauna Loa is a particular station, a daily/monthly average is not an annual average, and a global marine-surface estimate is not a station reading. The seasonal cycle on the Mauna Loa graphs reflects Northern Hemisphere vegetation uptake/decay over the year, superimposed on a long-term human-driven rise.

These statements mix vintages and annual-average versus within-year growth conventions.
