original_sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

original_sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Carbon units, stocks, flows and emissions charts; fingerprint 53486825eda1979d271237a20403c33c1e0ba9e54a5c9ef0191ae8468ecb2b9d. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Carbon units, stocks, flows and emissions charts

Which quantities can be compared when a chart says carbon, CO2, CO2-equivalent, concentration or per person? The optional-reading section supplies unit conversions and charts. Reading their units and boundaries is a foundation for both climate-policy comparisons and monetary costs per tonne. These pages are included because they are inside the selected supplied document, while retaining their “Voluntary readings” status. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 46–58

The map follows pp. 47–58 and uses p. 26's GWP definition to separate mass conversion from warming equivalence. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 26, 47–58

Carbon mass and the inverse price conversion

A tonne of carbon (t C) measures carbon atoms; a tonne of CO2 measures the whole molecule. Using source atomic masses 12 for C and 16 for O, molecular mass is \(12+2(16)=44\). Therefore

\[1\ \mathrm{tCO_2}=\frac{12}{44}\ \mathrm{tC}\approx0.2727\ \mathrm{tC},\qquad 1\ \mathrm{tC}=\frac{44}{12}\ \mathrm{tCO_2}\approx3.667\ \mathrm{tCO_2}.\]

For the same total payment, multiplying mass by \(44/12\) requires dividing price per mass by \(44/12\). Thus

\[100\ \$/\mathrm{tC}\times\frac{12}{44}=27.27\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2},\qquad 100\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2}\times\frac{44}{12}=366.67\ \$/\mathrm{tC}.\]

Confusing quantity conversion with price conversion reverses the comparison. Neither operation is a GWP conversion for methane or other gases. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 48

GWP and CO2-equivalent emissions

Global warming potential (GWP) compares the time-integrated radiative effect of a pulse mass of gas with an equal mass of CO2 over a stated horizon; CO2's value is one by definition. For a chosen metric, horizon and assessment,

\[E_{CO_2e}=\sum_g m_g GWP_g,\]

where \(m_g\) is emitted mass of gas \(g\). This is agent-expanded notation for the source's examples, not a new emissions estimate. A million tonnes of \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) at \(\mathrm{GWP}_{100}=25\) becomes \(25\) million tonnes \(\mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{e}\); a million tonnes of \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) at \(298\) becomes \(298\) million tonnes \(\mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{e}\). 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 25–26, 53

The p. 26 table explicitly identifies IPCC AR4 (2007) values; retain that vintage. Its complete entries are:

Gas Lifetime, years GWP20 GWP100 GWP500
CH4 12 72 25 7.6
N2O 114 289 298 153
HFC-23 270 12000 14800 12200
HFC-134a 14 3830 1430 425
SF6 3200 16300 22800 32600

These are the supplied historical values, not current universal constants or evidence that later charts use exactly the same assessment. A CO2e label needs its horizon and metric convention for exact comparison. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 26

Trace-gas concentration and AGGI

Physical p. 47 uses ppm for CO2, ppb for CH4/N2O and ppt for halocarbons. Each panel has its own scale. The historical plots show rising CO2, CH4 and N2O, peaking/declining CFC-11/CFC-12, and rising HCFC-22/HFC-134a over their displayed period ending around 2020. Heights across separate axes are not direct abundance comparisons. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 47

Physical p. 49 contrasts CO2-alone concentration with a CO2-equivalent mixing ratio obtained by matching forcing from long-lived gases, and a separate AGGI right axis. This equivalent concentration is not a sum of GWP-weighted emission tonnes. The slide does not explain AGGI's baseline. Supplementary definition: NOAA defines AGGI as long-lived-gas effective radiative forcing relative to its 1990 value, making 1990 equal one. It is a forcing ratio, not an emissions flow or forecast. NOAA AGGI, Introduction. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 49

Why a stable flow can increase an atmospheric stock

Concentration measures an atmospheric stock; emissions add mass per unit time and sinks remove it. A simple agent synthesis of this accounting is

\[A_{t+1}-A_t=E_t-R_t,\]

where \(A_t\) is atmospheric mass, \(E_t\) emissions and \(R_t\) net removal over the same interval, all in compatible mass units. A constant positive emission flow still increases \(A\) whenever \(E_t>R_t\). Stabilizing emissions differs from bringing net additions to zero. Connecting mass to ppm requires an atmospheric-mass conversion, which the source does not supply. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51

Physical p. 50 uses separate axes for concentration (ppm) and annual emissions (gigatonnes). Its 1751–2022 graph and caption's historical increase from about 5 Gt/year in the mid twentieth century to over 35 Gt/year illustrate different quantities, not a fitted causal coefficient. Physical p. 51 draws a flat emission line and rising concentration curve on uncalibrated x1–x20 axes with no dates, units or source. Its curved stock path does not follow from constant net additions alone, which would give a linear stock rise. Use it for stock-flow intuition, not a quantitative carbon-cycle law. NOAA's atmospheric-CO2 article independently explains that emissions exceeding sinks raise atmospheric abundance: “Fossil fuels overwhelm Earth's natural carbon cycle”. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 50–51

Sector quantities: gas and denominator first

Physical p. 52 is 2020 world per-capita CO2, with these displayed sector values in tonnes per person for the reported year: electricity/heat 1.93, transport 0.91, manufacturing/construction 0.79, buildings 0.35, industry 0.21, land-use/forestry 0.15, aviation/shipping 0.12 and fugitive emissions 0.03. It credits Climate Watch (2023) and population sources (2023). It is not an all-gas CO2e total, and no finer time aggregation is supplied. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 52

Physical p. 53 instead shows CH4 and N2O in CO2e, roughly 1990–2021, with a GWP100 footnote. Agriculture is largest in each panel; methane also has substantial fugitive and waste emissions. The other methane series are land-use/forestry, other fuel combustion and industry; the other N2O series are industry, waste, land-use/forestry, fugitive and other fuel combustion. The panels have different scales, so their line heights do not directly compare gas mass. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 53

Physical p. 54 combines all-gas CO2e by sector: electricity/heat, transport, manufacturing/construction, agriculture, fugitive emissions, industry, buildings, waste, land-use/forestry, aviation/shipping and other fuel combustion. Its source is Climate Watch (2023). End-period downturns in some historical series do not establish a permanent future trend. Exact comparison with the AR4 table requires checking the chart dataset's assessment convention, which the slide does not establish. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54

The complete graphic preserves each sector and its 100-year CO2e qualification. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 54

Per person, population and totals

Physical p. 55 encodes per-person emissions by rectangle height, population by width, and total emissions by area. A populous country can have a large area but lower per-person emissions than a small country. Labels emphasize countries with large totals rather than a complete per-capita ranking. Its title says CO2 but the vertical axis says tCO2e, so the supplied graphic leaves the gas/metric boundary ambiguous; do not silently treat the two labels as interchangeable. The illustration lacks a clear data-year citation and is not a current league table. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 55

The p. 56 map reports 2020 total GHG CO2e per person including land-use/forestry, credits Climate Watch (2023), and has a negative legend range and hatched “no data.” The p. 57 map reports 2021 CO2/CH4/N2O in GWP100 CO2e including land-use, credits Jones et al. (2023), and notes that land-use emissions can be negative. Different years, sources and gas/boundary labels mean their visual differences cannot be read as one harmonized annual change. Negative net land-use emissions and missing data are different categories: hatching is not zero emissions. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 56–57

Physical p. 58 compares 2018 CO2 per person with GDP per person in 2011 international dollars adjusted for purchasing power and inflation. Its GDP axis is logarithmic ($1000, $2000, $5000, $10000, $20000, $50000), so equal plot distances are not equal dollar increments. Emissions cover fossil fuels and cement, explicitly excluding land-use change. The positive cross-country association has considerable variation and does not identify a causal effect of income. Sources are the Global Carbon Project and Maddison Project Database 2020 (Bolt and van Zanden, 2020). 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 58

Unit consistency, stock-flow accounting and total-versus-per-person denominators are core foundations because they unlock these comparisons. Historical charts remain context; none is relabeled as current or used as an unqualified causal estimate. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 47–58

O018-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Use a declared hypothetical inventory with \(12\ \mathrm{tC}\) and price \(p_C=100\ \mathrm{currency\ units/tC}\). Convert mass and the price for the same total payment into tCO2 and price/tCO2. For separate emissions of 1 t CH4 and 0.5 t N2O, use the explicitly historical AR4 GWP100 factors 25 and 298 to compute tCO2e and distinguish it from CO2-equivalent atmospheric concentration/AGGI. With atmospheric mass \(A_t=100\), emissions \(10\) and removals \(6\) in common mass units over one interval, compute \(A_{t+1}\) and explain stable-flow versus stable-stock claims and missing ppm conversion. Constant net additions imply a linear stock increase, not the source’s uncalibrated curved law; mass-to-ppm conversion is absent. Country totals are \(10.00000000\) and \(5.00000000\) million tonnes: height is per person, width population, area total; a higher per-person value need not imply larger total. Complete solution and essential rubric: Mass scales as \(m_{CO_2}=m_C(44/12)=33.00000000\ \mathrm{tCO_2}\), while the equal-payment unit price scales inversely, \(p_{CO_2}=p_C(12/44)=21.81818182\) currency units/tCO2. Both products give the same total \(720.00000000\) currency units. This molecular-mass conversion is not methane GWP. Historical AR4 GWP100 gives \(E_{CO_2e}=1.5(25)+0.2(298)=97.10000000\) t CO2e; horizon/assessment must be declared, not treated as current universal constants. A forcing-equivalent atmospheric mixing ratio is another quantity; AGGI is an index of long-lived-gas forcing normalized to 1 in the base year 1990, not emitted tonnes. Stock accounting gives \(A_{t+1}=A_t+E_t-R_t=155.00000000\); a stable positive gross flow grows the stock whenever emissions exceed removals. Constant net additions imply a linear stock increase, not the source’s uncalibrated curved law; mass-to-ppm conversion is absent. Country totals are \(15.00000000\) and \(8.40000000\) million tonnes: height is per person, width population, area total; a higher per-person value need not imply larger total. Exact comparisons require common year/source/gas boundaries (CO2 versus all-gas CO2e, land-use inclusion), metric horizon and vintage. The source title/axis CO2/CO2e conflict is unresolved; negative net land-use is not missing/hatched data. sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, convert carbon quantities and audit stocks, flows and emissions charts.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Apply carbon/CO2price and mass conversions, stated historical GWPweights, stock-flow accounting and population/chart boundaries; retain voluntary-reading status.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Interpret harvest and waste capacity comparisons
  • Interpret concentration and temperature records with dates and baselines
Check the foundations

Does a renewable label prove harvest is sustainable without comparing same-interval growth? Is ppm concentration automatically a tonnes-per-year flow?

Reveal foundation explanation

No to both: harvest and yield need a comparable interval and net balance; ppm is an atmospheric fraction/stock measure, not an emissions flow.

sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
Which quantities can be compared when a chart says carbon, CO2, CO2-equivalent, concentration or per person? The optional-reading section supplies unit conversions and charts.

Reading their units and boundaries is a foundation for both climate-policy comparisons and monetary costs per tonne. These pages are included because they are inside the selected supplied document, while retaining their “Voluntary readings” status.

The map follows pp. 47–58 and uses p. 26's GWP definition to separate mass conversion from warming equivalence.

4.1 Carbon mass and the inverse price conversion

A tonne of carbon (t C) measures carbon atoms; a tonne of CO2 measures the whole molecule. Using source atomic masses 12 for C and 16 for O, molecular mass is \(12+2(16)=44\). Therefore

\[1\ \mathrm{tCO_2}=\frac{12}{44}\ \mathrm{tC}\approx0.2727\ \mathrm{tC},\qquad 1\ \mathrm{tC}=\frac{44}{12}\ \mathrm{tCO_2}\approx3.667\ \mathrm{tCO_2}.\]

For the same total payment, multiplying mass by \(44/12\) requires dividing price per mass by \(44/12\). Thus

\[100\ \$/\mathrm{tC}\times\frac{12}{44}=27.27\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2},\qquad 100\ \$/\mathrm{tCO_2}\times\frac{44}{12}=366.67\ \$/\mathrm{tC}.\]

Confusing quantity conversion with price conversion reverses the comparison. Neither operation is a GWP conversion for methane or other gases.

4.2 GWP and CO2-equivalent emissions

Global warming potential (GWP) compares the time-integrated radiative effect of a pulse mass of gas with an equal mass of CO2 over a stated horizon; CO2's value is one by definition. For a chosen metric, horizon and assessment,

\[E_{CO_2e}=\sum_g m_g GWP_g,\]

where \(m_g\) is emitted mass of gas \(g\). This is Explanation for the source's examples, not a new emissions estimate. A million tonnes of \(\mathrm{CH}_4\) at \(\mathrm{GWP}_{100}=25\) becomes \(25\) million tonnes \(\mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{e}\); a million tonnes of \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}\) at \(298\) becomes \(298\) million tonnes \(\mathrm{CO}_2\mathrm{e}\).

The p. 26 table explicitly identifies IPCC AR4 (2007) values; retain that vintage. Its complete entries are:

Gas Lifetime, years GWP20 GWP100 GWP500
CH4 12 72 25 7.6
N2O 114 289 298 153
HFC-23 270 12000 14800 12200
HFC-134a 14 3830 1430 425
SF6 3200 16300 22800 32600

These are the supplied historical values, not current universal constants or evidence that later charts use exactly the same assessment. A CO2e label needs its horizon and metric convention for exact comparison.

4.3 Trace-gas concentration and AGGI

uses ppm for CO2, ppb for CH4/N2O and ppt for halocarbons. Each panel has its own scale. The historical plots show rising CO2, CH4 and N2O, peaking/declining CFC-11/CFC-12, and rising HCFC-22/HFC-134a over their displayed period ending around 2020. Heights across separate axes are not direct abundance comparisons.

contrasts CO2-alone concentration with a CO2-equivalent mixing ratio obtained by matching forcing from long-lived gases, and a separate AGGI right axis. This equivalent concentration is not a sum of GWP-weighted emission tonnes.

The slide does not explain AGGI's baseline. Supplementary definition: NOAA defines AGGI as long-lived-gas effective radiative forcing relative to its 1990 value, making 1990 equal one. It is a forcing ratio, not an emissions flow or forecast. NOAA AGGI, Introduction.

4.4 Why a stable flow can increase an atmospheric stock

Concentration measures an atmospheric stock; emissions add mass per unit time and sinks remove it. A simple Explanation of this accounting is

\[A_{t+1}-A_t=E_t-R_t,\]

where \(A_t\) is atmospheric mass, \(E_t\) emissions and \(R_t\) net removal over the same interval, all in compatible mass units. A constant positive emission flow still increases \(A\) whenever \(E_t>R_t\). Stabilizing emissions differs from bringing net additions to zero. Connecting mass to ppm requires an atmospheric-mass conversion, which the source does not supply.

uses separate axes for concentration (ppm) and annual emissions (gigatonnes). Its 1751–2022 graph and caption's historical increase from about 5 Gt/year in the mid twentieth century to over 35 Gt/year illustrate different quantities, not a fitted causal coefficient. draws a flat emission line and rising concentration curve on uncalibrated x1–x20 axes with no dates, units or source.

Its curved stock path does not follow from constant net additions alone, which would give a linear stock rise. Use it for stock-flow intuition, not a quantitative carbon-cycle law.

NOAA's atmospheric-CO2 article independently explains that emissions exceeding sinks raise atmospheric abundance: “Fossil fuels overwhelm Earth's natural carbon cycle”.

4.5 Sector quantities: gas and denominator first

is 2020 world per-capita CO2, with these displayed sector values in tonnes per person for the reported year: electricity/heat 1.93, transport 0.91, manufacturing/construction 0.79, buildings 0.35, industry 0.21, land-use/forestry 0.15, aviation/shipping 0.12 and fugitive emissions 0.03. It credits Climate Watch (2023) and population sources (2023).

It is not an all-gas CO2e total, and no finer time aggregation is supplied.

instead shows CH4 and N2O in CO2e, roughly 1990–2021, with a GWP100 footnote. Agriculture is largest in each panel;

methane also has substantial fugitive and waste emissions. The other methane series are land-use/forestry, other fuel combustion and industry;

the other N2O series are industry, waste, land-use/forestry, fugitive and other fuel combustion. The panels have different scales, so their line heights do not directly compare gas mass.

combines all-gas CO2e by sector: electricity/heat, transport, manufacturing/construction, agriculture, fugitive emissions, industry, buildings, waste, land-use/forestry, aviation/shipping and other fuel combustion. Its source is Climate Watch (2023).

End-period downturns in some historical series do not establish a permanent future trend. Exact comparison with the AR4 table requires checking the chart dataset's assessment convention, which the slide does not establish.

The complete graphic preserves each sector and its 100-year CO2e qualification.

4.6 Per person, population and totals

encodes per-person emissions by rectangle height, population by width, and total emissions by area. A populous country can have a large area but lower per-person emissions than a small country.

Labels emphasize countries with large totals rather than a complete per-capita ranking. Its title says CO2 but the vertical axis says tCO2e, so the supplied graphic leaves the gas/metric boundary ambiguous;

do not silently treat the two labels as interchangeable. The illustration lacks a clear data-year citation and is not a current league table.

The p. 56 map reports 2020 total GHG CO2e per person including land-use/forestry, credits Climate Watch (2023), and has a negative legend range and hatched “no data.” The p. 57 map reports 2021 CO2/CH4/N2O in GWP100 CO2e including land-use, credits Jones et al. (2023), and notes that land-use emissions can be negative. Different years, sources and gas/boundary labels mean their visual differences cannot be read as one harmonized annual change.

Negative net land-use emissions and missing data are different categories: hatching is not zero emissions.

compares 2018 CO2 per person with GDP per person in 2011 international dollars adjusted for purchasing power and inflation. Its GDP axis is logarithmic ($1000, $2000, $5000, $10000, $20000, $50000), so equal plot distances are not equal dollar increments.

Emissions cover fossil fuels and cement, explicitly excluding land-use change. The positive cross-country association has considerable variation and does not identify a causal effect of income.

Sources are the Global Carbon Project and Maddison Project Database 2020 (Bolt and van Zanden, 2020).

Unit consistency, stock-flow accounting and total-versus-per-person denominators are core foundations because they unlock these comparisons. Historical charts remain context; none is relabeled as current or used as an unqualified causal estimate.

original_sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

original_sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation; fingerprint dc3f2be26999e63b812767c1b200564516dc4fb9a19243829ec7abf3f0ff1c90. Heading depth alone is adapted.

Climate scenarios, policy and adaptation

A climate scenario asks what follows if a coherent set of social, technological, emissions and policy conditions occurs. It is not an assigned probability or an unconditional forecast. The lecture uses older RCP projections alongside newer SSP-labelled examples; the two naming systems and their temperature baselines must be distinguished. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45

This map follows pp. 40–45 and 43's paired emissions/concentration graphic; it explains why the policy discussion needs both mitigation and adaptation. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45

SSP assumptions and RCP forcing pathways

The source presents SSP2, “middle of the road,” as its baseline socioeconomic narrative, extending major development trends without a large assumed policy/technology break. That is the lecture's baseline choice, not a universal definition that SSP2 equals one forcing outcome. Shared Socioeconomic Pathways describe demographic, economic and technological narratives; Representative Concentration Pathways describe emissions/concentration/forcing trajectories. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41, 43

Radiative forcing measures a change in Earth's energy balance in W/m², as the embedded comments on pp. 41–42 explain. RCP labels 2.6/4.5/6.0/8.5 refer to approximate 2100 forcing levels, with different trajectories toward them. The source associates 2.6/4.5/6.0 with approximately 490/650/850 ppm CO2-equivalent and leaves 8.5 unfinished. These are the slide's older shorthand values, not concentrations of CO2 alone; the exact trajectory and whether a quoted value is a peak or endpoint matter. Its claim that forcing is “declining” should not be read as monotonic decline throughout every RCP. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41

There is a source inconsistency: p. 41 calls RCP6.0 “close to SSP2,” whereas p. 42 calls RCP8.5 “close to SSP2.” A socioeconomic family does not uniquely identify a forcing path. Authoritative clarification: IPCC AR6 WGI SPM BoxSPM.1 and note 22 define SSPx-y as socioeconomic family x plus approximate 2100 forcing y. The supplied p. 43 itself shows SSP2-4.5 as intermediate, alongside SSP1-1.9/SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0/SSP5-8.5. IPCC AR6 WGI SPM, BoxSPM.1/note22. Thus neither conflicting “close to” statement is used as a one-to-one mapping. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 41–43

The AR5 temperature table needs its reference period

The supplied p. 42 table reports the following °C changes relative to 1986–2005, verified from IPCC 2014 Synthesis Report Table 2.1 (printed p. 60 and its notes). That missing baseline is essential: these are not automatically additional temperatures above the Paris preindustrial reference. Entries are means with the source's likely ranges; scenarios are conditional, and range width is not a probability assigned to the scenario itself. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42

RCP 2046–2065 mean (likely range),°C 2081–2100 mean (likely range),°C
2.6 1.0 (0.4–1.6) 1.0 (0.3–1.7)
4.5 1.4 (0.9–2.0) 1.8 (1.1–2.6)
6.0 1.3 (0.8–1.8) 2.2 (1.4–3.1)
8.5 2.0 (1.4–2.6) 3.7 (2.6–4.8)

The official table notes natural variability, forcing/model uncertainty and different confidence for the two horizons. Its observed baseline offset is not itself a complete uncertainty conversion rule, so do not add a constant and reuse the identical uncertainty range without qualification. IPCC2014 Synthesis Report, Table2.1 and notes. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 42

Physical p. 43 compares annual CO2 emissions (billions of tonnes/year) with resulting atmospheric CO2 concentrations (ppm). Low-emission paths bend down and can become net negative; concentrations need not follow emissions one-for-one because they reflect accumulated additions and removals. The caption says only central illustrative curves are shown, not the full uncertainty distribution. This graphic therefore illustrates scenario mechanisms rather than exact forecasts. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 43

Climate policy: source claims and verified chronology

Physical p. 44 names the UNFCCC, Kyoto arrangements and annual Conferences of the Parties (COPs). It refers to Annex I/II groupings and writes “DCM, JI”; the recognized Kyoto project mechanism is CDM, Clean Development Mechanism, alongside Joint Implementation. Annex groupings/targets are not all interchangeable: the official Kyoto overview distinguishes the Convention's annex structure and Kyoto Annex B commitments. Only that overview is needed here, not an invented treaty-law curriculum. Correction: the slide's “1996 Kyoto Protocol” is wrong; Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005. UNFCCC Kyoto overview, opening/market mechanisms. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44

The lecture describes Paris COP21 in 2015 as pursuing warming well below 2°C and efforts toward 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, with peaking as soon as possible and rapid subsequent reductions. Its discussion of INDCs concerns the pledges at that historical conference, not a checked present-day assessment of every NDC. The slide calls 4 November 2016 a “ratification” date; it is the Agreement's entry into force date. Adoption was 12 December 2015; individual parties ratify on their own dates. UNFCCC Paris overview. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44

The slide's subsequent conference list runs through COP30/Brazil 2025, naming Marrakesh 2016, Bonn 2017, Katowice 2018, Madrid 2019, the 2020 pandemic gap, Glasgow 2021, Cairo 2022, Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024. Location correction: COP27 was in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, not Cairo; the official proceedings state its 2022 venue. UNFCCC COP27 proceedings listing. These are the source's historical orientation, not a live future meeting schedule. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 44

Mitigation and adaptation solve different parts of the problem

Mitigation reduces climate-change drivers, such as net greenhouse-gas emissions; adaptation changes exposure/vulnerability and responses to climatic effects that still occur. Physical p. 45 combines a historical/projected warming panel with five escalating risk categories—unique/threatened systems, extreme weather, distribution of impacts, global aggregate impacts and large-scale singular events. Coloured transitions represent increasing risk, not cash damages or a uniform threshold for all outcomes. It overlays Paris NDC/aspiration labels on an AR5-era figure and concludes that even successful mitigation leaves impacts requiring adaptation. Read the overlay as a teaching illustration, not a current quantified forecast of the Paris pledges. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 45

The core reading path is assumptions→emissions→forcing→conditional climate→risks, then the complementary responses. Matching scenario type, baseline, date and uncertainty is prerequisite to using the numbers; conference chronology is supporting context with the source errors explicitly repaired here. 02_AQImp-ClimateChange.pdf, physical PDF p. 40–45

sections.title: Lesson outline

sections.html:
In this lesson, interpret conditional climate scenarios, policy chronology and adaptation.

2.1 What you’ll learn

  • Trace assumptions through emissions/forcing to conditional projections
  • Compare matching-baseline source means
  • Distinguish mitigation/adaptation and bounded historical treaty facts.

2.2 Before you begin

  • Explain radiative balance, heat storage and ocean chemistry
  • Interpret concentration and temperature records with dates and baselines
  • Convert carbon quantities and audit stocks, flows and emissions charts
Check the foundations

Is forcing a heat flux, concentration a stock fraction and annual emissions a mass flow? Can temperature changes with different reference periods be compared directly without checking the baseline?

Reveal foundation explanation

Yes to the first distinctions; no to direct different-baseline equivalence. Radiation/energy (O016), dated anomalies (O017) and emissions/stock units (O018) are different quantities. Require all;
sections.title: Introduction

sections.html:
• Scenario projection: A conditional model outcome under a specified pathway and assumptions.
  • Mitigation: Reducing the drivers of climate change.
  • Adaptation: Managing exposure and vulnerability to impacts that remain.
sections.title: Key definitions and concepts

sections.html:
A climate scenario asks what follows if a coherent set of social, technological, emissions and policy conditions occurs. It is not an assigned probability or an unconditional forecast. Use older RCP projections alongside newer SSP-labelled examples; the two naming systems and their temperature baselines must be distinguished.

This map follows pp. 40–45 and 43's paired emissions/concentration graphic; it explains why the policy discussion needs both mitigation and adaptation.

4.1 SSP assumptions and RCP forcing pathways

The source presents SSP2, “middle of the road,” as its baseline socioeconomic narrative, extending major development trends without a large assumed policy/technology break. That is the lecture's baseline choice, not a universal definition that SSP2 equals one forcing outcome.

Shared Socioeconomic Pathways describe demographic, economic and technological narratives; Representative Concentration Pathways describe emissions/concentration/forcing trajectories.

Radiative forcing measures a change in Earth's energy balance in W/m², as the embedded comments on pp. 41–42 explain. RCP labels 2.6/4.5/6.0/8.5 refer to approximate 2100 forcing levels, with different trajectories toward them.

The source associates 2.6/4.5/6.0 with approximately 490/650/850 ppm CO2-equivalent and leaves 8.5 unfinished. These are the slide's older shorthand values, not concentrations of CO2 alone;

the exact trajectory and whether a quoted value is a peak or endpoint matter. Its claim that forcing is “declining” should not be read as monotonic decline throughout every RCP.

There is a source inconsistency: p. 41 calls RCP6.0 “close to SSP2,” whereas p. 42 calls RCP8.5 “close to SSP2.” A socioeconomic family does not uniquely identify a forcing path. Authoritative clarification: IPCC AR6 WGI SPM BoxSPM.1 and note 22 define SSPx-y as socioeconomic family x plus approximate 2100 forcing y. The supplied p. 43 itself shows SSP2-4.5 as intermediate, alongside SSP1-1.9/SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0/SSP5-8.5. IPCC AR6 WGI SPM, BoxSPM.1/note22.

Thus neither conflicting “close to” statement is used as a one-to-one mapping.

4.2 The AR5 temperature table needs its reference period

The supplied p. 42 table reports the following °C changes relative to 1986–2005, verified from IPCC 2014 Synthesis Report Table 2.1 (printed p. 60 and its notes). That missing baseline is essential: these are not automatically additional temperatures above the Paris preindustrial reference.

Entries are means with the source's likely ranges; scenarios are conditional, and range width is not a probability assigned to the scenario itself.

RCP 2046–2065 mean (likely range),°C 2081–2100 mean (likely range),°C
2.6 1.0 (0.4–1.6) 1.0 (0.3–1.7)
4.5 1.4 (0.9–2.0) 1.8 (1.1–2.6)
6.0 1.3 (0.8–1.8) 2.2 (1.4–3.1)
8.5 2.0 (1.4–2.6) 3.7 (2.6–4.8)

The official table notes natural variability, forcing/model uncertainty and different confidence for the two horizons. Its observed baseline offset is not itself a complete uncertainty conversion rule, so do not add a constant and reuse the identical uncertainty range without qualification. IPCC2014 Synthesis Report, Table2.1 and notes.

compares annual CO2 emissions (billions of tonnes/year) with resulting atmospheric CO2 concentrations (ppm). Low-emission paths bend down and can become net negative;

concentrations need not follow emissions one-for-one because they reflect accumulated additions and removals. The caption says only central illustrative curves are shown, not the full uncertainty distribution.

This graphic therefore illustrates scenario mechanisms rather than exact forecasts.

4.3 Climate policy: source claims and verified chronology

names the UNFCCC, Kyoto arrangements and annual Conferences of the Parties (COPs). It refers to Annex I/II groupings and writes “DCM, JI”;

the recognized Kyoto project mechanism is CDM, Clean Development Mechanism, alongside Joint Implementation. Annex groupings/targets are not all interchangeable: the official Kyoto overview distinguishes the Convention's annex structure and Kyoto Annex B commitments.

Only that overview is needed here, not an invented treaty-law curriculum. Correction: the slide's “1996 Kyoto Protocol” is wrong; Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005. UNFCCC Kyoto overview, opening/market mechanisms.

Consider Paris COP21 in 2015 as pursuing warming well below 2°C and efforts toward 1.5°C above preindustrial levels, with peaking as soon as possible and rapid subsequent reductions. Its discussion of INDCs concerns the pledges at that historical conference, not a checked present-day assessment of every NDC.

The slide calls 4 November 2016 a “ratification” date; it is the Agreement's entry into force date.

Adoption was 12 December 2015; individual parties ratify on their own dates. UNFCCC Paris overview.

The slide's subsequent conference list runs through COP30/Brazil 2025, naming Marrakesh 2016, Bonn 2017, Katowice 2018, Madrid 2019, the 2020 pandemic gap, Glasgow 2021, Cairo 2022, Dubai 2023 and Baku 2024. Location correction: COP27 was in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, not Cairo; the official proceedings state its 2022 venue. UNFCCC COP27 proceedings listing.

These are the source's historical orientation, not a live future meeting schedule.

4.4 Mitigation and adaptation solve different parts of the problem

Mitigation reduces climate-change drivers, such as net greenhouse-gas emissions; adaptation changes exposure/vulnerability and responses to climatic effects that still occur. combines a historical/projected warming panel with five escalating risk categories—unique/threatened systems, extreme weather, distribution of impacts, global aggregate impacts and large-scale singular events.

Coloured transitions represent increasing risk, not cash damages or a uniform threshold for all outcomes. It overlays Paris NDC/aspiration labels on an AR5-era figure and concludes that even successful mitigation leaves impacts requiring adaptation.

Read the overlay as a teaching illustration, not a current quantified forecast of the Paris pledges.

The core reading path is assumptions→emissions→forcing→conditional climate→risks, then the complementary responses. Matching scenario type, baseline, date and uncertainty is prerequisite to using the numbers; conference chronology is supporting context with the source errors explicitly repaired here.

Solution: AR5changes are relative to 1986–2005. For scenario RCP2.6, the difference of displayed means is\(1.0-1.0=0.000000^\circ\mathrm{C}\);

late between-scenario mean gap is\(1.8-1.0=0.800000^\circ\mathrm{C}\). These mean differences are not new uncertainty intervals: preserve each likely range and model/natural-variability/horizon qualifications.

They are conditional projections, not assigned scenario probabilities or automatically values above preindustrial conditions. SSPs describe socioeconomic narratives;

RCPs describe forcing pathways. SSP2 alone does not uniquely select a forcing path, and SSP2-4.5 combines socioeconomic family 2 with approximate 2100 forcing 4.5 W/m².

The source’s RCP6.0/8.5 “close to SSP2” statements conflict and are not used as unique mappings. Older ppm CO2e shorthand is forcing-equivalent concentration, not CO2 alone or GWP-weighted tonnes.

The first action reduces climate drivers (mitigation); the second manages remaining exposure/vulnerability (adaptation).

Even successful mitigation leaves some impacts; the source’s coloured risk categories are neither cash damages nor one uniform threshold.

Kyoto was adopted 11 December 1997 and entered into force 16 February 2005; the mechanism is CDM with JI, not DCM.

Paris adoption 12 December 2015 and entry 4 November 2016 are distinct from each party’s ratification date. COP27 was Sharm el-Sheikh, not Cairo.

These bounded historical corrections and source COP30/Brazil 2025 pointer are not a checked live timetable or present NDC-effect assessment.
